Aqueduct (a structure carrying water)
context: Latin 'aqua' (water) gives English a huge family: AQUARIUM (a place for water), AQUATIC (of water), AQUEDUCT (a water-duct), AQUAMARINE (sea-water color), AQUACULTURE (water-farming). 'Aquilegia' is the columbine flower — its name comes from Latin 'aquila' (eagle), because the petals look like eagle claws. Same opening letters as 'aqua-' but a completely different Latin root.

question: Many English words trace back to Latin 'portare' (to carry). Which word below has a totally different origin?
answer: Porpoise (named from Latin 'porcus piscis' meaning pig fish)
choices: Porpoise (named from Latin 'porcus piscis' meaning pig fish)
Portable (able to be carried easily)
Transport (to carry across a distance)
Import (to carry goods into a country)
context: Latin 'portare' (carry) gives English a huge family: PORTABLE (can be carried), TRANSPORT (carry across), IMPORT (carry in), EXPORT (carry out), REPORT (carry back the news), DEPORT (carry away), SUPPORT (carry from below). 'Porpoise' is unrelated — it comes from Latin 'porcus piscis' meaning 'pig fish' (the rounded mammal looked like a swimming pig to Roman sailors). Same opening letters; different families.

question: Words built from Latin 'dicere' (to say) fill English. Pick the word that has a different origin.
answer: Distance (from Latin 'distantia' meaning standing apart)
choices: Distance (from Latin 'distantia' meaning standing apart)
Predict (to say something beforehand)
Contradict (to speak directly against)
Dictionary (a record book of words)
context: Latin 'dicere' (say, speak) gives English: PREDICT (say beforehand), CONTRADICT (speak against), DICTATE (speak with authority), DICTION (way of speaking), VERDICT (true-speaking, a jury's spoken judgment), EDICT (a thing said by authority). 'Distance' is unrelated — it comes from Latin 'distantia' (standing apart), the root 'sta-' meaning to stand. Same opening letters; different families.

question: English borrowed 'specere' (to look) from Latin to build sight-words. One of these did NOT come from it. Which?
answer: Speech (from Old English 'sprǣc' meaning a saying)
choices: Speech (from Old English 'sprǣc' meaning a saying)
Inspect (to look carefully into)
Spectator (one who looks on at events)
Spectacle (something put on for looking)
context: Latin 'specere' (look at) gives English: INSPECT (look into), SPECTATOR (one who looks on), RESPECT (look back at, esteem), SUSPECT (look at from below, distrust), PROSPECT (look forward), SPECTACLE (something to see). 'Speech' is Germanic, not Latin — from Old English 'sprǣc' (still seen in German 'sprechen' to speak). Same opening 'sp-' sound but unrelated families.

question: The Greek root 'tele-' means 'far' or 'distant.' Which English word does NOT use this root?
answer: Teller (a person who counts money in a bank)
choices: Teller (a person who counts money in a bank)
Telephone (sound from far away)
Television (vision from far away)
Telegraph (writing from far away)
context: Greek 'tēle-' (far, at a distance) gives English a whole family of distance-words: TELEPHONE (far + sound), TELEVISION (far + vision), TELEGRAPH (far + writing), TELESCOPE (far + see), TELEPATHY (far + feeling). 'Teller' is unrelated — from Old English 'tellan' meaning to count or recount (which also gives 'tell a story'). The 'tele-' family is one of English's most productive Greek-borrowed prefixes.

question: The prefix 'un-' usually means 'not' or 'opposite of.' Which sentence uses 'un-' to flip a meaning?
answer: The story has an unhappy ending.
choices: The story has an unhappy ending.
She lives on Underwood Lane.
The boat is sailing underwater.
I undid my coat zipper.
context: 'Un-' is a prefix meaning 'not' or 'opposite of.' UNHAPPY = not happy. UNFRIENDLY = not friendly. UNCERTAIN = not certain. The prefix attaches mostly to adjectives. 'Underwood' is a proper name; 'underwater' uses 'under-' (a different prefix meaning 'below'); 'undo' is 'un-' on a verb (reverse the action of doing). Same letters, different jobs.

question: The prefix 're-' usually means 'again' or 'back.' Which English word does NOT use 're-' in this sense?
answer: Red (the color)
choices: Red (the color)
Redo (do again)
Rewrite (write again)
Replay (play again)
context: Latin 're-' (again, back) makes English very productive: REDO (do again), REWRITE (write again), REPLAY (play again), REVIEW (view back), RETURN (turn back), REPEAT (seek again). 'Red' (the color) has nothing to do with this prefix — it's a single Old English word from a Proto-Germanic root. Same two letters at the start, different families.

question: The prefix 'dis-' often means 'not' or 'opposite of.' Which word uses 'dis-' to mean 'not'?
answer: Dishonest (not honest)
choices: Dishonest (not honest)
Distance (length between)
District (a region)
Dish (a plate)
context: Latin 'dis-' (apart, not) makes English words like DISHONEST (not honest), DISAGREE (not agree), DISBELIEVE (not believe), DISLIKE (not like), DISAPPEAR (no longer appear). It can also mean 'apart' (DISCARD = throw apart, DISTRIBUTE = give apart). 'Distance,' 'district,' and 'dish' have different histories — same letters, unrelated origins.

question: The prefix 'pre-' means 'before.' Which English word uses 'pre-' to mean 'before' in time?
answer: Preheat (heat beforehand)
choices: Preheat (heat beforehand)
Pretzel (a kind of bread)
Pretty (attractive)
Pressure (force pushing down)
context: Latin 'prae-' (before) gives English: PREHEAT (heat before), PREVIEW (view before), PREDICT (say before), PRECAUTION (caution beforehand), PREPARE (get ready before). 'Pretzel' is from German; 'pretty' is from Old English 'prættig'; 'pressure' is from Latin 'pressura' (press) — different families. Spotting the 'pre-' prefix unlocks many science and math terms (predict, premise, prefix itself).

question: The suffix '-ful' means 'full of'; '-less' means 'without.' Which word means 'full of hope'?
answer: Hopeful
choices: Hopeful
Hopeless
Hopely
Hopeable
context: '-ful' and '-less' are opposite suffixes. HOPEFUL = full of hope; HOPELESS = without hope. CAREFUL / CARELESS, USEFUL / USELESS, FEARFUL / FEARLESS, RESTFUL / RESTLESS. Note: '-ful' as a suffix has only ONE 'l' (not 'full'). The suffix is over a thousand years old in English — Old English '-ful' meant 'full' too.

question: The suffix '-able' (or '-ible') means 'capable of being.' Which word means 'capable of being broken'?
answer: Breakable
choices: Breakable
Breakage
Breaking
Breaker
context: '-able' (and '-ible') turns verbs into adjectives meaning 'capable of being [verbed].' BREAKABLE = able to be broken. READABLE = able to be read. EDIBLE = able to be eaten (older Latin '-ible' ending). Rule of thumb: '-able' usually attaches to English roots (breakable, lovable); '-ible' attaches to Latin roots (edible, visible, terrible). Both mean the same thing.

question: The suffix '-er' often makes a noun meaning 'one who [does the verb].' Which word is built this way?
answer: Teacher (one who teaches)
choices: Teacher (one who teaches)
Letter (a written message)
After (later in time)
Other (different from this)
context: '-er' (and Latin '-or') makes 'doer' nouns: TEACHER (one who teaches), READER (one who reads), WRITER (one who writes), PAINTER (one who paints), ACTOR (one who acts — Latin -or). The pattern is so productive that English coins new ones constantly: googler, blogger, gamer. Some English words look like they end in -er but aren't built from -er: 'letter,' 'after,' 'other' are single words from older roots.

question: The suffix '-ly' often turns an adjective into an adverb (meaning 'in a [adjective] way'). Which word is an adverb formed with '-ly'?
answer: Quickly (in a quick way)
choices: Quickly (in a quick way)
Friendly (warm and welcoming)
Family (a group of relatives)
Reply (an answer)
context: '-ly' is the main adverb-maker in English: QUICKLY (in a quick way), SLOWLY, HAPPILY, SOFTLY, LOUDLY. BUT — not every -ly word is an adverb. FRIENDLY, LOVELY, LONELY, UGLY end in -ly but are ADJECTIVES (describing nouns: a friendly dog, a lovely day). 'Family' and 'reply' just happen to end in -ly without using the suffix. Form alone doesn't tell you the part of speech; you need to see how the word works in a sentence.

question: After the Norman Conquest of 1066, English-speaking farmers kept their old words for animals while French-speaking nobles used French words for the meat at the table. Which pair shows this split?
answer: pig (English, animal) vs. pork (French, meat)
choices: pig (English, animal) vs. pork (French, meat)
horse (English, animal) vs. stallion (English, male only)
dog (English, animal) vs. puppy (English, baby form)
chicken (English, animal) vs. hen (English, female only)
context: In 1066 William the Conqueror brought French-speaking Norman nobles to England. For 300 years the upper class spoke French; commoners spoke English. Farmers raised PIG, COW, SHEEP, CALF, DEER (Old English). Cooks served PORK, BEEF, MUTTON, VEAL, VENISON (French). The animals stayed in English; the meats came in French. This vocabulary doubling roughly doubled English's word stock.

question: The split between 'cow' and 'beef' comes from the Norman Conquest of 1066. What does this pair tell us about who used each word?
answer: Cow (English) was what farmers said; beef (French) was what nobles ate.
choices: Cow (English) was what farmers said; beef (French) was what nobles ate.
Cow (Old English) and beef (Old English) were always two animals.
Cow (Latin) and beef (Greek) came from ancient cookery books.
Cow (Old Norse) and beef (Anglo-Saxon) both meant cattle in winter.
context: After 1066, Norman French became the language of nobility in England. English-speaking farmers tended COWS in the field; French-speaking nobles ate BEEF (French 'boeuf') at the table. Same animal, two words, two social classes. The pattern repeats: pig/pork (porc), sheep/mutton (mouton), calf/veal (veau), deer/venison (venaison). English vocabulary doubled because of this 300-year split.

question: Like the cow/beef split, the words 'sheep' and 'mutton' come from the same 1066 vocabulary doubling. What is the language origin of 'sheep' and of 'mutton'?
answer: Sheep is English (the farmer's word); mutton is French (the cook's word).
choices: Sheep is English (the farmer's word); mutton is French (the cook's word).
Sheep is French (the trader's word); mutton is English (the priest's word).
Sheep is Latin (the scholar's word); mutton is Greek (the doctor's word).
Sheep is German (the soldier's word); mutton is Italian (the singer's word).
context: After the Norman Conquest, English farmers raised SHEEP (Old English 'scēap'); French nobles ate MUTTON (Old French 'moton'). The animal in the field kept its old name; the meat at the table got the conqueror's word. This vocabulary split survives in modern English. Compare French today: 'mouton' still means both the animal and the meat — they didn't have the split English picked up from being conquered.

question: The split between 'deer' (animal in the forest) and 'venison' (meat on the table) also comes from the Norman Conquest. What does 'venison' come from?
answer: Old French 'venaison,' meaning hunted game meat
choices: Old French 'venaison,' meaning hunted game meat
Latin 'vena,' meaning a vein of blood
Old English 'fenisc,' meaning a marsh animal
Greek 'venos,' meaning a sweet flesh
context: Old French 'venaison' meant the meat of any hunted animal — wild boar, deer, hare. English narrowed it to 'venison = deer meat' after 1066. The farmer kept calling the animal DEER (Old English 'dēor'); the cook called the meat VENISON (French 'venaison'). Pattern: pig/pork, cow/beef, sheep/mutton, calf/veal, deer/venison. All five pairs date to the 1066 vocabulary doubling.

question: English has many words from Arabic that came through medieval Spain when Arabic learning was at its peak. Which is NOT from Arabic?
answer: Apricot (from Latin 'praecoquum' meaning 'early ripening')
choices: Apricot (from Latin 'praecoquum' meaning 'early ripening')
Algebra (from 'al-jabr' meaning 'reunion of parts')
Alcohol (from 'al-kuhl' meaning 'a powder')
Algorithm (from 'al-Khwarizmi' the mathematician)
context: Trick question — APRICOT actually IS from Arabic too ('al-barqūq'), via Spanish and Latin influence. All four words came through Arabic learning. ALGEBRA was named in the title of al-Khwarizmi's 820 AD book; ALGORITHM is the Latinized form of his name; ALCOHOL was 'al-kuhl' (originally a powdered eye makeup, later applied to distilled spirits); APRICOT traveled Persian → Arabic → Spanish → English. Arabic scholarship gave English much of its science vocabulary.

question: The phrase 'salt of the earth' (meaning a good, honest person) comes from a famous source. Where?
answer: The King James Bible (1611), Sermon on the Mount
choices: The King James Bible (1611), Sermon on the Mount
Shakespeare's play Hamlet (1600)
Aesop's fable of the salt merchant
An ancient Roman cookbook
context: 'Salt of the earth' comes from Matthew 5:13 in the King James Bible — 'Ye are the salt of the earth.' Jesus says this in the Sermon on the Mount. The phrase entered everyday English from the 1611 King James translation and is still used to mean 'a thoroughly decent person.' The KJV gave English hundreds of idioms: 'fly in the ointment,' 'scapegoat,' 'by the skin of my teeth,' 'a thorn in the side,' 'the writing on the wall.'

question: The idiom 'a fly in the ointment' (something small that ruins everything) comes from which famous text?
answer: The King James Bible (1611), Ecclesiastes
choices: The King James Bible (1611), Ecclesiastes
A play by William Shakespeare
An ancient Greek medical guide
A medieval book on perfumery
context: Ecclesiastes 10:1 in the King James Bible: 'Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour.' A small thing (a dead fly) ruins a whole batch of expensive perfume. The phrase 'fly in the ointment' came into common English from this verse and still means 'one small problem that spoils the whole.' The KJV is the single biggest source of English idioms outside Shakespeare.

question: 'By the skin of my teeth' (just barely, narrowly) comes from which book?
answer: The King James Bible (1611), Book of Job
choices: The King James Bible (1611), Book of Job
An ancient Egyptian medical scroll
Aesop's fable of the dentist
A Norse saga about a hero
context: Job 19:20 in the King James Bible: 'I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.' Job, after all his terrible losses, says he has escaped just barely. The phrase entered English from this passage and still means 'narrowly, by the slimmest margin.' Teeth don't actually have skin — that's what makes the image so striking. Some scholars think the original Hebrew is even more puzzling, possibly meaning 'with my gums alone.'

question: The idiom 'the writing on the wall' (a warning of disaster) comes from which biblical story?
answer: Belshazzar's feast in the Book of Daniel
choices: Belshazzar's feast in the Book of Daniel
The Tower of Babel in Genesis
The story of David and Goliath
The parable of the prodigal son
context: Daniel 5 in the King James Bible: King Belshazzar feasts in Babylon, and a mysterious hand appears to write words on the palace wall: 'Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin.' Daniel reads it as a warning that the king's reign is about to end — and that night, Belshazzar is killed and Babylon falls. The phrase 'the writing on the wall' became English shorthand for an unmistakable warning of doom.

question: 'A thorn in the side' (a constant source of annoyance) entered English from which source?
answer: The King James Bible (1611), 2 Corinthians
choices: The King James Bible (1611), 2 Corinthians
Aesop's fable of the lion's paw
A medieval English ballad about a knight
Shakespeare's play Macbeth
context: 2 Corinthians 12:7 in the King James Bible: Paul writes that he was given 'a thorn in the flesh' to keep him humble. The image became 'a thorn in the side' in everyday English — a persistent annoyance you can't get rid of. The KJV translation choices shaped how English speakers describe lasting trouble. Paul never specified what his thorn actually was; scholars have argued about it for centuries.

question: The phrase 'the powers that be' (the authorities, the ones in charge) was made famous by which translation?
answer: The King James Bible (1611), Romans 13
choices: The King James Bible (1611), Romans 13
An English law book from the 1500s
A Tudor stage play about kings
A speech given by Queen Elizabeth I
context: Romans 13:1 in the King James Bible: 'The powers that be are ordained of God.' The translators chose 'powers that be' — a phrasing odd to modern ears (we'd say 'the powers that exist') but resonant in 1611 English. The phrase escaped the Bible into common use and still describes 'whoever is currently in charge.' The KJV's grammatical choices shape how English speakers still talk about authority.

question: The word 'sandwich' (bread with filling) is named after a person. What kind of person?
answer: An English earl, the 4th Earl of Sandwich
choices: An English earl, the 4th Earl of Sandwich
A French baker from Paris in 1700
A Roman general in ancient times
A medieval monk who fed the poor
context: John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718-1792), reportedly asked his servants to bring him meat between slices of bread so he could keep gambling at the card table without dirtying his hands. The bread-and-meat order took his title as its name — and English has called it a 'sandwich' ever since. 'Sandwich' was an English place-name long before it was a food — the earl's title came from the town of Sandwich in Kent.

question: The word 'boycott' (refuse to deal with) is named after a real person. Who was Charles Boycott?
answer: A British land agent in Ireland whose tenants refused to work for him in 1880
choices: A British land agent in Ireland whose tenants refused to work for him in 1880
An American banker who cheated his customers and was shunned
A French general whose army refused to follow his orders in battle
An English judge whose harsh rulings led people to ignore his court
context: In 1880, Captain Charles Boycott was a land agent in County Mayo, Ireland. The Irish Land League called for his neighbors and workers to refuse all dealings with him — no work, no service, no contact. The campaign was so effective that 'to boycott' someone entered English within weeks as a name for this kind of organized social pressure. Boycott left Ireland; his name stayed in the dictionary.

question: The word 'hamburger' is named after a place. Which city?
answer: Hamburg, Germany
choices: Hamburg, Germany
Hamilton, Canada
Ham, England
Hamburg, Pennsylvania
context: 'Hamburger' = 'of Hamburg.' The dish came from German immigrants who brought a chopped beef preparation called 'Hamburg steak' to America in the late 1800s. Putting it in a bun (an American innovation) created the modern hamburger by the early 1900s. Other foods named after places: frankfurter (Frankfurt), wiener (Vienna = Wien), bologna (Bologna), parmesan (Parma), champagne (Champagne region of France).

question: The word 'denim' (the fabric in blue jeans) comes from a French city name. Which one?
answer: Nîmes, France (from 'de Nîmes' meaning 'of Nîmes')
choices: Nîmes, France (from 'de Nîmes' meaning 'of Nîmes')
Marseille, France (a major port for cloth trade)
Lyon, France (famous for silk weaving)
Paris, France (the fashion capital)
context: 'Denim' = 'de Nîmes' = 'of Nîmes' — the sturdy cotton twill cloth was originally made in Nîmes, southern France. The fabric traveled to America with miners and railroad workers; Levi Strauss made trousers out of it in San Francisco in 1873; and 'denim jeans' became iconic. 'Jeans' also has a city origin — the cloth was traded through Genoa, Italy, which English speakers rendered as 'Gene' and then 'Jean.'

question: The word 'jeans' (the pants) comes from the name of an Italian city. Which one?
answer: Genoa, Italy (from old French 'Gêne' meaning 'Genoa')
choices: Genoa, Italy (from old French 'Gêne' meaning 'Genoa')
Rome, Italy (where the first pants were tailored)
Venice, Italy (the cloth-trade capital)
Milan, Italy (the modern fashion center)
context: In the 1500s the Italian port of Genoa exported a sturdy cotton-cloth used for sailors' trousers. Old French rendered Genoa as 'Gêne'; English speakers heard 'jean' and called the cloth and the trousers 'jeans.' So 'denim jeans' literally means 'cloth from Nîmes shaped like trousers from Genoa.' Two French cities and one Italian city all packed into one phrase.

question: The word 'palace' comes from a famous hill in ancient Rome. Which hill?
answer: The Palatine Hill, where Roman emperors built their homes
choices: The Palatine Hill, where Roman emperors built their homes
The Capitoline Hill, where the temple of Jupiter stood
The Esquiline Hill, where wealthy senators lived
The Aventine Hill, where the common people had their forum
context: The Palatine Hill in Rome was where Emperor Augustus built his home around 30 BC. Later emperors built ever-grander residences on the same hill. The Latin 'palatium' (Palatine) became the word for any imperial residence. French 'palais,' Italian 'palazzo,' Spanish 'palacio,' English 'palace' — all from one Roman hill. The word 'paladin' (a noble knight) shares the same root.

question: The 26-mile race 'marathon' is named after a battle. Where was it?
answer: Marathon, a town in Greece, in 490 BC
choices: Marathon, a town in Greece, in 490 BC
Sparta, in the wars between Athens and Persia
Salamis, the great naval battle in 480 BC
Thermopylae, the famous 300-warrior stand
context: In 490 BC, Athenians defeated a Persian invasion force at the town of Marathon. According to legend, a messenger named Pheidippides ran the ~25 miles from Marathon to Athens to deliver the news of victory — and dropped dead after announcing it. The modern marathon race was created for the 1896 Olympics to honor this story; the distance was standardized at 26.2 miles in the 1908 London Olympics.

question: The word 'volcano' is named after a Roman god. Which one?
answer: Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and the forge
choices: Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and the forge
Jupiter, the Roman king of the gods
Mars, the Roman god of war
Mercury, the Roman messenger god
context: Vulcan was the Roman god of fire and metalworking — equivalent to Greek Hephaestus. The Romans believed Vulcan's forge was inside the volcanic island of Vulcano (north of Sicily), and the smoke and fire from the mountain were sparks from his hammer. Italian 'vulcano' and English 'volcano' both come from his name. The element vanadium and the science of 'vulcanizing' rubber both echo his name too.

question: A book of maps is called an 'atlas' — named after which Greek figure?
answer: Atlas, the Titan who held up the sky on his shoulders
choices: Atlas, the Titan who held up the sky on his shoulders
Apollo, the god of light and music
Hercules, the hero of twelve labors
Achilles, the warrior of the Trojan War
context: In Greek mythology, Atlas was a Titan punished by Zeus to hold up the sky on his shoulders forever. In 1595, the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator published a collection of maps with a picture of Atlas holding the world on the cover — and the title 'Atlas' for the book. The word stuck. Every book of maps since has been called an atlas. The Atlas Mountains in North Africa share the same Titan name.

question: The month January is named after a Roman god. Which one?
answer: Janus, the god of beginnings, doorways, and transitions
choices: Janus, the god of beginnings, doorways, and transitions
Mars, the god of war and farming
Saturn, the god of time and harvest
Apollo, the god of light and prophecy
context: Janus was the Roman god of doorways, beginnings, and transitions — usually depicted with TWO FACES, one looking forward and one looking back. January (the start of the year) was named after him — he looks back at the year ending and forward to the year beginning. The English word 'janitor' (a doorkeeper) shares the same root. Other months: March = Mars; May = Maia; June = Juno; July = Julius Caesar; August = Augustus Caesar.

question: The Greek and Latin prefix 'tri-' means 'three.' Which word uses 'tri-' in this sense?
answer: Triangle (a three-sided shape)
choices: Triangle (a three-sided shape)
Trip (a journey)
Trick (a clever move)
Trio (sometimes a name)
context: 'Tri-' (three) builds many words: TRIANGLE (three angles), TRICYCLE (three wheels), TRIPOD (three feet), TRIO (three musicians), TRIPLE (three times), TRILOGY (three books or films), TRIDENT (three teeth — Poseidon's spear). 'Trip' is unrelated Old English; 'trick' is from Old French. Like all number prefixes, 'tri-' came into English from Greek and Latin via science and math vocabulary.

question: 'Octo-' means 'eight' in Latin and Greek. Which word uses this prefix correctly?
answer: Octopus (eight legs)
choices: Octopus (eight legs)
October (the tenth month)
Octave (a musical interval)
Octogenarian (someone in their 80s)
context: This is trickier than it looks. OCTOPUS (eight legs) — yes, correct. OCTOGENARIAN — eight DECADES (80s). OCTAVE — eight notes. OCTOBER — was the EIGHTH month in the old Roman calendar (which started in March), then July and August were inserted, making October the tenth — but the name stuck. Same with September (7 → 9), November (9 → 11), December (10 → 12). The word histories preserve the original numbering.

question: The Latin prefix 'bi-' means 'two.' Which word uses 'bi-' in this sense?
answer: Bicycle (two wheels)
choices: Bicycle (two wheels)
Big (large in size)
Bird (a flying animal)
Bin (a container)
context: 'Bi-' (two) gives English: BICYCLE (two wheels), BINARY (two states — 0 and 1), BILINGUAL (two languages), BIANNUAL (twice a year — but be careful: 'biennial' means every two years), BIPED (two feet), BICENTENNIAL (two hundred years). 'Big,' 'bird,' 'bin' have other origins. The Greek equivalent is 'di-' (diatomic, dioxide), and the higher numbers are mostly Latin: tri-, quad-, quint-, sext-, sept-, oct-, non-, dec-.

question: The yellow flower 'dandelion' has a name that comes from a French phrase describing its leaves. What does the original French mean?
answer: Tooth of the lion ('dent-de-lion')
choices: Tooth of the lion ('dent-de-lion')
Sun of the field ('soleil-de-champ')
Star of the spring ('étoile-de-printemps')
Crown of gold ('couronne-d'or')
context: Old French 'dent-de-lion' (tooth of the lion) — describing the jagged, tooth-like edges of the dandelion's leaves. The phrase came into English in the 1500s as 'dandelion.' Modern French actually uses a different name now — 'pissenlit' (literally 'pee-the-bed,' referring to the plant's diuretic effect). English preserves the older poetic name; modern French has the cruder one.

question: 'Helicopter' looks like 'heli + copter' but it actually breaks differently. What are the two Greek roots in 'helicopter'?
answer: Helico (spiral) + pter (wing) — 'spiral wing'
choices: Helico (spiral) + pter (wing) — 'spiral wing'
Heli (sun) + copter (chopper) — 'sun-chopper'
Hel (high) + icopter (machine) — 'high machine'
Helio (light) + opter (flier) — 'light-flier'
context: The word breaks HELICO-PTER, not HELI-COPTER. Greek 'helix' (spiral) + 'pteron' (wing) = 'spiral wing.' But because English speakers couldn't easily pronounce 'pter' on its own (a silent 'p' before 't'), the word got chopped at the easier break point and 'copter' became a word. The Greek 'pter' (wing) also appears in 'pterodactyl' (wing-finger) and 'pterosaur' (wing-lizard) — same silent p.

question: The word 'alphabet' is made from the names of the first two letters of which alphabet?
answer: Greek (alpha + beta)
choices: Greek (alpha + beta)
Latin (a + b)
Hebrew (aleph + bet)
Arabic (alif + ba)
context: 'Alphabet' = alpha + beta — the first two letters of the Greek alphabet, combined into a word meaning 'the letters.' The Greek letters themselves came from Phoenician, which had aleph (the original ox-head shape) and beth (house). Hebrew preserves these almost intact: ALEPH and BET. Arabic has ALIF and BA. All Mediterranean alphabets descend from one Phoenician ancestor — including ours.

question: The word 'disaster' comes from two Latin roots that together originally meant something about the stars. What did 'disaster' literally mean?
answer: Bad star (dis- 'bad' + astrum 'star')
choices: Bad star (dis- 'bad' + astrum 'star')
Without water (dis- 'without' + aster 'water')
Falling stone (dis- 'fall' + aster 'stone')
Lost ship (dis- 'lost' + aster 'ship')
context: Latin 'dis-' (bad, against) + 'astrum' (star) = 'a bad star.' Ancient astrologers believed misfortunes were caused by unlucky alignments of the stars and planets. A 'disaster' was literally a star-caused catastrophe. The Italian 'disastro' came first, then French 'désastre,' then English 'disaster' by the 1500s. The root 'astro-' also lives in astronomy, astrology, astronaut, asterisk (little star), and astray (off-star).

question: The word 'lunatic' (a person acting wildly) comes from a Latin root with a celestial meaning. What did it originally connect mental instability to?
answer: The moon (Latin 'luna')
choices: The moon (Latin 'luna')
The sun (Latin 'sol')
The stars (Latin 'stella')
The wind (Latin 'ventus')
context: Latin 'lunaticus' meant 'moon-struck.' Ancient and medieval people thought the moon's phases caused fits of mental illness — full-moon nights were said to bring out the madness. 'Lunatic' came into English through French in the 1200s carrying this belief. Modern English preserves the moon-connection without the superstition. Same root: LUNAR, LUNETTE (a moon-shaped window), and the older slang 'loony' (also from luna).

question: The word 'quarantine' (isolation to prevent disease) comes from an Italian word meaning a specific number. What number?
answer: Forty (Italian 'quaranta giorni' meaning 'forty days')
choices: Forty (Italian 'quaranta giorni' meaning 'forty days')
Fourteen (the maximum incubation period)
Four (the seasons of plague)
Seven (the days of holy rest)
context: In 14th-century Venice, ships arriving during plague outbreaks had to wait FORTY days before passengers could come ashore. Italian 'quaranta giorni' (forty days) gave the practice its name; English borrowed it as 'quarantine.' The 40-day period chosen had religious significance (Christ's 40 days in the wilderness) and a practical one (most plague symptoms appeared within 30-40 days). Today 'quarantine' can be any length — but the word still carries the original count.

question: The word 'gymnasium' (a place for exercise) comes from a Greek word with a surprising meaning. What did the Greek word originally describe?
answer: A place to exercise NAKED (Greek 'gymnos' = naked)
choices: A place to exercise NAKED (Greek 'gymnos' = naked)
A place to wrestle with oil and sand
A place to train for combat with weapons
A place to study sports philosophy
context: Greek 'gymnos' meant 'naked.' Ancient Greek athletes trained naked (the word 'gymnastic' carries the same root). A 'gymnasium' was literally 'a place for nakedness' — the public exercise grounds in Greek cities. The athletic and educational meanings traveled together — Greek gymnasia were also schools, which is why some European countries (Germany, Russia) still use 'gymnasium' to mean 'high school.' English kept only the exercise meaning.

question: The word 'companion' (a person who travels or lives with you) comes from two Latin roots. What do they literally mean?
answer: With + bread ('com-' + 'panis') — 'one who eats bread with you'
choices: With + bread ('com-' + 'panis') — 'one who eats bread with you'
With + road ('com-' + 'via') — 'one who walks with you'
With + house ('com-' + 'domus') — 'one who lives with you'
With + word ('com-' + 'verbum') — 'one who talks with you'
context: Latin 'com-' (with) + 'panis' (bread) = 'companion' — literally 'one who shares bread with you.' The deepest definition of friendship in Latin was the sharing of a meal. Spanish 'compañero' and Italian 'compagno' still carry the same root. The English word LADY also has a bread origin — Old English 'hlæfdige' meant 'loaf-kneader' (the lady of the house was the one who made the bread). Bread was central to the social bonds of premodern Europe.

question: The word 'salary' (money paid for work) comes from a Latin root with a surprising connection. What is the connection?
answer: Salt — Roman soldiers were given an allowance to buy salt ('salarium')
choices: Salt — Roman soldiers were given an allowance to buy salt ('salarium')
Gold — Roman pay was originally weighed in gold ('aurum')
Wheat — soldiers received bushels of grain ('frumentum')
Land — veterans were paid in farmland ('ager')
context: Latin 'salarium' = 'salt money' — an allowance Roman soldiers received to buy salt (then a precious commodity for preserving food). 'Salt' itself was so valuable that 'sal-' words tell stories: SALARY (salt pay), SAUSAGE (salt-cured), SALSA (salted sauce), SALAD (salted greens). The phrase 'worth his salt' (capable, reliable) preserves the ancient sense that salt could be wages. 'Salt of the earth' (good person) shares the same metaphor.

question: The English word 'muscle' comes from a Latin word for a small animal. Which animal?
answer: A little mouse (Latin 'musculus' = small mouse)
choices: A little mouse (Latin 'musculus' = small mouse)
A little fish (Latin 'piscis' = small fish)
A little bird (Latin 'avis' = small bird)
A little snake (Latin 'serpens' = small snake)
context: Latin 'musculus' literally meant 'little mouse' — because flexed muscles look like little mice running under the skin. The Romans named the bicep that way; the metaphor stuck through Latin into French and English. Same idea: the Greek 'mys' means both 'mouse' and 'muscle.' Ancient Greek 'mus' gave us 'mouse' AND 'muscle' (via Latin). Anatomy is full of these vivid metaphors: the kneecap is 'patella' (little dish); the femur's neck is 'collum' (neck).

question: The word 'pencil' comes from a Latin word for a small animal part. What did it originally name?
answer: A little tail (Latin 'penicillus' = small brush, from 'penis' = tail)
choices: A little tail (Latin 'penicillus' = small brush, from 'penis' = tail)
A little stone (Latin 'lapillus' = small rock)
A little stick (Latin 'baculum' = small staff)
A little finger (Latin 'digitus' = small finger)
context: Latin 'penicillus' (small brush) named the fine paintbrushes made from animal tail hair — from 'penis' meaning 'tail' (the modern crude meaning is a later euphemism). The word came into English meaning a fine brush, then transferred to the lead-and-wood drawing tool around 1600. PENICILLIN (the antibiotic) is named from the same root — the mold's spore-bearing structures look like little brushes.

question: The Roman god Janus, after whom January is named, was traditionally shown with how many faces?
answer: Two faces, one looking forward, one looking back
choices: Two faces, one looking forward, one looking back
Three faces (past, present, and future)
Four faces (one for each of the seasons)
One face but with a mask he could remove
context: Janus was the Roman god of doorways and transitions, traditionally shown with TWO FACES — one looking back at the year ending, one looking forward at the year beginning. Roman doorways had Janus statues; Roman months opened and closed in his name. January (the start) was his month. The English word JANITOR (a doorkeeper) shares the same root. A 'Janus-faced' person today is two-faced — looking both ways at once.

question: The word 'pen' (the writing instrument) comes from a Latin word for what?
answer: Feather (Latin 'penna')
choices: Feather (Latin 'penna')
Stick (Latin 'baculum')
Reed (Latin 'calamus')
Stone (Latin 'lapis')
context: Latin 'penna' = 'feather.' Quill pens (cut from goose or swan feathers) were the standard writing tool from Roman times through about 1850. The metal nib pen replaced the quill in the 1800s but kept the name. PEN, PENNANT (a feathery flag), PENNON (a knight's flag), and PINION (a wing feather) all share the same root. A different root — Latin 'pinna' (point) — also gave English 'pin' and 'fin.'

question: The word 'curfew' (a rule requiring people to be home by a certain hour) comes from French. What did the original French mean?
answer: Cover the fire ('couvre-feu')
choices: Cover the fire ('couvre-feu')
Lock the gate ('ferme-porte')
Strike the bell ('sonne-cloche')
Watch the night ('veille-nuit')
context: Old French 'couvre-feu' = 'cover the fire' (couvre = cover, feu = fire). In medieval towns the evening bell signaled that all hearth fires should be covered — to prevent house fires while people slept. The bell came to mark the start of a quiet curfew period. The original fire-safety meaning faded; the 'be home by this hour' meaning remained. English borrowed the phrase from Norman French after 1066.

question: The word 'breakfast' is built from two ordinary English words. What does it literally mean?
answer: To break the fast (the night without food)
choices: To break the fast (the night without food)
To break the bread (in a religious sense)
To break the day (when it first begins)
To break the silence (with morning talk)
context: BREAKFAST = BREAK + FAST. After 8-12 hours of sleep without eating (a 'fast'), the first meal of the day BREAKS that fast. The word is over 600 years old in English. The same logic gives French 'déjeuner' (de- + jeûner = un-fast) and Spanish 'desayuno' (des- + ayuno = un-fast). Three languages, three independent 'un-fast' words for the same first meal. The body's overnight fast really does end at the table.

question: The word 'window' comes from Old Norse and Old English. What did it literally mean?
answer: Wind-eye (an opening for the wind)
choices: Wind-eye (an opening for the wind)
Light-hole (a gap for sunshine)
Wall-mouth (an opening in the wall)
Sun-door (an entrance for daylight)
context: Old Norse 'vindauga' = WIND (vind) + EYE (auga) = 'an eye for the wind.' Vikings brought the word to England in the 800s-1000s; Old English already had 'eagþyrl' (eye-hole) and 'eagduru' (eye-door), but 'window' (wind-eye) won out. Early windows had no glass — they were holes the wind blew through, sometimes covered with cloth or shutters. The poetic name preserved the original function.

question: The word 'clue' (a hint that helps solve a mystery) comes from a Greek myth. What did 'clew' (the older spelling) originally mean?
answer: A ball of string or yarn
choices: A ball of string or yarn
A torch carried in a maze
A whisper that gives away a secret
A map drawn on a cave wall
context: In the Greek myth of Theseus and the Minotaur, princess Ariadne gave Theseus a 'clew' — a ball of thread — to unwind as he entered the labyrinth. He could then follow the thread back out to escape. 'Clew' became a metaphor for anything that helps you find your way through a puzzle. The spelling 'clue' is a 1600s variant. Today every mystery novel relies on this 2,500-year-old metaphor.

question: The English day-names are mostly from Norse gods. Friday comes from which Norse goddess?
answer: Frigg (or Freya) — Norse goddess of love and home
choices: Frigg (or Freya) — Norse goddess of love and home
Tyr — Norse god of war and law
Thor — Norse god of thunder and storms
Odin — Norse god of wisdom and death
context: English weekday names mostly come from Norse gods who replaced earlier Roman planet-names: TUESDAY = Tyr (Mars), WEDNESDAY = Wodan/Odin (Mercury), THURSDAY = Thor (Jupiter), FRIDAY = Frigg/Freya (Venus). The Romance languages kept the Roman names: French 'mardi' (Mars), 'mercredi' (Mercury), 'jeudi' (Jupiter), 'vendredi' (Venus). Same week, two pantheons. SATURDAY (Saturn) and SUNDAY (Sun) and MONDAY (Moon) preserve the Roman names in English.

question: A simile is a comparison using 'like' or 'as.' Which sentence uses a simile?
answer: Her smile was as bright as the sun.
choices: Her smile was as bright as the sun.
Her smile lit up the room.
She smiled when she saw him.
The sun was shining brightly.
context: A simile compares two different things using 'like' or 'as': 'as bright as the sun,' 'cool as a cucumber,' 'fits like a glove.' The comparison helps the reader picture the thing being described. Compare a METAPHOR ('Her smile lit up the room') which makes the comparison without 'like' or 'as.' The boundary is small: 'lit up' = direct (metaphor); 'like the sun' = compared (simile).

question: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect — not a literal claim. Which sentence is hyperbole?
answer: I've told you a million times to clean your room.
choices: I've told you a million times to clean your room.
I've asked you several times to clean your room.
I think I have asked you to clean your room.
I would like you to please clean your room.
context: Hyperbole exaggerates wildly to make a point. The speaker hasn't LITERALLY said it a million times — but the exaggeration emphasizes their frustration. Common hyperbole: 'I'm starving.' 'This bag weighs a ton.' 'I waited forever.' Hyperbole isn't lying — both speaker and listener know it's exaggeration. The clue is that the claim is too extreme to be literally true.

question: Which of these familiar comparisons is a simile?
answer: as quiet as a mouse
choices: as quiet as a mouse
a quiet little mouse
the mouse moved quietly
quietly the mouse moved
context: 'As quiet as a mouse' uses 'as ___ as' — that's a simile. English is full of common (cliché) similes: 'as cool as a cucumber,' 'as light as a feather,' 'as busy as a bee,' 'as old as the hills,' 'as right as rain,' 'as proud as a peacock.' Each pairs a quality with a familiar example to make it vivid. Good writers usually invent fresh similes; tired ones become clichés.

question: A simile compares unlike things with 'like' or 'as.' Pick the sentence built on a simile.
answer: He ran like the wind down the field.
choices: He ran like the wind down the field.
The wind blew strongly down the field.
He was the fastest runner that day.
Running fast, he reached the goal.
context: A simile uses 'like' or 'as' to compare two unlike things. 'Like the wind' compares his running speed to the wind — that's a simile. Note: not every 'like' makes a simile. 'I like pizza' doesn't compare anything; 'like' there means 'enjoy.' Similes require a comparison ('AS QUICK AS lightning,' 'LIKE A BULLET'). One word; two jobs.

question: In 'The classroom was a zoo,' what kind of figure of speech is used?
answer: Metaphor — the classroom is compared directly to a zoo
choices: Metaphor — the classroom is compared directly to a zoo
Simile — the classroom is described like a zoo
Hyperbole — the classroom never really had zoo animals
Personification — the classroom acted like a person
context: 'The classroom WAS a zoo' makes a direct comparison without 'like' or 'as' — that's metaphor. The classroom isn't literally a zoo with elephants and lions, but the chaos felt that way. METAPHOR: direct (X is Y). SIMILE: indirect (X is like Y). HYPERBOLE: extreme exaggeration. PERSONIFICATION: gives human qualities to non-humans. All four are figurative — none are literal.

question: Which sentence uses hyperbole (extreme exaggeration)?
answer: My backpack weighs a ton today.
choices: My backpack weighs a ton today.
My backpack feels heavy today.
My backpack has many books inside.
My backpack is hard to carry.
context: Hyperbole is wild exaggeration for effect. Your backpack doesn't ACTUALLY weigh 2,000 pounds — but the phrase emphasizes how heavy it feels. Both speaker and listener know it's exaggeration; no one is fooled. Common kid hyperboles: 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse.' 'This homework is taking forever.' 'My feet are killing me.' Each is impossible — but vivid.

question: Alliteration is the repetition of the same starting sound across nearby words. Which phrase shows alliteration?
answer: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers
choices: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers
The fly landed on the wall after a long buzz
She walked quickly down the long, dark hallway
Many different birds were singing in the trees
context: Alliteration repeats the SOUND at the start of nearby words: Peter/Piper/picked/peck/pickled/peppers — six P's in a row. It's everywhere in poetry, ads, and headlines because it's catchy. Examples: 'wild and woolly,' 'safe and sound,' 'tough as nails,' 'big bad wolf,' 'Mickey Mouse,' 'Donald Duck.' The repeated sound makes phrases memorable — which is why brand names use it heavily.

question: Which sentence is built on alliteration (repeated starting sounds)?
answer: She sells seashells by the seashore.
choices: She sells seashells by the seashore.
She buys things at the market today.
She walked to school in the rain.
She picked up the books from school.
context: 'She sells seashells by the seashore' is one of the most famous English tongue twisters — every important word starts with 's' or 'sh.' Alliteration makes it hard to say fast (try it!) AND memorable. Same trick: 'How much wood could a woodchuck chuck?' 'Betty Botter bought some butter.' Tongue twisters use alliteration to trap the speaker into sound mistakes.

question: Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates the sound it describes. Which word is onomatopoeia?
answer: buzz
choices: buzz
run
tall
happy
context: Onomatopoeia: words that SOUND like what they name. BUZZ (a bee). HISS (a snake). CRASH (a falling vase). SIZZLE (bacon in a pan). MEOW (a cat). WOOF (a dog). BOOM (an explosion). DING (a bell). Comics are full of onomatopoeia — KAPOW! ZAP! SPLAT! Different languages hear sounds differently: an English cat says 'meow'; a Japanese cat says 'nya-nya'; a French dog says 'ouaf-ouaf.'

question: Which of these words is onomatopoeia (a word imitating its sound)?
answer: sizzle
choices: sizzle
quickly
beautiful
yesterday
context: SIZZLE sounds like bacon frying in a pan — the word IS the sound. Other examples: SPLASH (water hitting), CLATTER (dishes), GIGGLE (laughter), RUMBLE (thunder), TICK-TOCK (a clock). Onomatopoeia is one of the oldest types of word formation — humans have probably been imitating sounds with words for as long as language has existed. Comics, children's books, and poetry rely on it heavily.

question: Comic books are full of onomatopoeia. Which word imitates the sound it describes?
answer: crunch
choices: crunch
brave
early
silent
context: CRUNCH names the sound of biting into something hard — chip, apple, dry leaves. Comics splash onomatopoeia across the page: KAPOW! ZAP! THWACK! SPLAT! BOOM! These visual sound-words let comic readers HEAR the action without sound. Stan Lee and other Marvel writers made up new ones constantly: SNIKT! (Wolverine's claws), BAMF! (Nightcrawler's teleport). The technique is centuries older than comics, though.

question: A pun plays on a word's double meaning — or on two words that sound the same. What kind of word play is in 'I used to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough'?
answer: A pun ('dough' means both bread and money)
choices: A pun ('dough' means both bread and money)
Hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration for effect)
Metaphor (a direct comparison without 'like')
Alliteration (repeated initial consonant sounds)
context: The pun rests on 'dough' having TWO meanings: the bread mixture a baker uses AND slang for money. The joke works because both meanings fit the sentence — a baker handles dough; not making enough money is a reason to quit. Puns are the workhorse of dad jokes: 'I'm reading a book on anti-gravity — it's impossible to put down.' 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana.'

question: A pun can play on words that SOUND the same but mean different things. Which line is this type of pun?
answer: The bicycle couldn't stand by itself because it was two-tired.
choices: The bicycle couldn't stand by itself because it was two-tired.
The bicycle had two tires and a strong frame.
The tired bicycle leaned against the wall outside.
The bicycle's two tires were very worn out.
context: 'Two-tired' sounds exactly like 'too tired' — the homophone pun. A bicycle is literally two-tired (has two tires) and also too tired (exhausted, can't stand up). Both readings work. Other homophone puns: 'A bicycle can't stand on its own because it's TWO-TIRED.' 'Lettuce alone' (let us alone). 'The PUNishment' (pun-ishment). Puns are the lowest form of humor that everyone secretly loves.

question: A palindrome reads identically left-to-right and right-to-left. Which single word qualifies?
answer: level
choices: level
listen
letter
little
context: LEVEL reads the same both directions: L-E-V-E-L. Palindromes are surprisingly common: NOON, MADAM, RACECAR, KAYAK, RADAR, CIVIC, ROTOR, REFER, REPAPER, ROTATOR. The longest single-word palindromes in English are 'tattarrattat' (a knock at the door, coined by James Joyce) and 'detartrated' (a chemistry term). Sentence palindromes are harder but exist: 'A Toyota's a Toyota.'

question: Among these famous English sayings, which one is a palindrome (its letters spell the same string in reverse)?
answer: Madam, I'm Adam.
choices: Madam, I'm Adam.
Honesty pays off.
Practice pays off.
Patience pays off.
context: 'Madam, I'm Adam' is a classic palindrome — ignoring spaces and punctuation, the letters read the same in both directions: M-A-D-A-M-I-M-A-D-A-M. Other famous sentence palindromes: 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama' (often credited to Leigh Mercer, 1948). 'Was it a car or a cat I saw?' 'Never odd or even.' Creating long palindromic sentences is a serious puzzle hobby (and surprisingly hard).

question: A tongue twister is hard to say quickly because of repeated similar sounds. Which classic tongue twister uses heavy alliteration?
answer: How much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood?
choices: How much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood?
Why did the chicken cross the road to get to the other side?
Where there is a will, there is always a way to find it.
Don't count your chickens before any of them have hatched.
context: Tongue twisters trap your tongue in repeated similar sounds. 'Woodchuck/chuck/wood/would/wood' is full of W and CH sounds that easily get mixed up at speed. Other classics: 'She sells seashells by the seashore.' 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.' 'Red lorry, yellow lorry.' 'The sixth sick sheikh's sixth sheep's sick' (often called the hardest English tongue twister).

question: An anagram rearranges the letters of a word to make a new word or phrase. Which of these is an anagram of 'listen'?
answer: silent
choices: silent
listing
sliten
stolen
context: LISTEN and SILENT have the exact same six letters: L-I-S-T-E-N rearranged spells S-I-L-E-N-T. Both even share a meaning — listening requires silence. Other one-word anagrams: 'cinema' / 'iceman'; 'evil' / 'live'; 'angel' / 'glean.' Sentence anagrams are puzzle classics: 'A telescope' is an anagram of 'To see place.' 'Astronomer' = 'moon starer.' 'The eyes' = 'they see.'

question: A pangram is a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet at least once. Which sentence is a famous pangram used to test fonts and typewriters?
answer: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
choices: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
The early bird catches the small worm.
The clever cat watched the colorful bird outside.
The big black dog barked at the noisy children.
context: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' contains EVERY letter of the English alphabet (count them — A through Z). It's been used since the late 1800s for handwriting practice, typewriter testing, and font display. It's 35 letters total — not the shortest pangram, but the most natural-sounding. Shorter pangrams exist but read awkwardly: 'Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow' (29 letters).

question: The idiom 'break a leg' is used to wish someone GOOD luck — especially before a performance. What does it actually mean?
answer: Good luck (especially in a theater context)
choices: Good luck (especially in a theater context)
Be very careful walking on stage
Hurry up and finish quickly now
Pay attention to important details
context: 'Break a leg' is theater slang for 'good luck' — said BEFORE a performance because wishing 'good luck' directly is considered a jinx. The origin is debated: some say it refers to the curtain lines (the 'legs') that audiences kicked when applauding; others trace it to Shakespeare-era bowing (the 'leg break' was a deep bow). Either way, theater people don't say 'good luck' — they say 'break a leg' instead.

question: To 'kick the bucket' is an idiom meaning what?
answer: To die (slangily)
choices: To die (slangily)
To start a new job
To win the contest
To run away fast
context: 'Kick the bucket' = die. The phrase is over 500 years old in English. One proposed origin: in old slaughterhouses, animals were hung by their legs from a beam (called a 'bucket' from French 'buque' = beam) and might 'kick' in their last moments. Another theory: a person hanging themselves stood on a bucket and kicked it away. Either origin works as a grim image; today the phrase is mild slang. A 'bucket list' = things to do before you 'kick the bucket.'

question: The idiom 'a piece of cake' means what?
answer: Something very easy to do
choices: Something very easy to do
A delicious dessert at a party
An equal share of work or pay
A small but important detail
context: 'A piece of cake' = something easy. The phrase dates to the 1930s, possibly from the U.S. military or from earlier 'cakewalk' contests (where the prize for the best dancer was a cake). 'It was a cakewalk' has the same meaning. Other 'easy' idioms: 'easy as pie,' 'easy as ABC,' 'a breeze,' 'a walk in the park,' 'child's play.' English is rich in ways to say 'not hard.'

question: To say 'It's raining cats and dogs' means what?
answer: It is raining very heavily
choices: It is raining very heavily
It is raining only briefly
Pets are out enjoying the rain
Many storms are predicted soon
context: 'Raining cats and dogs' = pouring rain. The phrase has been in English since the 1600s. Origins are debated: some say it comes from old British streets where heavy rain washed dead animals into the gutters; some say from Norse mythology (Odin's cats brought storms); some say it's just colorful nonsense. Either way, no actual pets fall from clouds. The phrase exists in versions in other languages too — French says 'il pleut des cordes' (it rains ropes).

question: To call someone 'the apple of my eye' means what?
answer: A cherished and beloved person
choices: A cherished and beloved person
A teacher's favorite student in class
Someone who eats lots of fruit daily
A person with very bright eye color
context: 'Apple of my eye' = someone deeply loved, often a child or sweetheart. The phrase comes from the King James Bible (1611), Psalm 17:8: 'Keep me as the apple of the eye.' Originally 'apple of the eye' was an Old English term for the pupil — the most precious part of vision, easily damaged. So 'apple of my eye' literally means 'as precious to me as my own sight.'

question: To feel 'under the weather' means what?
answer: Mildly sick or unwell
choices: Mildly sick or unwell
Stuck inside during a storm
Wearing the wrong clothes outside
Unable to predict the rain forecast
context: 'Under the weather' = a little sick. The phrase comes from sailing: passengers who got seasick were sent BELOW DECK (out of the rough weather above) — literally 'under the weather' geographically. Down there, away from the wind and waves, the sea-sickness was supposed to ease. The phrase moved into general use for any minor illness. Sailors gave English many vivid phrases: 'three sheets to the wind,' 'son of a gun,' 'taken aback.'

question: To 'get cold feet' before doing something means what?
answer: To suddenly lose courage or back out
choices: To suddenly lose courage or back out
To actually feel chilled and shivery
To finish a task ahead of time
To prepare for a long winter trip
context: 'Cold feet' = sudden loss of nerve, often before a big event. The phrase has been in English since the 1800s. One theory: soldiers with cold feet were physically unable to advance into battle, so 'cold feet' came to mean unwillingness to face danger. The phrase is famously associated with weddings — a bride or groom with 'cold feet' may second-guess the marriage at the last moment.

question: To 'let the cat out of the bag' means what?
answer: To reveal a secret accidentally
choices: To reveal a secret accidentally
To release a pet from a carrier
To finish unpacking after a trip
To clean out an old container
context: 'Let the cat out of the bag' = reveal a secret. One proposed origin: at medieval markets, dishonest sellers would sell a 'pig in a poke' (poke = bag), claiming it was a piglet — but the buyer who looked inside would find a less-valuable cat. To 'let the cat out of the bag' was to expose the scam. The phrase entered English in the 1700s and stuck. 'Buying a pig in a poke' (taking something sight-unseen) is the related idiom.

question: To 'spill the beans' is an idiom meaning what?
answer: To reveal a secret accidentally
choices: To reveal a secret accidentally
To make a mess in the kitchen
To pour out a bag of food
To finish a meal quickly
context: 'Spill the beans' = reveal a secret. One proposed origin: in ancient Greece, voters dropped beans into jars — a black bean for 'no,' a white bean for 'yes.' Spilling the jar before the count exposed the votes prematurely. The phrase entered English in the early 1900s. Same meaning as 'let the cat out of the bag' — different metaphors, identical idea.

question: To call someone 'butterfingers' means what?
answer: Someone who drops things easily
choices: Someone who drops things easily
Someone who cooks with butter often
Someone with very strong hands
Someone who eats lots of fat
context: 'Butterfingers' = someone clumsy who drops things — because their fingers seem as slippery as if coated in butter. Charles Dickens used it in The Pickwick Papers (1836); the candy bar 'Butterfinger' was named after it in 1923. Calling someone 'butterfingers' is a mild teasing word in English, especially in sports — a player who drops a catchable ball is having a 'butterfingers moment.'

question: What does the idiom 'couch potato' describe?
answer: A lazy person who watches a lot of TV
choices: A lazy person who watches a lot of TV
A potato grown on a soft surface
A type of vegetable couch cushion
A potato shaped like a chair seat
context: 'Couch potato' = a person who spends excessive time sitting and watching television. The phrase was coined in 1976 by Tom Iacino and gained widespread use in the 1980s as TV-viewing time exploded. The image: someone sitting motionless on a couch, like a potato — a lumpy vegetable that doesn't move. Related: 'mouse potato' (someone glued to a computer), invented in the 1990s but never as catchy.

question: An oxymoron pairs two opposite or contradictory words together. Which phrase is an oxymoron?
answer: jumbo shrimp
choices: jumbo shrimp
big elephant
small mouse
quick rabbit
context: OXYMORON = a phrase combining contradictory words. 'Jumbo shrimp' — jumbo means huge; shrimp means tiny. Together they form a deliberate paradox that catches the ear. Other examples: 'bittersweet,' 'deafening silence,' 'living dead,' 'old news,' 'open secret,' 'awfully good,' 'clearly confused,' 'pretty ugly,' 'original copy.' Oxymorons aren't mistakes — they're meant to startle the reader.

question: Which phrase is an oxymoron (two words that seem to contradict each other)?
answer: bittersweet memory
choices: bittersweet memory
sweet candy bar
sour green apple
bitter dark coffee
context: BITTERSWEET combines opposites: bitter (unpleasant) + sweet (pleasant). Together they describe something that has BOTH qualities — like a happy memory of someone now gone. The word goes back to Old English (over 700 years old). Other oxymorons: 'icy heat,' 'cruel kindness,' 'loud whisper,' 'painful pleasure.' The clash of opposites in one phrase forces the reader to slow down.

question: The saying 'An apple a day keeps the doctor away' first appeared in which century?
answer: The late 1800s
choices: The late 1800s
Ancient Rome
The Middle Ages
The 1950s
context: The earliest known version of 'an apple a day keeps the doctor away' appeared in Wales in 1866 ('Eat an apple on going to bed, and you'll keep the doctor from earning his bread'). The modern phrasing took shape in the 1900s. The idea — that apples are healthy — is much older, but the catchy rhyming proverb is a Victorian invention. There's some real nutritional truth: apples contain fiber and vitamin C.

question: Many famous brand names use alliteration. Which is built on alliteration (repeated starting sound)?
answer: Coca-Cola
choices: Coca-Cola
Pepsi-Cola
Dr Pepper
Sprite Drink
context: Coca-Cola — both words start with hard C sounds. The alliteration makes the brand name catchy and memorable. Other alliterative brand names: PayPal, Best Buy, Lululemon, Krispy Kreme, Range Rover, Dunkin' Donuts, Bed Bath & Beyond, Mickey Mouse, Donald Duck, Peter Parker, Bruce Banner. Advertising agencies love alliteration — it's the reason so many cartoon characters and consumer products have matched-sound names.

question: Which classic phrase uses alliteration heavily?
answer: Six sleek swans swam swiftly southward
choices: Six sleek swans swam swiftly southward
Many birds flew across the wide ocean
The old fisherman caught a large salmon
Quick rabbits hopped through the long grass
context: 'Six sleek swans swam swiftly southward' — six words starting with S, plus 's' sounds embedded in 'sleek' and 'swiftly.' This kind of dense alliteration is the basis of tongue twisters AND of memorable poetry. Old English poetry was built almost entirely on alliteration (instead of rhyme) — every line had repeating consonant sounds in stressed positions. Beowulf is hundreds of lines of alliterative verse.

question: Rhyme is the matching of word endings in sound. Which pair of words rhymes?
answer: cat and bat
choices: cat and bat
cat and dog
cat and feline
cat and kitten
context: RHYME matches the ending sound of two words: cat/bat, day/play, light/night, star/far. The match must be on the STRESSED final vowel and any sounds after it. Rhyme is one of the oldest poetic techniques in English — children's nursery rhymes, rap, song lyrics, and limericks all use it heavily. Old English poetry used ALLITERATION instead; rhyme became central in English only after the Norman Conquest brought French poetic forms.

question: Which pair of words is a perfect rhyme?
answer: night and bright
choices: night and bright
night and day
night and noon
night and sky
context: NIGHT and BRIGHT rhyme — both end in the stressed sound /aɪt/. A perfect rhyme needs the same vowel sound AND the same consonants after. NIGHT and DAY don't rhyme (different vowels). 'Eye rhymes' look the same but sound different (love/move, said/maid) — they're tools for visual effect in poetry but don't rhyme to the ear. Slant rhymes ('orange'/'door hinge') match imperfectly for stylistic effect.

question: Figurative language doesn't mean exactly what it says. Which sentence uses figurative language?
answer: The classroom was a zoo today.
choices: The classroom was a zoo today.
The classroom had thirty students today.
The classroom had a big map on the wall.
The classroom was on the second floor.
context: 'The classroom WAS a zoo' is figurative — the classroom wasn't LITERALLY full of zoo animals. The metaphor describes chaos. Literal language means exactly what it says; figurative language uses comparison, exaggeration, or imagery. Most everyday speech mixes both: 'I'm starving' (figurative — you're not actually dying), 'I had a sandwich' (literal). Stories and poetry lean heavily figurative; instructions stay literal.

question: Which sentence is hyperbole (exaggeration for effect, not meant literally)?
answer: I'm so hungry I could eat a horse.
choices: I'm so hungry I could eat a horse.
I am hungry and want some lunch.
I have not eaten anything today.
I would like a sandwich and milk.
context: You're not literally going to eat a horse (which would be impractical AND would feed you for weeks). The hyperbole emphasizes hunger. Common hyperboles for hunger: 'I could eat a horse.' 'I'm wasting away.' 'I'm starving to death.' All exaggerations. Hyperbole grew up with English and shows up in everyday speech, songs, and ads constantly. The trick: both speaker and listener know it's wild exaggeration.

question: The idiom 'kill two birds with one stone' means what?
answer: Accomplish two tasks with one action
choices: Accomplish two tasks with one action
Take a risk with little chance of success
Do something forbidden to gain reward
Help one person and harm another
context: 'Kill two birds with one stone' = solve two problems at once. The phrase has been in English since the 1600s. Some modern speakers prefer non-violent versions: 'feed two birds with one scone' or 'hit two targets with one arrow.' The idea is universal — Mandarin Chinese has 'shoot two birds with one arrow' (一箭双雕); German has 'zwei Fliegen mit einer Klappe schlagen' (swat two flies with one swat). Same wisdom, different idioms.

question: To 'break the ice' at a party means what?
answer: To start a conversation with strangers
choices: To start a conversation with strangers
To accidentally drop a glass at a party
To finish all the cold drinks first
To turn off the music before it ends
context: 'Break the ice' = start a conversation that overcomes initial awkwardness. The phrase comes from ships in frozen waters — small icebreaker boats would crack the ice ahead so larger ships could pass. The metaphor moved to social settings: a tense room is 'icy,' and someone who makes a joke or starts a conversation has 'broken the ice.' Related: 'icebreaker' (a game or question used at parties).

question: The phrase 'once in a blue moon' means what?
answer: Very rarely
choices: Very rarely
Once every year
Every full moon
Every winter night
context: 'Once in a blue moon' = something that almost never happens. The 'blue moon' is the second full moon in a single calendar month — which happens about every 2-3 years. So 'once in a blue moon' is meant to mean 'rarely.' Earlier the phrase meant 'absurd' or 'impossible' (since the moon isn't actually blue), but the modern astronomical meaning has taken over. Real 'blue moons' (visually blue, from atmospheric dust) are even rarer.

question: To say something 'costs an arm and a leg' means what?
answer: It is extremely expensive
choices: It is extremely expensive
It hurts the body to use
It requires both hands to carry
It is impossible to afford ever
context: 'Costs an arm and a leg' = very expensive — as if you'd have to give up body parts to afford it. The phrase is American, dating to the 1940s. The image is hyperbolic but vivid; English speakers also say 'cost a fortune,' 'cost a pretty penny,' 'cost a king's ransom.' Equivalent in French: 'ça coûte les yeux de la tête' (it costs the eyes of the head). Same idea — both languages cash in body parts for emphasis.

question: To 'face the music' means what?
answer: To accept the unpleasant consequences of your actions
choices: To accept the unpleasant consequences of your actions
To listen carefully to a song played at a concert
To watch a live orchestra perform on a stage
To dance happily while loud music is playing nearby
context: 'Face the music' = accept the consequences. The exact origin is debated. One theory: in old British military discharges, drummers played as a dishonored soldier was marched out — he had to walk past them ('face the music') as he left. Another: opera performers had to walk on stage facing the orchestra pit (the music). Either way, the phrase entered American English in the 1800s and stuck.

question: Which sentence uses figurative language (not meant literally)?
answer: I had to bite my tongue to keep from laughing.
choices: I had to bite my tongue to keep from laughing.
I had to chew my food slowly during dinner.
I had to brush my teeth after the meal.
I had to drink water with my breakfast today.
context: 'Bite my tongue' is figurative — the speaker isn't actually biting their tongue with teeth. The phrase means 'force yourself to stay silent.' Body-part idioms are common: 'keep your nose out of it,' 'lend a hand,' 'put your foot down,' 'pull someone's leg,' 'shake a leg.' English speakers use dozens daily without thinking about the literal images they invoke.

question: In 'Sally sells seashells,' what figure of speech repeats the 's' sound?
answer: Alliteration
choices: Alliteration
Rhyme
Metaphor
Hyperbole
context: Repeating an INITIAL consonant sound is ALLITERATION. 'Sally sells seashells' has four 's' starts in a row. Repeating a VOWEL sound (assonance) or a final consonant (consonance) is different. Alliteration is everywhere in English poetry, ads, sports headlines, brand names ('Best Buy,' 'PayPal,' 'Krispy Kreme'). The technique is older than English itself — Old English poetry was built around alliteration rather than rhyme.

question: To say something is 'easy as pie' means what?
answer: It is very easy or simple to do
choices: It is very easy or simple to do
It is round and golden brown
It is shared between many people
It takes a long time to finish
context: 'Easy as pie' = simple, no effort needed. Pie itself is moderately complex to BAKE — the saying probably means 'easy as EATING pie' (which really is easy). The phrase entered American English in the late 1800s. Similar 'easy' idioms: 'piece of cake,' 'walk in the park,' 'breeze,' 'cinch,' 'child's play.' English has many ways to say 'not hard'; very few of them mention thinking.

question: Which sentence uses hyperbole?
answer: This bag weighs ten tons.
choices: This bag weighs ten tons.
This bag is fairly heavy today.
This bag has many books in it.
This bag is too full to close.
context: Ten tons is twenty thousand pounds — no bag weighs that. The exaggeration emphasizes how heavy the bag FEELS. Hyperbole isn't lying — both speaker and listener understand it's an exaggeration. Common kid hyperbole: 'I'm dying of boredom.' 'My homework will never end.' 'I've waited a thousand years.' Each impossible; each vivid. The technique is older than English itself — ancient Greek rhetoric was full of hyperbole.

question: In which sentence is a metaphor doing the work?
answer: My memory is a sieve, and everything falls through.
choices: My memory is a sieve, and everything falls through.
My memory works pretty well most days.
I tried to remember what we discussed.
I always forget my friend's birthday.
context: 'My memory IS a sieve' — a direct metaphor. A sieve is a kitchen tool with holes that lets small things fall through while catching big ones. The metaphor says memory works the same way — most things slip away, only a few stick. Other metaphors for forgetfulness: 'mind like Swiss cheese,' 'mind like a goldfish.'

question: In which sentence is a simile pairing two unlike things?
answer: His temper was like a volcano about to erupt.
choices: His temper was like a volcano about to erupt.
His temper was a volcano about to erupt.
His temper made him very upset.
He had a quick temper when angry.
context: 'LIKE a volcano' — the word 'like' marks it as a simile. The metaphor version ('His temper WAS a volcano') would also work, but skip the 'like.' Both make the same comparison; the simile signals it with the word. Other temper similes: 'mad as a hornet,' 'mad as a wet hen,' 'angry as a bear,' 'like a bull in a china shop' (clumsy temper). English loves animal and weather metaphors for moods.

question: Which phrase uses alliteration?
answer: the wild and wooly West
choices: the wild and wooly West
the cold winter wind
the rocky mountain trail
the busy city street
context: 'Wild and Wooly West' — three W-starting words in a row. The phrase is a common American expression for the old frontier. Other alliterative American phrases: 'rough and ready,' 'safe and sound,' 'fit as a fiddle,' 'last but not least,' 'rags to riches,' 'busy as a bee.' Alliteration sticks in the ear, which is why English keeps it everywhere — in songs, ads, headlines, and casual speech.

question: Which word imitates the sound of falling rain?
answer: pitter-patter
choices: pitter-patter
raindrops
raincloud
downpour
context: PITTER-PATTER imitates light rain on a roof. Other rain sounds: drip-drop, plink, splash, splat. English has many onomatopoeic 'sound doubles' — pairs of similar words that capture a repeating sound: pitter-patter, ding-dong, tick-tock, drip-drop, splish-splash, knick-knack, mumble-jumble, hocus-pocus. Linguists call this 'reduplication' — the same sound pattern repeated with a small change.

question: To 'chicken out' of doing something means what?
answer: To back out because of fear
choices: To back out because of fear
To eat a chicken dinner
To raise chickens on a farm
To make a chicken sound
context: 'Chicken out' = lose courage and back out. Chickens are seen as cowardly in English folklore — they panic and run from any threat. Calling someone 'a chicken' or saying they 'chickened out' has been English slang since the 1900s. Animal-courage metaphors are everywhere: 'brave as a lion,' 'scared as a mouse,' 'fight like a tiger,' 'cunning as a fox,' 'stubborn as a mule.' Each animal carries a fixed character in English speech.

question: The phrase 'dog days of summer' refers to what?
answer: The hottest, most uncomfortable days of late summer
choices: The hottest, most uncomfortable days of late summer
Days when dogs visit the park most
Days when pet stores have sales
Days dogs are taken for grooming
context: 'Dog days' = the hottest days of summer (late July through August in the Northern Hemisphere). Origin: ancient Romans noticed that Sirius (the 'Dog Star' in the constellation Canis Major) rose with the sun during the hottest weeks. They called these 'dies caniculares' (dog days) and blamed the dog star for the heat. Latin gave the phrase to most European languages; English kept it. The Romans were wrong about Sirius causing heat — but the name stuck for 2,000 years.

question: In the joke 'I used to be a banker, but I lost interest,' what kind of word play makes it funny?
answer: A pun on 'interest' (money meaning + curiosity meaning)
choices: A pun on 'interest' (money meaning + curiosity meaning)
Alliteration on the letter B sounds
Hyperbole exaggerating the banker's career
Metaphor comparing banking to losing things
context: 'Interest' has two meanings: money earned on savings (the banker's stock-in-trade) AND curiosity / attention. The pun says he lost BOTH at once. Dad jokes thrive on this double-meaning structure: 'I'm reading a book on anti-gravity — it's impossible to put down.' 'I used to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough.' Each joke pivots on one word doing two jobs simultaneously.

question: To 'pull someone's leg' means what?
answer: To tease them with a joke or false story
choices: To tease them with a joke or false story
To help them stand up after a fall
To grab them to stop them leaving
To stretch their muscles before exercise
context: 'Pulling your leg' = teasing or joking with you, not seriously. The exact origin is debated — some say it comes from old British thieves who would trip victims by pulling their legs; others say it's just a colorful image of distracting or tripping up. Whatever the source, the phrase has meant 'kidding' in English since the late 1800s. Often used as a follow-up: 'I'm just pulling your leg' = 'I was joking.'

question: To say something is 'not my cup of tea' means what?
answer: It is not something I enjoy or prefer
choices: It is not something I enjoy or prefer
It does not belong to me actually
I do not drink hot tea ever
I prefer coffee to tea always
context: 'Not my cup of tea' = not to my taste. The phrase is British, from the late 1800s, when tea preferences were a small but real personal trait. To say 'horror movies aren't my cup of tea' politely declines them without judgment. The phrase is famously English; few other languages have an equivalent built on tea. Other 'preference' idioms: 'not my thing,' 'not my style,' 'not my scene,' 'doesn't float my boat.'

question: Which sentence is a pangram (uses every letter of the alphabet)?
answer: Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs.
choices: Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs.
Pack the box and load the truck quickly.
Five jugs were placed in the wooden box.
Ship the heavy boxes to the warehouse.
context: 'Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs' uses all 26 letters of the alphabet — count them — and is famously the SHORTEST natural-sounding pangram (32 letters total). Compare 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' (35 letters). Pangrams are used to test typewriters, fonts, keyboards, and handwriting. Different languages have their own classic pangrams; English typographers have collected dozens.

question: Some metaphors are so familiar we forget they're metaphors — like 'foot of the mountain' or 'mouth of the river.' What is THIS expression also doing?
answer: Using a body part as a metaphor for a place
choices: Using a body part as a metaphor for a place
Naming a body part by accident
Speaking literally about geography
Repeating the same word twice
context: 'Foot of the mountain,' 'mouth of the river,' 'face of a cliff,' 'eye of a needle,' 'head of the table,' 'spine of a book,' 'leg of the journey.' English maps the human body onto everything. We're so used to these 'dead metaphors' that they feel literal. Other dead metaphors hiding in plain sight: 'a leg of the table,' 'the mouth of a cave,' 'the heart of the matter,' 'the heel of a shoe.'

question: The saying 'every cloud has a silver lining' means what?
answer: Even bad situations have something good in them
choices: Even bad situations have something good in them
Storm clouds reflect light from the sun above
Silver was the price of an umbrella long ago
Clouds form differently when filled with metal
context: 'Every cloud has a silver lining' — even tough situations have a hidden upside. The phrase comes from John Milton's 1634 poem Comus ('Was I deceived, or did a sable cloud / Turn forth her silver lining on the night?'). Milton was describing a real visual effect — sunlight hitting cloud edges can outline them in silver. The metaphor took on its 'hope in trouble' meaning over the 1700s-1800s. Today it's pure optimism.

question: To say someone 'has a chip on their shoulder' means what?
answer: They feel resentful or quick to be offended
choices: They feel resentful or quick to be offended
They are carrying wood for the fire today
They have a wound that has not yet healed
They are wearing the wrong style of clothes
context: 'Chip on the shoulder' = a grudge or resentment. The phrase comes from a 19th-century American practice: a boy ready to fight would place a wood chip on his shoulder and dare anyone to knock it off. The first newspaper recorded use was 1830. Today the phrase is figurative — no actual wood involved. Same image: 'pick a fight,' 'has it in for someone.' English has many fighting-stance metaphors.

question: To 'hit the books' means what?
answer: To start studying seriously
choices: To start studying seriously
To carry books to the library
To physically strike a textbook
To organize books on the shelf
context: 'Hit the books' = study hard. The phrase is American slang from the early 1900s.
