A keeper of libraries professionally (from 'biblion,' library).
A reader of scripture daily (from 'biblion,' bible).
A learner of foreign languages (from 'biblion,' tongue).
context: Greek '-phil-' (love, attraction) gives: BIBLIOPHILE (book-lover), AUDIOPHILE (sound-lover), FRANCOPHILE (France-lover), TECHNOPHILE (technology-lover). The opposite '-phob-' (fear, aversion) gives the parallel set: BIBLIOPHOBE, TECHNOPHOBE, etc. -PHIL- and -PHOB- form natural mirror pairs across the Greek-rooted vocabulary.

question: The Greek combining form 'TELE-' means 'far' or 'at a distance.' Which word does NOT use this prefix?
answer: tellurium (from Latin 'tellus,' the earth)
choices: tellurium (from Latin 'tellus,' the earth)
telephone (sound from a distance)
television (sight from a distance)
telescope (a looker over a distance)
context: Greek 'tele-' (far, distant) gives: TELEPHONE (far-sound), TELEVISION (far-sight, with Latin 'videre' as the second half), TELESCOPE (far-looker), TELEGRAPH (far-writer), TELEGRAM (far-message), TELEPATHY (far-feeling). 'Tellurium' is the chemical element 52, named from Latin 'tellus' (earth) — completely unrelated to the Greek prefix despite the similar look.

question: The Greek combining form 'CHRON-' means 'time.' Which word does NOT use this prefix?
answer: chrome (from 'chroma,' color)
choices: chrome (from 'chroma,' color)
chronological (in order of time)
chronic (lasting a long time)
anachronism (out of time-place)
context: Greek 'chronos' (time) gives: CHRONOLOGY (study of time-order), CHRONOLOGICAL (time-ordered), CHRONIC (lasting in time), CHRONICLE (a time-record), ANACHRONISM (out-of-time-place), SYNCHRONOUS (with-time-together), DIACHRONIC (through time). Different root: 'chrome' comes from 'chroma' (color, hue), giving CHROMOSOME (color-body, since they take up stains), MONOCHROME (single-color), POLYCHROME (many-colors).

question: Greek 'POLY-' means 'many.' What does POLYGLOT mean?
answer: A person who speaks many languages (from 'glotta,' tongue).
choices: A person who speaks many languages (from 'glotta,' tongue).
A person from many places at once (from 'glotta,' place).
A person who reads many books quickly (from 'glotta,' book).
A person who travels many roads (from 'glotta,' road).
context: Greek 'poly-' (many) gives: POLYGLOT (many tongues), POLYGON (many angles, 'gōnia'), POLYTHEISM (many gods, 'theos'), POLYGAMY (many marriages, 'gamos'), POLYHEDRON (many sides, 'hedra'), POLYMER (many parts, 'meros'), POLYTECHNIC (many skills, 'techne'). Opposite: MONO- (one). The English 'multi-' and Greek 'poly-' often coexist for the same meaning (multilingual = polyglot).

question: The word 'ALGEBRA' came into English from Arabic — through medieval European scholarship. What does Arabic 'al-jabr' originally mean?
answer: The reunion of broken parts — the original mathematical sense of solving equations.
choices: The reunion of broken parts — the original mathematical sense of solving equations.
The setting of the morning sun — a metaphor for new beginnings.
The dividing of a herd — the original use in livestock accounting.
The pouring of clear water — a metaphor for clarity of thought.
context: 'Algebra' comes from the title of a 9th-century book by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi (who also gives his name to ALGORITHM): 'Kitab al-jabr wa-l-muqabala' ('The Book of Restoration and Balancing'). 'Al-jabr' meant the operation of moving subtracted terms to the other side of an equation — 'reuniting broken parts.' The book's Latin translation was the standard math text in medieval Europe.

question: The word 'ALCOHOL' came into English from Arabic. What does Arabic 'al-kuhul' originally name?
answer: A fine powder — originally a black eye-makeup made from antimony (kohl).
choices: A fine powder — originally a black eye-makeup made from antimony (kohl).
A clear liquid — the original spirit produced by distillation.
A drinking ceremony — the formal sharing of wine after dinner.
A sweet syrup — the medicinal preparation given to royal patients.
context: 'Alcohol' comes from Arabic 'al-kuhul' — a fine cosmetic powder (the eye-darkening kohl still sold in Middle Eastern markets). European alchemists used the word for any FINE ESSENCE distilled from a substance. Eventually it was applied to the 'alcohol of wine' — and the modern sense (the intoxicating ingredient) became the only one. The original eye-makeup sense survives in 'kohl.'

question: Many English star names start with 'AL-' — Aldebaran, Altair, Algol. Why?
answer: Medieval Arab astronomers cataloged the stars; their Arabic names (with 'al-,' meaning 'the') entered Europe via Latin translations.
choices: Medieval Arab astronomers cataloged the stars; their Arabic names (with 'al-,' meaning 'the') entered Europe via Latin translations.
Galileo named most stars himself in the 1600s using Arabic-sounding phonetics to suggest mystery.
Modern astronomy chose Arabic-style names in the 1900s when older systems became politically complicated.
Persian poets invented these names in the 1300s and they spread through European folklore literature.
context: Between roughly 800 and 1200 CE, Arab astronomers (working in Baghdad, Damascus, and across the Islamic world) preserved and extended Greek astronomy. Their star catalogs — with Arabic names beginning with 'al-' (the) — became the standard. When European astronomy revived (1100s onward), Latin translations of these texts carried the names along. ALDEBARAN ('the follower'), ALTAIR ('the eagle'), ALGOL ('the demon' — actually a variable star whose dimming was known to Arab observers).

question: The English word 'ZENITH' (the highest point) comes from Arabic. What was the original Arabic phrase?
answer: Samt al-ras — 'the path overhead' (literally the direction of the head).
choices: Samt al-ras — 'the path overhead' (literally the direction of the head).
Zayn al-hil — 'the gem at the peak' (a Persian poetic phrase).
Hawa al-zur — 'the air's center' (a desert weather term).
Daqa al-shams — 'the sun's strike' (a noon-time observation).
context: 'Zenith' came into Latin via Arabic 'samt al-ras' — 'the direction of the head,' meaning the point in the sky directly above an observer. Medieval Latin scribes misread the Arabic 'samt' as 'senit' (the 'm' and the long s being similar), and that became Latin 'zenit,' English 'zenith.' The opposite point — directly below — is 'nadir,' from Arabic 'nazir' (opposite). Both came from medieval Arab astronomy.

question: Why does English have so many words starting with 'AL-' that come from Arabic (algebra, alcohol, almanac, alkali, alchemy)?
answer: Arabic 'al' means 'the' — and was absorbed into the borrowed words as part of the term in European languages.
choices: Arabic 'al' means 'the' — and was absorbed into the borrowed words as part of the term in European languages.
Arabic 'al' marks the female form of a noun — picked up by chemists during the Renaissance.
Arabic 'al' is the standard scientific prefix — invented in the 1800s for taxonomy and chemistry.
Arabic 'al' indicates a Persian, not Arabic, origin — confusing many medieval European linguists.
context: In Arabic, 'al-' is the definite article (the equivalent of English 'the'). When medieval Europeans borrowed Arabic words, they took 'al-' along with the noun, treating it as part of the word. So 'algebra' (the-restoration), 'alcohol' (the-fine-powder), 'almanac' (the-calendar), 'alchemy' (the-chemistry), 'alkali' (the-ashes). Spanish has 'el' from the same pattern: 'el azúcar' (the sugar — Arabic 'al-sukkar'). The article got grafted permanently.

question: The word 'COFFEE' came into English via Turkish from Arabic. What did Arabic 'qahwa' originally also mean?
answer: Wine (the word originally applied to wine before being repurposed for the coffee-drink).
choices: Wine (the word originally applied to wine before being repurposed for the coffee-drink).
A hot bath (the original sense being warming or invigorating).
A morning ritual (the prayer time after sunrise).
A brown stone (the color of the bean rather than the drink).
context: Arabic 'qahwa' originally meant wine (it appears with this sense in classical Arabic poetry). When coffee-drinking spread from Yemen and Ethiopia (1400s) through the Islamic world, 'qahwa' was repurposed — possibly because coffee, like wine, gave a kind of mental lift but was permissible under Islamic law. Turkish 'kahve' came from the same Arabic source, and that's what passed through Italian 'caffè' into English 'coffee.'

question: The English word PAJAMAS came from Hindi-Urdu via British colonial contact. What did Persian-rooted 'pāy-jāma' originally mean?
answer: Leg-garment — referring to the loose drawstring trousers worn in South Asia.
choices: Leg-garment — referring to the loose drawstring trousers worn in South Asia.
Sleep-clothing — the formal Persian word for bed attire across all classes.
House-shirt — a tunic worn only indoors among Persian nobility.
Cold-cover — a quilted under-garment worn during northern winters.
context: British officials in colonial India encountered 'pāy-jāma' — Persian-rooted Hindi-Urdu for 'leg-garment.' These were loose drawstring trousers worn for everyday comfort. The British borrowed both the garment AND the word, using 'pyjamas' (British spelling) for nightwear once they brought the style home. The American spelling 'pajamas' came later. The Persian/Hindi-Urdu sense was just 'pants.'

question: The English word SHAMPOO comes from Hindi. What did 'champo' originally mean?
answer: To press, knead, or massage (a head and body massage, not a hair wash).
choices: To press, knead, or massage (a head and body massage, not a hair wash).
To pour clean water from a copper vessel before evening prayers.
To collect plant juices for skin softening among the nobility.
To wash with a hot sand mixture in the desert tradition of India.
context: Hindi 'champo' (imperative of 'champna,' to press or knead) meant a massage — typically of the head and body. British colonial visitors to India encountered this as a refreshing service offered with bath-houses. They brought the word back, narrowed it to head-washing specifically, and 'shampoo' became the hair-cleansing product.

question: The English word BUNGALOW came from Hindi 'bangla.' What does that mean literally?
answer: Of Bengal — a house in the style typical of the Bengal region of India.
choices: Of Bengal — a house in the style typical of the Bengal region of India.
Of the bamboo — a structure built from local plant materials.
Of the season — a house for monsoon rains rather than dry weather.
Of the village — a hut used by farmers near rice paddies.
context: 'Bungalow' came from Hindi 'bangla' — meaning 'of Bengal,' from 'Bangala' (Bengal, eastern India). British colonial officials lived in single-story houses with broad verandas in the Bengali style; they brought the word home and applied it to single-story houses generally. Today 'bungalow' has come to mean any small single-story house — far from its origin as a Bengal-style colonial residence.

question: Which set of English words ALL come from Hindi-Urdu via British colonial contact in India?
answer: loot, thug, bandana, guru
choices: loot, thug, bandana, guru
guitar, sugar, magazine, zero
sushi, karate, tycoon, typhoon
ketchup, tea, kowtow, tofu
context: From Hindi/Urdu/Sanskrit via British colonialism: LOOT ('lūṭ,' booty), THUG ('thag,' a member of a violent gang), BANDANA ('bandhnu,' tie-dyed cloth), GURU ('guru,' teacher), JUNGLE ('jangal,' forest), CHEETAH ('chita,' spotted), DUNGAREES ('dungri,' cloth), PUNDIT ('pandit,' scholar). The other groups are from Arabic (sugar, magazine, zero), Japanese (sushi, karate), and Chinese (ketchup, tea, kowtow).

question: The English word THUG (a violent criminal) came from Hindi 'thag.' What did the original term name?
answer: A member of an organized Indian band of robbers (the Thuggee, suppressed by the British in the 1830s).
choices: A member of an organized Indian band of robbers (the Thuggee, suppressed by the British in the 1830s).
A roving merchant traveling between cities to trade silver coins.
A street performer in colonial Calcutta who juggled torches.
A village wrestler who served as a local protector by tradition.
context: The Thuggee were organized robber bands in pre-1840 India who killed travelers (often by strangulation) and robbed them. British administrator William Sleeman led a suppression campaign in the 1830s. The Hindi word 'thag' (cheat, robber) entered English as 'thug,' eventually losing the specific Thuggee meaning and broadening to any violent criminal. (Sleeman's campaign is what gave the word its colonial-era English currency.)

question: The English word JUNGLE came from Hindi 'jangal.' What did the original Sanskrit-derived term name?
answer: Uncultivated land — wilderness, scrub, or wild ground (not specifically tropical rainforest).
choices: Uncultivated land — wilderness, scrub, or wild ground (not specifically tropical rainforest).
Tropical rainforest — the dense canopy and undergrowth specifically.
Swamp — marshy land near rivers used for rice cultivation.
Mountain forest — high elevation tree groves above farmland.
context: Hindi 'jangal' (from Sanskrit 'jangala') meant uncultivated land — wilderness, scrub, or rough ground of any kind, including dry scrubland. The British borrowed the word for any wild place and gradually narrowed it (in English) to dense tropical forest. The Sanskrit/Hindi original had a much broader sense. Many English-readers picture only rainforest — that's a narrowing that happened in English specifically.

question: Some popular word-origin stories are FALSE, invented after the fact. Which of these phrases has a TRUE origin story?
answer: 'Decimate' really did come from the Roman military practice of killing 1 in 10 mutineers.
choices: 'Decimate' really did come from the Roman military practice of killing 1 in 10 mutineers.
'Rule of thumb' came from a law allowing wife-beating with sticks no thicker than a thumb.
'OK' came as an acronym for 'oll korrect' from a 1700s Boston shopkeeper named O. Kraft.
'Posh' came from luxury cabin assignments labeled Port Out Starboard Home on liners.
context: DECIMATE is genuine: Latin 'decimare,' from 'decimus' (tenth), really did name a Roman discipline where 1 in 10 soldiers was killed by lot. The other three are folk etymologies: no English law allowed wife-beating with sticks; OK has a different origin (1839 Boston Morning Post abbreviation craze); POSH was used long before any cabin-assignment claim and the story is undocumented.

question: The popular story that 'RULE OF THUMB' comes from a law allowing wife-beating with a stick no thicker than a thumb is FALSE. What is the actual origin?
answer: From rough-measurement traditions, where carpenters, brewers, and gardeners used the thumb as a quick gauge.
choices: From rough-measurement traditions, where carpenters, brewers, and gardeners used the thumb as a quick gauge.
From a Welsh legal tradition that defined inheritance shares by hand width across generations.
From a medieval thumbprint identification system used in trade ledgers across England.
From a Latin proverb 'pollex regula' applied to the choosing of a king in old elections.
context: No English law ever permitted wife-beating with a stick measured by thumb width. The myth was popularized in the 1970s and has been thoroughly debunked by legal historians. The phrase actually comes from rough-measurement practices: carpenters using the thumb's width as a rough inch, brewers testing temperature with a thumb, gardeners using thumb-pinches as planting depth gauges.

question: The folk-etymology that 'TIP' (a gratuity) comes from 'To Insure Promptness' is FALSE. What's wrong with the backronym theory?
answer: The word 'tip' meaning a gratuity existed long before the supposed acronym; the meaning came from thieves' slang.
choices: The word 'tip' meaning a gratuity existed long before the supposed acronym; the meaning came from thieves' slang.
The phrase 'insure promptness' is grammatically modern and could not have produced a 17th-century word.
Tips were illegal in 18th-century England and could not have been named after their purpose.
Backronyms only emerged in the 1900s and could not have generated any older English vocabulary.
context: 'Tip' (a small gift of money) appeared in English by the early 1600s. Acronyms (words formed from initials) are rare before the 20th century — they're mostly a modern phenomenon. The 'To Insure Promptness' explanation is a BACKRONYM (a fake acronym invented after the word). The word 'tip' actually comes from 17th-century thieves' cant — meaning 'to give, hand over' (also seen in 'tip the wink,' 'tip the hat'). Similar fake-acronym myths: POSH, NEWS, GOLF, SOS — almost all are backronyms.

question: The folk story that 'POSH' means 'Port Out, Starboard Home' (allegedly luxury cabin assignments on India-bound ships) is unfounded. What is the likely real origin?
answer: From a 19th-century slang word 'posh' meaning a dandy or stylish person; origin uncertain but documented before any ship-cabin claim.
choices: From a 19th-century slang word 'posh' meaning a dandy or stylish person; origin uncertain but documented before any ship-cabin claim.
From a Hindi word 'pash' meaning a wealthy traveler; borrowed during the British colonial period in India.
From the Polish surname 'Posz' brought by 19th-century immigrants who opened expensive London shops.
From an abbreviation 'po. sh.' on parliamentary records meaning 'post-shilling' luxury fees.
context: The 'Port Out Starboard Home' story is a classic BACKRONYM. No ticket records show cabins booked that way, and the explanation surfaces only in the 1930s, long after 'posh' was current English slang. The most likely real source is older slang 'posh' (dandy, swell), used in late-1800s British music halls. The exact origin is uncertain, but the ship-cabin story is documented as folklore, not history.

question: The folk story that 'GOLF' is an acronym for 'Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden' is false. What's the actual origin?
answer: From an old Scots word 'gowf' (or 'goff') meaning to strike; the game appears in 1457 Scottish records.
choices: From an old Scots word 'gowf' (or 'goff') meaning to strike; the game appears in 1457 Scottish records.
From a Dutch word 'kolf' (a club or bat); although the games are unrelated, the words look similar.
From a French phrase 'jeu de la golfe' (game of the cove); played by sailors waiting for the tide.
From a Greek mythological figure named Golfias, a wandering shepherd who invented stick-and-ball play.
context: 'Golf' comes from a Scots word for a game using a club to hit a ball, first appearing in records of 1457 when the Scottish parliament tried to ban it because it distracted men from archery practice. The 'Gentlemen Only Ladies Forbidden' acronym is a backronym from the 1990s, fake from the start. The word's evolution traces through Scottish dialect, not any acronym.

question: The popular story that the word 'SINCERE' comes from Latin 'sine cera' ('without wax') — supposedly from sculptors hiding cracks with wax — is FALSE. What's the actual Latin origin?
answer: Latin 'sincerus' — meaning 'clean, pure, sound' — a single word, not a compound.
choices: Latin 'sincerus' — meaning 'clean, pure, sound' — a single word, not a compound.
Greek 'syngeneia' — meaning 'kinship' — referring to honest family relations.
Old French 'senceire' — meaning 'open-hearted' — from a chivalric code term.
Anglo-Saxon 'sinncere' — meaning 'truthful at all times' — from a moral oath.
context: 'Sincere' comes from Latin 'sincerus,' a single word meaning 'clean, pure, sound.' The popular 'sine cera' story (sculptors hiding cracks with wax — therefore 'without wax' = 'genuine') is a FOLK ETYMOLOGY: it sounds plausible, has zero documentary support, and falls apart on inspection of Latin grammar. 'Sincerus' is one word, not a compound 'sine + cera.' The fake story has been repeated for centuries — which is exactly how folk etymologies thrive.

question: What's the actual origin of the abbreviation 'OK' (or 'okay')?
answer: Boston newspaper humor in 1839, a deliberately misspelled 'oll korrect,' part of an abbreviation fad.
choices: Boston newspaper humor in 1839, a deliberately misspelled 'oll korrect,' part of an abbreviation fad.
An acronym 'Oll Korrect' invented seriously in office work by accountants in the 1880s.
A backronym for 'Order Known' used by the British army in the 1840s for marching commands.
A trademark of the Olympic Kerosene Company in the 1860s, popularized through advertising.
context: Linguist Allen Walker Read documented 'OK' as appearing in the Boston Morning Post on March 23, 1839, part of an abbreviation craze (also producing 'KY' for 'know yuse' and 'NCsm' for 'no use'). It was a JOKE: deliberate misspelling of 'all correct' as 'oll korrect' = O.K. The 1840 presidential campaign of Martin Van Buren (nicknamed 'Old Kinderhook') gave it a political boost, and the abbreviation stuck.

question: Some old stories about word origins get repeated forever even when they're wrong. What's the technical name for such a popular-but-false origin story?
answer: Folk etymology (a popular explanation invented after the fact, not historically supported).
choices: Folk etymology (a popular explanation invented after the fact, not historically supported).
Backformation (a real linguistic process where a shorter word is created from a longer one).
Bracketing (when speakers re-divide a phrase into different word boundaries over time).
Reanalysis (when grammar reshapes a word's role; a real shift, not a fake story).
context: Folk etymology has two technical meanings: (1) the popular-but-false origin stories that get retold forever even after debunking; and (2) the real linguistic process where speakers reshape a word to look like a more familiar word (Old English 'sand-blind' = 'half-blind' got reanalyzed as 'sand-blind' because 'sand' looked more familiar than the old prefix 'sam-'). The first sense, fake origin stories, is the one to flag and dismiss.

question: Which English word means 'a sudden insight' and comes from Greek through religious vocabulary?
answer: epiphany (from Greek 'epiphaneia,' an appearance or showing)
choices: epiphany (from Greek 'epiphaneia,' an appearance or showing)
encore (from French 'encore,' meaning 'again' in theater)
ennui (from French 'ennui,' meaning boredom or weariness)
espresso (from Italian 'espresso,' meaning pressed out fast)
context: 'Epiphany' came from Greek 'epiphaneia' (literally 'a showing forth'). In the Christian tradition it names the manifestation of Christ to the Magi (January 6). The word generalized to mean any sudden burst of understanding — James Joyce in particular wrote about literary 'epiphanies.' The other three words come from French and Italian and have nothing to do with Greek.

question: The word ROBOT was coined for a 1920 Czech play by Karel Capek. What does Czech 'robota' originally mean?
answer: Forced labor or drudgery (the play imagined manufactured workers doing such labor).
choices: Forced labor or drudgery (the play imagined manufactured workers doing such labor).
A puppet on strings (the play used puppet imagery from Czech folk theater).
A man of iron (the play imagined a knight of metal serving a king).
A clever servant (the play imagined a Czech peasant outwitting an emperor).
context: 'Robot' was coined by Karel Capek for his 1920 play 'R.U.R.' (Rossum's Universal Robots). The Czech word 'robota' (forced labor, drudgery — the labor of a peasant tied to a lord's estate) had no science-fiction sense before Capek used it. Within a decade, 'robot' had spread to every European language as the name for a machine that does work. One of the few science-fiction terms that became universal vocabulary.

question: What is the difference between a METAPHOR and a SIMILE?
answer: A simile uses 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor compares directly without those words.
choices: A simile uses 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor compares directly without those words.
A metaphor is longer than a simile; a simile is always a short phrase.
A metaphor is positive; a simile compares one thing favorably to another.
A metaphor names a category; a simile names just one specific feature.
context: Both metaphor and simile compare two unlike things. SIMILE uses an explicit comparison word: 'like,' 'as,' 'than.' ('Her smile was LIKE the sun.') METAPHOR makes the comparison direct, without the comparison word: 'Her smile WAS the sun.' Metaphors are stronger; similes are gentler. Both are figurative — neither claims literal identity.

question: Which sentence is a SIMILE?
answer: She sings like an angel.
choices: She sings like an angel.
She is an angel when she sings.
Her voice carries the listener away.
Her singing changed the room's mood.
context: A simile uses 'like' or 'as' to compare two unlike things. 'Sings LIKE an angel' is a simile (uses 'like'). The first distractor is a metaphor (direct identification, no 'like'). The other two are figurative in different ways but not similes — they describe effects rather than make explicit comparisons.

question: Which is an EXTENDED METAPHOR (a single metaphor developed across multiple sentences or images)?
answer: All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players; they have their exits and their entrances.
choices: All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players; they have their exits and their entrances.
Shakespeare wrote dozens of plays; many include famous lines that we still quote today.
The world is a stage in many ways, since people perform roles for those around them.
Shakespeare's characters speak in verse, and they sometimes break the fourth wall to address us.
context: Extended metaphor sustains one metaphor through related images. Shakespeare's 'As You Like It' opens with Jaques saying 'All the world's a stage,' then develops the metaphor: men and women are players, with exits and entrances, playing many parts in their lifetimes — the seven ages of man. The image keeps unfolding. Shorter metaphors strike fast and stop; extended ones build an entire world.

question: Which is a MIXED METAPHOR (two metaphors that clash when combined)?
answer: We need to nip this in the bud before it snowballs out of control.
choices: We need to nip this in the bud before it snowballs out of control.
We need to address this problem before it spirals out of control.
We need to handle this situation before it gets out of hand.
We need to stop this trend before it has time to grow.
context: A mixed metaphor combines two unrelated metaphors that don't make sense together. 'Nip in the bud' (a gardening metaphor — pinch a flower bud before it blooms) plus 'snowball' (a winter-weather metaphor — a snowball rolling downhill grows) clash because plants don't snowball. Writers often slip into mixed metaphors when they're combining clichés without picturing the image — and the result is often unintentionally funny.

question: What does the metaphor 'time is money' suggest about time?
answer: Time can be spent, saved, wasted, or invested, just like money.
choices: Time can be spent, saved, wasted, or invested, just like money.
Time is literally a form of currency that you can use to buy things.
Time is exactly equal to money in every situation and culture today.
Time is the most expensive resource in modern American economies.
context: 'Time is money' (Benjamin Franklin, 1748) is a metaphor that organizes our entire vocabulary about time: we SPEND time, SAVE time, WASTE time, INVEST time, BUDGET time, BORROW time. This is a CONCEPTUAL metaphor — one that shapes how we think, not just how we speak.

question: Which sentence is figurative (a simile or metaphor), not literal?
answer: She has a heart of stone.
choices: She has a heart of stone.
She has a strong heart for her age.
She has a slow heart rate naturally.
She has had a heart condition for years.
context: 'A heart of stone' is a METAPHOR — her heart isn't literally made of stone (that would mean she was dead, or a statue). It means she's emotionally hard or unfeeling. The other three sentences describe a literal heart. Figurative language uses concrete images to communicate abstract qualities — and the kid's job is to NOT take it literally.

question: Which sentence is LITERAL — not figurative?
answer: The tower stands fifty meters tall.
choices: The tower stands fifty meters tall.
The tower stands as tall as a giant.
The tower stands like a guardian over the city.
The tower stands sleepless watch over the village.
context: Literal language describes things as they actually are. 'Fifty meters tall' is a measurable physical fact about the tower. The other three use figurative language: simile ('as tall as a giant'), simile with personification ('like a guardian'), and pure personification ('sleepless watch'). Figurative language gives towers human or mythic qualities; literal language gives the measurement.

question: Of these four sentences describing a door, which uses PERSONIFICATION?
answer: The old door GROANED as it opened.
choices: The old door GROANED as it opened.
The old door swung open slowly.
The old door was painted bright red.
The old door had rusted hinges.
context: Personification attributes a HUMAN action or quality to something non-human. 'Groaned' is a sound humans make — usually when in pain or annoyed. Applying it to a door brings the door to life as a tired, complaining character. The other three describe the door without personifying it. Sound-words ('whispered,' 'groaned,' 'sighed,' 'screamed') are the easiest personification triggers.

question: Why is 'The sun SMILED on the meadow' personification?
answer: Smiling is a human action; assigning it to the sun makes the sun seem person-like.
choices: Smiling is a human action; assigning it to the sun makes the sun seem person-like.
Smiles always require lips, so the sun's rays must be working as lip-like beams.
The sun is being addressed directly, which is the only mark of personification.
The sun appears in fairy tales as a character, and this is a reference to those.
context: Personification = giving HUMAN traits to non-humans. Smiling is uniquely human (the sun has no face, no muscles to smile). The image works because we picture the warmth and brightness AS IF the sun were a happy person. Personification doesn't require literal facial features — just the human action assigned to a non-human thing.

question: Three of these sentences personify the river. Which one is LITERAL (no personification)?
answer: The river flowed downhill toward the sea.
choices: The river flowed downhill toward the sea.
The river argued with the rocks in its bed.
The river sang its way through the canyon.
The river forgot to be quiet that afternoon.
context: Rivers can literally FLOW — that's a normal river verb, no personification. But rivers can't 'argue,' 'sing,' or 'forget' — those are human mental actions. The other three each project a human capacity onto the river, making it sound alive. The test for personification: ask whether the verb names a uniquely human action.

question: Personification often appears in poems. What is the personifying verb here: 'Time flies on swift wings'?
answer: flies
choices: flies
swift
wings
Time
context: 'Flies' attributes the act of flying — and by implication, having wings — to Time, which is abstract and cannot literally fly. The phrase 'on swift wings' completes the personification. Notice how a single verb can carry the whole figure: any verb that requires a living agent (flies, dances, mourns, hesitates) personifies its non-human subject.

question: Which line by Carl Sandburg from his poem 'Fog' uses personification?
answer: The fog comes on little cat feet.
choices: The fog comes on little cat feet.
The fog is thicker by the river.
The fog rises off the cold water.
The fog hides the lighthouse light.
context: Carl Sandburg's 1916 poem 'Fog' opens with one of the most famous American examples of personification: 'The fog comes on little cat feet.' Fog can't have feet — let alone cat feet. The image makes the fog feel quiet, soft-stepping, and alive. The whole poem is six lines: 'The fog comes / on little cat feet. // It sits looking / over harbor and city / on silent haunches / and then moves on.' Pure personification throughout.

question: Which sentence is personification — but uses an ABSTRACT idea (not a thing) as the personified subject?
answer: Hope spreads its wings and sings to the heart.
choices: Hope spreads its wings and sings to the heart.
The bird spread its wings and sang to its mate.
She held the bird gently and listened to it sing.
The hopeful song of the bird filled the morning.
context: Personification can apply to ABSTRACT ideas (hope, time, love, death, justice) — giving them human or living-thing actions. 'Hope spreads its wings' makes an abstract concept act like a bird. This is a particularly powerful kind of personification because abstractions don't otherwise have any sensory shape: poetry brings them to life by giving them a body of action.

question: Which sentence personifies an OBJECT (not a force or abstract idea)?
answer: The teakettle screamed for attention on the stove.
choices: The teakettle screamed for attention on the stove.
The thunder rolled across the dark valley.
Loneliness wrapped its arms around her.
The seasons danced their slow rotation.
context: All four sentences use personification — but they personify different KINDS of things. 'Teakettle' is an object (a thing). The others personify a force (thunder), an emotion (loneliness), and a process (seasons). Object-personification often produces the most concrete, almost cartoonish effects — like Disney films where teacups talk and candlesticks dance.

question: HYPERBOLE is extreme exaggeration for effect (not meant literally). Which is the clearest example?
answer: I've told you a million times to put your shoes away.
choices: I've told you a million times to put your shoes away.
I've told you several times to put your shoes away.
I've told you twice today to put your shoes away.
I asked you politely to put your shoes away.
context: Hyperbole uses extreme numbers or claims for effect: 'a million times' (not literal), 'I'm starving' (when just hungry), 'this bag weighs a ton' (it doesn't). The other three choices give literal or moderate descriptions. Hyperbole is everywhere in everyday speech — it's how English speakers emphasize feelings without sounding flat.

question: Which everyday phrase is an example of hyperbole?
answer: I could eat a horse.
choices: I could eat a horse.
I am very hungry tonight.
I would like dinner soon, please.
I haven't eaten since this morning.
context: 'I could eat a horse' is HYPERBOLE — extreme exaggeration. Nobody can actually eat a horse, but the image conveys intense hunger in a way 'I'm very hungry' cannot. Common hyperbolic phrases: 'I've been waiting forever,' 'this homework is killing me,' 'my feet are aching to death.' Notice the literal-impossibility test: the more clearly impossible, the more hyperbolic.

question: Which choice is LITERAL — not hyperbole?
answer: The line at the grocery store took fifteen minutes.
choices: The line at the grocery store took fifteen minutes.
The line at the grocery store took absolutely forever.
The line at the grocery store was a mile long today.
The line at the grocery store stretched to infinity.
context: Hyperbole exaggerates beyond literal possibility. 'Forever,' 'a mile long,' 'to infinity' are all exaggerations meant for emotional effect. 'Fifteen minutes' is a literal time (could be a real measurement) and so isn't hyperbolic. Test: would a stopwatch agree? If yes, it's literal. If no, you're in hyperbole territory.

question: What is the opposite of HYPERBOLE — a deliberate UNDERSTATEMENT?
answer: Saying 'It's just a flesh wound' when an arm has been chopped off (Monty Python).
choices: Saying 'It's just a flesh wound' when an arm has been chopped off (Monty Python).
Saying 'I am thirteen feet tall' when standing on a small platform stool.
Saying 'I love this so much' when receiving an unwanted birthday present.
Saying 'I'm starving for breakfast' before eating a normal-sized morning meal.
context: Understatement (also called LITOTES in its formal version) is hyperbole's opposite — describing something as LESS than it really is, for effect. 'A bit of a setback' (when actually devastating), 'not bad' (when wonderful), 'somewhat upset' (when furious). The Monty Python sketch — the Black Knight losing limbs and insisting 'tis but a scratch' — is the canonical comic example.

question: Why do speakers use hyperbole when literal description would be more accurate?
answer: Hyperbole communicates feeling and emphasis better than literal numbers can.
choices: Hyperbole communicates feeling and emphasis better than literal numbers can.
Hyperbole is required in formal writing whenever a sentence describes time.
Hyperbole is only used in poetry, not in everyday speech among regular speakers.
Hyperbole is used to confuse the listener into agreeing with the speaker's point.
context: Hyperbole signals INTENSITY of feeling. 'I'm so tired I could sleep for a week' communicates exhaustion more vividly than 'I'm extremely tired.' Speakers and listeners both understand the literal exaggeration; the figure of speech does the emotional work. Children intuitively use hyperbole before they know its name ('a million,' 'forever,' 'the biggest ever').

question: Which common phrase is hyperbole?
answer: I'd give my right arm for a slice of pizza.
choices: I'd give my right arm for a slice of pizza.
I would prefer some pizza for dinner tonight.
I am willing to pay for a slice of pizza now.
I really want to order pizza at the moment.
context: 'I'd give my right arm' is hyperbole — nobody seriously trades a limb for pizza. The phrase conveys strong desire. Common right-arm and limb hyperboles cluster around want: 'I'd kill for a coffee,' 'I'd give my right arm,' 'I'd sell my soul.' All overstate the trade-off for comic emphasis.

question: METONYMY substitutes a closely associated word for the thing meant. What does 'the crown' stand for in 'The crown announced new policies'?
answer: The monarchy or the king/queen as ruler.
choices: The monarchy or the king/queen as ruler.
A jeweled crown sitting on a museum stand for display.
A crown of laurels (an ancient Greek victory wreath).
A crown molding (an architectural ceiling feature).
context: Metonymy is using a closely associated thing to stand for the main thing. 'The crown' (the physical object) stands for the institution of monarchy. Other classic metonymies: 'the pen' (writing), 'the sword' (military), 'the bench' (the judiciary), 'the White House' (the U.S. executive). The substitution works because the chosen image is strongly linked to what's meant.

question: Which sentence uses METONYMY (substitute an associated thing for the real subject)?
answer: The pen is mightier than the sword.
choices: The pen is mightier than the sword.
The writer's argument was stronger than the soldier's force.
Words can persuade more deeply than weapons frighten.
Writing has more lasting power than military victory.
context: The famous phrase 'the pen is mightier than the sword' (Edward Bulwer-Lytton, 1839) uses METONYMY: 'the pen' stands for writing/persuasion, and 'the sword' stands for military force. The three distractors say roughly the same thing literally, without metonymy. Metonymy compresses the idea into two vivid objects — that's what makes the phrase memorable.

question: SYNECDOCHE uses a PART to stand for the WHOLE (or vice versa). Which is an example?
answer: All hands on deck!
choices: All hands on deck!
All sailors here!
Crew, report now!
Topside, everyone!
context: Synecdoche substitutes a PART for the WHOLE: 'all hands' means 'all sailors' (their hands stand for the whole sailor). Other examples: 'a fleet of fifty sails' (sails stand for ships), 'a hired gun' (a gun stands for an armed man), 'don't grow up to be a suit' (a suit stands for a corporate worker). The whole-for-part variety is rarer: 'America won the gold' (the whole country stands for the athlete).

question: Which sentence uses synecdoche (part-for-whole or whole-for-part)?
answer: Lend me your ears.
choices: Lend me your ears.
Please listen.
Pay attention.
Hear me out.
context: 'Lend me your ears' (Mark Antony in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar) is SYNECDOCHE — 'ears' stand for the whole act of listening attention. Shakespeare's speech is one of the most quoted examples of the figure. Other synecdoches: 'wheels' for car, 'mouths to feed' for people, 'hired hands' for workers, 'a roof over my head' for shelter.

question: What is the difference between METONYMY and SYNECDOCHE?
answer: Metonymy substitutes a CLOSELY ASSOCIATED thing; synecdoche specifically substitutes a PART or WHOLE.
choices: Metonymy substitutes a CLOSELY ASSOCIATED thing; synecdoche specifically substitutes a PART or WHOLE.
Metonymy is a stronger figure of speech; synecdoche is weaker and only used in poetry.
Metonymy applies only to abstract ideas; synecdoche applies only to physical objects.
Metonymy is a modern English term; synecdoche is the older Greek version of the same.
context: Both substitute one word for another, but the relationship differs. METONYMY: closely associated thing ('the White House' for 'the executive branch,' 'the crown' for 'the monarchy'). SYNECDOCHE: a PART for the WHOLE ('all hands' for 'all sailors') or a WHOLE for a PART ('Brazil won the World Cup' = Brazil's team). Synecdoche is technically a special case of metonymy, but the two are usually taught separately.

question: In 'Brazil won the World Cup,' the figure of speech is:
answer: Synecdoche (the whole country stands for the team)
choices: Synecdoche (the whole country stands for the team)
Metaphor (Brazil compared to a winning person)
Hyperbole (the country exaggerated as one entity)
Personification (Brazil given human victory traits)
context: When we say 'Brazil won the World Cup,' we mean Brazil's national TEAM (a small part of Brazil) won. The whole country stands for one specific group within it — SYNECDOCHE in the whole-for-part direction. We do this constantly in sports talk: 'America won the gold,' 'Japan beat Korea,' 'France played beautifully today.' Each sentence substitutes the whole nation for the actual team.

question: Which sentence uses metonymy involving a place name standing for an institution?
answer: Washington has not commented on the new policy.
choices: Washington has not commented on the new policy.
Washington, D.C. is a popular tourist destination.
Washington was the first U.S. president to serve.
Washington State borders the Pacific Ocean on the west.
context: Place names often stand by metonymy for institutions: 'Washington' (the U.S. federal government), 'Downing Street' (the British Prime Minister's office), 'the Vatican' (the Catholic Church), 'Wall Street' (American finance), 'Silicon Valley' (the U.S. tech industry). The other three sentences use 'Washington' literally — as a city, a person, or a state.

question: In the phrase 'The pen is mightier than the sword,' what does 'the sword' stand for?
answer: Military force or violence (metonymy: the weapon stands for warfare itself).
choices: Military force or violence (metonymy: the weapon stands for warfare itself).
A specific historic sword used by an ancient general (the literal weapon).
Soldiers' training (metonymy: practice with the weapon stands for skill).
An ornamental ceremony (metonymy: ceremonial swords stand for tradition).
context: In Bulwer-Lytton's famous phrase, 'the sword' is metonymy for military force or warfare — the weapon stands for the kind of action it represents. The same kind of substitution lets 'the pen' stand for writing and persuasion. Both are figures: nobody is really claiming a physical pen weighs more than a physical sword.

question: What kind of figure of speech is 'The Pentagon announced a new strategy'?
answer: Metonymy (the building stands for the U.S. Department of Defense).
choices: Metonymy (the building stands for the U.S. Department of Defense).
Metaphor (the Department of Defense is compared to a pentagon-shaped object).
Hyperbole (the building is exaggerated as having the power to speak).
Personification (the building is given the human ability to announce things).
context: 'The Pentagon' literally refers to the five-sided building in Arlington, Virginia, where the U.S. Department of Defense is headquartered. By METONYMY, the building name stands for the institution housed in it — and the announcement is actually made by officials, not by the building. Similar institutional metonymies: 'the White House,' 'Number 10' (Downing Street), 'the Élysée' (the French presidency), 'the Kremlin.'

question: Which figure of speech is in 'I bought a new set of WHEELS' (meaning car)?
answer: Synecdoche (part for whole)
choices: Synecdoche (part for whole)
Metaphor (a direct comparison)
Hyperbole (an exaggeration)
Personification (human qualities)
context: 'Wheels' for car is SYNECDOCHE — using a PART (the wheels) to stand for the WHOLE (the car). It's the same move as 'all hands on deck' (hands for sailors). Synecdoche tends to feel more casual and colorful than metonymy: 'wheels,' 'threads' (for clothes), 'hired hands' (for workers), 'mouths to feed' (for hungry people).

question: An OXYMORON pairs two contradictory words for effect. Which phrase is an oxymoron?
answer: deafening silence
choices: deafening silence
rushing wind
shining sun
falling rain
context: Oxymoron pairs two words whose dictionary meanings clash: 'deafening' (loud enough to deafen) + 'silence' (no sound). The contradiction makes you stop and think. Famous oxymorons: 'jumbo shrimp,' 'bittersweet,' 'civil war,' 'open secret,' 'awfully good,' 'living dead,' 'pretty ugly.' The other three choices have agreeing words.

question: Which is NOT an oxymoron (the two words AGREE rather than clash)?
answer: boiling hot
choices: boiling hot
jumbo shrimp
civil war
bittersweet
context: 'Boiling hot' has two agreeing words (boiling implies hot — they reinforce each other). The other three are classic OXYMORONS: 'jumbo' (huge) + 'shrimp' (small thing); 'civil' (polite, orderly) + 'war' (violence); 'bitter' + 'sweet' (opposite tastes). The contradiction in each is what makes the phrase memorable.

question: A PARADOX is a self-contradictory statement that nevertheless reveals a truth. Which famous phrase is a paradox?
answer: Less is more.
choices: Less is more.
Less is better.
More is more.
Less makes sense.
context: 'Less is more' (architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, popularizing a 19th-century phrase) is a PARADOX — it seems to say something impossible (less can't equal more) but reveals a truth (a simpler design often has more impact than an ornate one). Other paradoxes: 'the more I know, the less I understand'; 'I always lie' (the liar's paradox); 'the only constant is change.' Paradoxes invite second thinking.

question: What is the difference between an OXYMORON and a PARADOX?
answer: An oxymoron is a two-word contradiction; a paradox is a longer self-contradictory statement that reveals a truth.
choices: An oxymoron is a two-word contradiction; a paradox is a longer self-contradictory statement that reveals a truth.
An oxymoron is humorous; a paradox is serious and only used in academic writing.
An oxymoron is always false; a paradox is always true on second reading.
An oxymoron is from Latin; a paradox is from Greek by linguistic origin.
context: OXYMORON: a tight, often two-word, contradiction ('deafening silence,' 'jumbo shrimp'). PARADOX: a longer statement that contradicts itself but expresses a deeper truth ('to find yourself, you must lose yourself'; 'less is more'). The line between them blurs — some oxymorons act paradoxically; some paradoxes have oxymoronic kernels. But the scale differs: oxymoron = phrase; paradox = sentence or claim.

question: Which sentence is a PARADOX?
answer: The more we know, the more we realize we do not know.
choices: The more we know, the more we realize we do not know.
The more we know, the easier the questions become.
The more we know, the more we can teach others quickly.
The more we know, the better our test scores get.
context: Socrates is often credited with the paradox: 'I know that I know nothing.' The longer English version — 'the more we know, the more we realize we don't know' — captures the paradoxical insight that learning expands awareness of ignorance, not just knowledge. The other three are straightforward statements without contradiction.

question: Which is an OXYMORON used in everyday American English?
answer: awfully good
choices: awfully good
really good
very good
extremely good
context: 'Awfully good' pairs 'awfully' (full of awe, originally — and now meaning 'terribly') with 'good' (positive) — a clash that creates an OXYMORON. We use it without thinking: 'awfully nice of you,' 'awfully expensive,' 'terribly sweet,' 'frightfully good.' The negative-positive pairing reflects how language shifts intensifiers ('awfully,' 'terribly,' 'frightfully') from their literal meanings.

question: A DANGLING MODIFIER is an opening phrase that doesn't logically attach to the subject. Which sentence has one?
answer: Running down the street, the trees looked beautiful.
choices: Running down the street, the trees looked beautiful.
Running down the street, I saw the beautiful trees.
The trees looked beautiful as I ran down the street.
While running down the street, I admired the trees.
context: A dangling modifier opens with a phrase that should describe the SUBJECT of the main clause, but doesn't. 'Running down the street' should describe whoever was running — but in the first choice the subject is 'the trees,' which weren't running. The fix is to make the subject match the modifier ('I' is doing the running, so 'I' should be the subject).

question: Why is 'Walking through the park, the flowers were stunning' a DANGLING modifier?
answer: The opening phrase implies the FLOWERS were walking, which doesn't make sense.
choices: The opening phrase implies the FLOWERS were walking, which doesn't make sense.
The opening phrase is incomplete and needs more words to finish out.
The opening phrase uses the wrong tense, since it should be 'walked.'
The opening phrase is too long for the rest of the sentence to balance.
context: 'Walking through the park' is a participial phrase. Grammatically, it modifies whoever is the SUBJECT of the main clause. Here the subject is 'flowers,' which weren't doing any walking. The result is a sentence that literally says the flowers were walking. Fix: 'Walking through the park, I saw stunning flowers' (now I'M walking, which makes sense).

question: Which sentence is correctly FIXED — the modifier now attaches properly?
answer: Climbing the steep hill, the hikers grew tired.
choices: Climbing the steep hill, the hikers grew tired.
Climbing the steep hill, the path grew muddy.
Climbing the steep hill, the view became dramatic.
Climbing the steep hill, the rocks were slippery.
context: In 'Climbing the steep hill, the hikers grew tired,' the opening modifier 'Climbing the steep hill' correctly attaches to the subject 'hikers' (who are doing the climbing). In the other three sentences, the subjects ('path,' 'view,' 'rocks') aren't climbing — those are dangling modifiers. The fix is always to make the subject match what the modifier describes.

question: What's the FUNNIEST reading of 'After eating the cat, I went to bed'?
answer: The narrator ate the cat (the phrasing attaches 'eating the cat' to 'I').
choices: The narrator ate the cat (the phrasing attaches 'eating the cat' to 'I').
The cat ate something else, and the narrator went to bed.
The narrator put the cat to bed, gently and carefully.
Someone else ate the cat while the narrator slept later.
context: Without a comma after 'eating' (or a clearer phrasing), the sentence can read as 'after eating the cat,' meaning the narrator was the one who ate the cat. The fix: 'After eating, the cat and I went to bed' OR (intended meaning) 'After feeding the cat, I went to bed.' This is a misread structure that produces an absurd image — the same principle as the famous comma-saves-Grandma joke.

question: Which is the CORRECTED version of 'Looking out the window, the rain stopped'?
answer: Looking out the window, I saw the rain stop.
choices: Looking out the window, I saw the rain stop.
Looking out the window, the storm cleared up.
Looking out the window, the sun came out.
Looking out the window, the umbrella was wet.
context: 'Looking out the window' must describe whoever is doing the looking. In the original ('the rain stopped'), the rain isn't doing the looking — that's a dangling modifier. The fix introduces a subject ('I') who can actually be looking out the window. The other corrections in the choices still have danglers — none of those subjects can look out a window.

question: Which sentence has a MISPLACED modifier (positioned where it modifies the wrong word)?
answer: She only ate the cake at the party.
choices: She only ate the cake at the party.
She ate only the cake at the party.
She ate the cake only at the party.
Only she ate the cake at the party.
context: 'Only' is a modifier whose position changes the meaning. Each version of this sentence means something different: 'She ONLY ate' (didn't drink/socialize); 'She ate ONLY the cake' (not the pizza or ice cream); 'She ate the cake ONLY at the party' (not at home); 'ONLY she ate the cake' (no one else did). The first version is ambiguous, often interpreted as 'she ONLY ate it' but meaning depends on tone.

question: Why does the garden-path sentence 'The old man the boats' work?
answer: 'Old' is briefly read as adjective + 'man' as noun, but the real parse is 'the old' (people) + 'man' (verb meaning to staff).
choices: 'Old' is briefly read as adjective + 'man' as noun, but the real parse is 'the old' (people) + 'man' (verb meaning to staff).
The sentence is missing a verb, and the reader has to fill one in from context.
The word order is reversed, and the reader rearranges it mentally for sense.
The pronouns are ambiguous, and the reader picks the most likely referent.
context: 'The old man the boats' first reads as a fragment (subject 'the old man' + the boats). But 'man' here is the VERB (meaning to staff or operate), and 'the old' is the subject (older people). The sentence means 'older people staff the boats.' This is GARDEN-PATH — the early reading forces re-analysis. The kid who notices the re-parse has done parsing on the fly — a useful syntax-awareness exercise.

question: Which sentence uses ALLITERATION (repeated initial consonant sounds)?
answer: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
choices: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
Peter ate his apple after he finished his work.
The bird sang sweetly when the sun came up high.
We watched the movie at home on Saturday night.
context: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds at the START of stressed words. 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers' is the canonical alliteration tongue-twister — every stressed word starts with /p/. Other examples: 'big bad wolf,' 'wild and woolly,' 'rough and ready.' Different from ASSONANCE (repeated vowel sounds: 'how now, brown cow') and CONSONANCE (repeated consonant sounds not necessarily at the start).

question: What does the figure of speech ASSONANCE repeat?
answer: Vowel sounds across nearby words (e.g., 'How now, brown cow').
choices: Vowel sounds across nearby words (e.g., 'How now, brown cow').
Consonant sounds at the start of words (this is alliteration).
Words at the start of clauses (this is anaphora).
Words at the end of lines (this is end-rhyme).
context: Assonance is repeated VOWEL sounds in nearby words (the 'ow' sound in 'How now, brown cow'). Alliteration is repeated CONSONANT sounds at word-starts. Consonance is repeated consonant sounds anywhere ('pitter-patter,' the /t/ and /r/ throughout). Rhyme is repetition of full sound (vowel + final consonant) at line endings. These four sound figures shape poetry, song lyrics, and memorable prose.

question: Which is an example of ONOMATOPOEIA (a word that imitates the sound it names)?
answer: buzz, hiss, crash, sizzle
choices: buzz, hiss, crash, sizzle
joy, fear, hope, doubt
above, below, near, far
today, tomorrow, never, soon
context: Onomatopoeia (Greek: 'name-making') gives a word a sound that imitates what it names. 'Buzz' sounds buzzy; 'hiss' has the actual hiss in it; 'crash' has the harsh consonants of an impact; 'sizzle' has the s's of a hot pan. Other examples: bang, click, snap, drip, splash, whoosh, plop. Onomatopoeia varies across languages — a rooster says 'cock-a-doodle-doo' in English but 'kikeriki' in German and 'cocorico' in French.

question: A PUN exploits two meanings of a word or two similar-sounding words. What kind of pun is in 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana'?
answer: A pun on grammatical structure — 'flies' shifts from verb (time flies) to noun (fruit flies).
choices: A pun on grammatical structure — 'flies' shifts from verb (time flies) to noun (fruit flies).
A pun on spelling — flies the verb is spelled differently from flies the noun.
A pun on imagery — both lines compare time and fruit to the same flying arrow.
A pun on rhyme — arrow and banana share an end-syllable sound completing the joke.
context: The double-take in this joke (often attributed to Groucho Marx but probably originating with linguist Anthony Oettinger around 1966) comes from re-reading 'flies' as a different part of speech. First reading: 'time FLIES (verb) like an arrow' (passes quickly). Second reading: 'fruit FLIES (noun) like a banana' (insects called fruit flies enjoy bananas). The pun works on grammar, not spelling.

question: Which is a HOMOPHONE PUN (two words that sound the same)?
answer: I used to be a banker but I lost interest.
choices: I used to be a banker but I lost interest.
I used to be a banker but the job was boring.
I used to be a banker but I quit last year.
I used to be a banker before I changed careers.
context: The pun is on 'interest' — which means both (1) curiosity/enthusiasm and (2) the financial-interest rate a banker deals in. The same WORD has two meanings; the joke exploits both at once. Other pun-on-double-meaning examples: 'Why was the math book sad? It had too many problems.' 'The grammar club discontinued because there was no tense moment.'

question: What is a PALINDROME?
answer: A word or phrase that reads the same forward and backward.
choices: A word or phrase that reads the same forward and backward.
A word that has two unrelated meanings in the same language.
A word that rhymes exactly with another word in the same line.
A word that is made up of two smaller words joined together.
context: Palindromes read the same in both directions, ignoring spaces, punctuation, and capitalization. Famous palindromes: 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'; 'Madam, I'm Adam'; 'Was it a car or a cat I saw?'; 'A Toyota's a Toyota.' Single-word palindromes: level, radar, civic, racecar, kayak. The longest English-word palindrome is a tossup, but 'tattarrattat' (a Joyce coinage in 'Ulysses') is sometimes cited.

question: Which of these is a PALINDROME — a phrase whose letters spell the same backward?
answer: Madam, I'm Adam.
choices: Madam, I'm Adam.
Adam met a polite madam.
Madam Adam knew grammar.
Adam, the polite man, bowed.
context: Read 'Madam, I'm Adam' letter by letter forward and backward (ignoring spaces, apostrophe, and comma): M-A-D-A-M-I-M-A-D-A-M. Same both ways. This famously plays on Adam's introduction to Eve in the Garden of Eden ('madam' being a polite form). The joke combines biblical reference with the palindrome trick.

question: An IDIOM is a phrase whose meaning isn't literal. What does 'break a leg' mean?
answer: Good luck (especially before a performance).
choices: Good luck (especially before a performance).
A warning to be careful at theatre stairs.
A long break or vacation in theatre slang.
Disagreement on stage during performance.
context: 'Break a leg' is theatre slang for 'good luck' — typically said before a performance. The origin is debated: theatrical superstition holds that wishing 'good luck' brings bad luck, so the opposite is said instead. The phrase has spread from theatre to general use. Other anti-wish idioms: 'merde' (used by ballet dancers, French for a vulgar word), 'toi toi toi' (German theatrical version).

question: What does the idiom 'red herring' mean?
answer: A misleading clue intended to distract from the real issue.
choices: A misleading clue intended to distract from the real issue.
A flavorful smoked fish served at British breakfasts.
A dangerous warning sign in old maritime tradition.
A festive decoration used in autumn celebrations only.
context: A 'red herring' (originally an actual smoked, reddish fish) was supposedly used to train hunting dogs by dragging a strong-smelling fish across the trail to test their focus. By extension, the phrase means a distracting clue or false lead — particularly in detective stories. Some historians say the dog-training story is folk etymology, and the idiomatic sense came purely from political writing in the 1800s. Either way, the modern meaning is established.

question: The idiom 'BITE THE BULLET' means to endure something painful. Where does the phrase come from?
answer: From battlefield surgery before anesthesia, when soldiers literally bit a bullet to brace against pain.

context: Before chloroform and ether became standard surgical anesthesia (mid-1800s), battlefield surgeons asked soldiers to bite down on a soft lead bullet during operations — a way to brace against the pain. The bullet absorbed the bite without breaking teeth. The phrase 'bite the bullet' carried the literal action into figurative meaning: to endure something painful with grit. The expression entered general English around 1891.

question: Which sentence uses a SPOONERISM (swapped initial sounds, often producing comic results)?
answer: I have in my bosom a half-warmed fish.
choices: I have in my bosom a half-warmed fish.
I have in my heart a half-formed wish.
I have in my bag a half-eaten apple.
I have in my pocket a half-folded note.
context: A spoonerism swaps the initial sounds of two nearby words, usually accidentally and often comically. 'I have in my bosom a half-warmed fish' is the intended Reverend Spooner version — the SOURCE phrase was 'half-formed wish' (formed → warmed; wish → fish, with letters swapped). Reverend William Archibald Spooner (1844-1930) of Oxford was famous for such slips. Many attributed slips are apocryphal — but spoonerisms as a category bear his name.

question: What is a MALAPROPISM?
answer: Using a wrong word that sounds like the right one (often with comic results).
choices: Using a wrong word that sounds like the right one (often with comic results).
Mispronouncing a word that is spelled correctly in the text.
Adding extra syllables to long Latin-derived English words.
Reversing letters within a word while speaking quickly out loud.
context: Malapropism uses a wrong word that sounds similar to the correct one. The name comes from Mrs. Malaprop, a character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's 1775 play 'The Rivals,' who specialized in such errors ('He is the very pineapple of politeness' — meaning 'pinnacle'; 'comparisons are odorous' — meaning 'odious'). Yogi Berra was famous for them: 'It's like déjà vu all over again,' 'nobody goes there anymore — it's too crowded.'

question: What is an EGGCORN?
answer: A misheard phrase reshaped into a similar-sounding plausible one (e.g., 'for all intensive purposes').
choices: A misheard phrase reshaped into a similar-sounding plausible one (e.g., 'for all intensive purposes').

A type of yellow stone polished and worn as a pendant in old times.

context: An eggcorn is a mishearing that produces a new phrase that sort of makes sense. The name comes from a documented case of someone writing 'eggcorn' instead of 'acorn' — and the resulting word makes a kind of intuitive sense (acorns are egg-shaped corn-of-trees). Other eggcorns: 'for all intensive purposes' (for all intents and purposes), 'one in the same' (one and the same), 'should of' (should have), 'old-timers' disease' (Alzheimer's disease). The eggcorn category was named in 2003 by linguist Geoff Pullum.

question: What is IRONY in its most common verbal sense?
answer: Saying the opposite of what you mean for effect, especially humor or critique.
choices: Saying the opposite of what you mean for effect, especially humor or critique.
Speaking using elevated formal language to mark a serious occasion.
Using metaphors more often than literal description in a passage.
Repeating a key word multiple times for rhythmic emphasis in speech.
context: Verbal irony says one thing and means the opposite. Walking out into a downpour, you say 'Beautiful weather!' — verbal irony. Compare with SITUATIONAL irony (the outcome is opposite to expectation: the fire station burns down) and DRAMATIC irony (the audience knows what the characters don't — Romeo doesn't know Juliet is just sleeping). Sarcasm is verbal irony with a bite — using the opposite of what you mean to mock.

question: What is SARCASM?
answer: Verbal irony with the intent to mock or criticize.
choices: Verbal irony with the intent to mock or criticize.
Any exaggeration used to make a serious point.
Repetition of a question for rhetorical effect.
Any joke that exploits double meaning in English.
context: Sarcasm is irony aimed at mocking. 'Oh, brilliant idea' said with a flat tone after someone does something dumb — sarcastic irony. Sarcasm differs from non-sarcastic irony in INTENT: irony notes a mismatch; sarcasm uses the mismatch to mock. The word 'sarcasm' comes from Greek 'sarkasmos' (literally 'tearing of flesh'). Sarcasm is harder to catch in text than in speech because tone of voice usually signals it.

question: Romeo finds Juliet apparently dead and kills himself, but the audience already knows she took a sleeping potion. What kind of irony is this?
answer: Dramatic irony (the audience knows what a character does not).
choices: Dramatic irony (the audience knows what a character does not).

Cosmic irony (the universe seems to work against the protagonist).
context: DRAMATIC irony exploits the gap between what the audience knows and what a character knows. In Romeo and Juliet, the audience knows Juliet has taken a sleeping potion — Romeo doesn't. When he finds her 'dead' and kills himself, the gap is unbearable. Dramatic irony is the engine of tragedy: the audience watches a character walk toward disaster, knowing what they don't.

question: Which is correct: 'less than ten cookies' or 'fewer than ten cookies'?

Modern usage often blurs the rule in casual speech ('10 items or less' at the grocery store), but careful writing keeps the distinction.

question: Which sentence uses LESS correctly (for a non-countable quantity)?

The other three use LESS with countable nouns (cups, mugs, cans) — those should be FEWER. Quick rule: if you can put a number directly in front of the noun, use FEWER. If you need to add a measurement word, use LESS.

question: Which is correct: 'less than five miles' or 'fewer than five miles'?

question: The supermarket sign says '10 items or less.' What's the prescriptive grammar critique?

Others kept 'less' arguing that it's the natural conversational form.

question: Which sentence correctly uses BOTH 'less' and 'fewer'?

question: Choose the correct word: '___ going to love this restaurant.'
answer: You're
choices: You're
Your
Youre
U'r
context: YOU'RE = contraction of 'you are.' YOUR = possessive (belonging to you). 'YOU'RE going to love' = 'you are going to love.' Substitute 'you are' to test: if it fits, use YOU'RE. Memory: apostrophe = letters missing. YOU'RE has the apostrophe because the A in 'are' has been replaced.

question: Choose the correct word: 'Where did you put ___ jacket?'
answer: your
choices: your
you're
youre
yore
context: YOUR = possessive (belonging to you). 'Your jacket' = the jacket that belongs to you. The other option, YOU'RE, means 'you are' — which would not fit here. Test: substitute 'you are.' 'Where did you put you are jacket?' Doesn't fit. So use YOUR. (YORE is an unrelated word meaning 'long ago' — 'days of yore.')

question: Why is the YOUR/YOU'RE confusion so common in writing?
answer: They sound the same in speech, and only writing must distinguish them.
choices: They sound the same in speech, and only writing must distinguish them.
They have only recently become separate words in English usage rules.
They are interchangeable in casual writing across all American style guides.
They mean the same thing, but the apostrophe is preferred in formal writing.
context: YOUR and YOU'RE are HOMOPHONES — they sound identical. Speech doesn't distinguish them, but writing must. The contraction YOU'RE drops the A from 'you are' and replaces it with an apostrophe. YOUR is the possessive (parallel to MY, HIS, HER). The same pattern recurs: their/they're, its/it's, whose/who's. The fix for all of these: substitute the full form (you are, they are, it is, who is) and see if it fits.

question: Choose the correct word: 'The kitten chased ___ tail in circles.'
answer: its
choices: its
it's
its'
it
context: ITS (no apostrophe) = possessive (belonging to it). IT'S (with apostrophe) = contraction of 'it is' or 'it has.' 'The kitten chased ITS tail' = the kitten's tail. Substitute 'it is' to test: 'The kitten chased it is tail' makes no sense. So use ITS. The most counterintuitive English possessive: unlike most possessives, IT'S with apostrophe is the contraction.

question: Choose the correct word: '___ raining outside.'
answer: It's
choices: It's
Its
Its'
It
context: IT'S = contraction of 'it is' (or 'it has'). 'IT'S raining' = 'it is raining.' The apostrophe replaces the missing letter I from 'is.' ITS (no apostrophe) is possessive ('its tail,' 'its color'). Test: substitute 'it is.' If it fits, use IT'S. If not, use ITS. This is one of English's most frequent grammar mistakes.

question: Choose the correct word: '___ at the door?'
answer: Who's
choices: Who's
Whose
Whos'
Who
context: WHO'S = contraction of 'who is' or 'who has.' WHOSE = possessive (belonging to whom). 'WHO'S at the door' = 'who is at the door.' Substitute 'who is' to test. WHOSE would be possession: 'Whose book is this?' = to whom does the book belong?

question: Choose the correct word: '___ car is parked outside?'
answer: Whose
choices: Whose
Who's
Whos'
Whose'
context: WHOSE = possessive (belonging to whom). 'WHOSE car' = to whom does this car belong? WHO'S = contraction of 'who is.' Substitute 'who is': 'Who is car is parked outside?' makes no sense, so use WHOSE. The same pattern as ITS/IT'S — apostrophe = contraction; no apostrophe = possessive. (English's irregularity: most possessives have apostrophes; the pronoun-possessives don't.)

question: William Strunk's most famous rule, in 'The Elements of Style' (1918), is what?
answer: Omit needless words.
choices: Omit needless words.
Use long sentences for dignity.
Use the passive voice always.
Use Latin words for elegance.
context: William Strunk Jr. (with E.B. White's later revision) wrote: 'Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts.' OMIT NEEDLESS WORDS is the heart of Strunk's style philosophy. White (the children's author of 'Charlotte's Web') revised the book in 1959 and added the famous closing essay.

question: Strunk's rule 'Omit needless words.' Which version of this sentence is the most concise (Strunkian)?
answer: The committee decided.
choices: The committee decided.
The committee made the decision.
A decision was reached by the committee.
It was the committee that made the decision.
context: Strunk's rule applies here: 'made the decision' = 'decided.' 'Was reached by' adds passive voice and a 'by' phrase. 'It was X that Y' adds cleft-sentence framing. Each version says the same thing — but 'The committee decided' uses the fewest words. Concise prose is harder to write than wordy prose; Strunk teaches you to spot and cut the bloat.

question: Which Strunk-style revision tightens 'In view of the fact that he was late, he missed the train'?
answer: Because he was late, he missed the train.
choices: Because he was late, he missed the train.
Due to the fact that he was late, he missed the train.
It is on account of the fact that he was late that he missed the train.
He missed the train, in view of the fact that he was late.
context: 'In view of the fact that' (6 words) = 'because' (1 word). Strunk lists this kind of bloated phrase as a target for cutting. Other examples in 'The Elements of Style': 'the question as to whether' = 'whether'; 'there is no doubt but that' = 'doubtless' or 'no doubt'; 'this is a subject that' = 'this subject.' Slash these and the prose snaps to attention.

question: Which version is most concise, in the spirit of Strunk?
answer: She arrived early.
choices: She arrived early.
She arrived at an early time.
She made an early arrival.
It was early when she arrived.
context: 'She arrived early' is 3 words and says everything. The other versions add nominalizations ('made an early arrival') and cleft-frames ('it was X when Y') without adding meaning. Strunk's principle: every unnecessary word weakens the sentence. The exception, of course, is when extra words add nuance or rhythm — but most bloat is just bloat.

question: Strunk taught: 'Use the active voice.' Which version is in active voice?
answer: The dog chased the cat.
choices: The dog chased the cat.
The cat was chased by the dog.
Chased by the dog was the cat.
It was the cat that was chased by the dog.
context: Active voice: SUBJECT does the action (the dog chased). Passive voice: subject RECEIVES the action (the cat was chased). Strunk preferred active voice because it's almost always shorter and more direct. Passive voice has its uses (when the doer is unknown or unimportant), but Strunk treated those as exceptions, not the default.

question: Which is Strunk's principle for concrete language?
answer: Use specific, definite, and concrete language.
choices: Use specific, definite, and concrete language.
Use as many adjectives as possible for color and depth.
Use abstract terms to elevate the formal register of the prose.
Use the longest available word to demonstrate vocabulary range.
context: Strunk wrote: 'Prefer the specific to the general, the definite to the vague, the concrete to the abstract.' Compare 'A period of unfavorable weather set in' (vague) to 'It rained every day for a week' (concrete). The first sounds bureaucratic; the second creates a picture in the reader's mind. Strunk's specific-and-concrete rule is the writing-craft cousin of his omit-needless-words rule.

question: Why did Strunk's rules become so popular in American schools?
answer: E.B. White (his former student) revised and published the book in 1959, and it became the standard college English text.
choices: E.B. White (his former student) revised and published the book in 1959, and it became the standard college English text.
Strunk himself toured American schools in the 1920s, lecturing teachers on his approach to clear writing.
The federal government adopted Strunk's rules as the official style for all U.S. government documents.
Strunk's rules were embedded in the Constitution as the standard for legal writing in American courts.
context: Strunk wrote 'The Elements of Style' for his Cornell University students in 1918. E.B. White (later the author of 'Charlotte's Web' and a longtime New Yorker writer) had been his student. In 1959, White revised the book for general American readers — adding a famous essay on style. The 'Strunk and White' version sold over 10 million copies and became the standard text in American college composition classes.

question: Which choice tightens 'There are many students who are studying for the exam' (Strunk style)?
answer: Many students are studying for the exam.
choices: Many students are studying for the exam.
Students are many who are studying for the exam.
There are many students who, in fact, are studying for the exam.
It is the case that many students are studying for the exam.
context: 'There are X who Y' is one of Strunk's classic targets for cutting. 'There are many students who are studying' (8 words to the verb) tightens to 'Many students are studying' (4 words). The 'there are' empty-subject construction can almost always be reduced. Watch for: 'There is/are X that/who Y' — usually a candidate for tightening.

question: What is PRESCRIPTIVE grammar?
answer: An approach that tells how language SHOULD be used (rules-based).
choices: An approach that tells how language SHOULD be used (rules-based).
An approach that focuses only on written language, never speech.
An approach used only in elementary schools, never university classes.
An approach that records examples of native-speaker errors only.
context: Prescriptive grammar TELLS PEOPLE WHAT THE RULES ARE. It prescribes correct usage — like a doctor prescribing medicine. Most school grammar is prescriptive: 'don't split infinitives,' 'don't end a sentence with a preposition,' 'use whom for objects.' Famous prescriptivists: Bishop Robert Lowth (1762), William Strunk (1918), William Safire. The opposite approach (descriptive) studies how people actually use language.

question: How is DESCRIPTIVE grammar different from prescriptive grammar?
answer: Descriptive grammar OBSERVES how speakers actually use language; prescriptive TELLS them how they should.
choices: Descriptive grammar OBSERVES how speakers actually use language; prescriptive TELLS them how they should.
Descriptive grammar is used only in elementary schools; prescriptive is the college-level standard.
Descriptive grammar prefers regional dialects; prescriptive prefers educated city speech only.
Descriptive grammar emphasizes formal writing; prescriptive emphasizes casual conversation only.
context: Descriptive grammar OBSERVES how people ACTUALLY use language. A descriptivist notes: 'In casual speech, English speakers often say who instead of whom in object position.' The descriptivist describes what speakers do, not what they should do. Modern linguistics is mostly descriptive. The two approaches aren't fully opposed: descriptivists describe the rules; prescriptivists try to enforce specific ones.

question: Bishop Robert Lowth in 1762 declared splitting infinitives improper. Why was his rule controversial?
answer: He imported the rule from Latin, where infinitives are single words and CAN'T be split.
choices: He imported the rule from Latin, where infinitives are single words and CAN'T be split.
He imported the rule from French, where infinitives are mandatory in formal writing.
He imported the rule from German, where infinitives appear at the end of clauses.
He imported the rule from Greek, where the practice was banned by ancient grammarians.
context: Latin infinitives are SINGLE WORDS — 'amare' (to love), 'ridere' (to laugh). You literally cannot split them. English infinitives are TWO WORDS ('to love,' 'to laugh') and CAN be split: 'to boldly go.' Lowth imposed a Latin rule on English where the rule didn't naturally fit.
