answer: Veal — from Old French 'veel,' the calf meat served at noble tables.
choices: Veal — from Old French 'veel,' the calf meat served at noble tables.
Tripe — from Old French 'tripe,' which actually denotes the cleaned-stomach offal.
Cutlet — from Old French 'costelette,' meaning a small rib of any young animal.
Roast — from Old French 'rost,' meaning meat that has been cooked over a fire.
context: The cow/beef, pig/pork, sheep/mutton, calf/veal, deer/venison split shaped English vocabulary permanently. The Norman pattern: Old English farm-yard word for the animal, Old French table-word for the meat. 'Calf' (Old English 'cealf') is the animal; 'veal' (Old French 'veel,' from Latin 'vitellus' — little calf) is the meat. Other entries in the same vocabulary doubling: 'sheep' / 'mutton' (Old French 'moton'); 'deer' / 'venison' (Old French 'venesoun'). The pattern doesn't appear in food vocabulary in most other European languages because they lacked the linguistic class split.

question: Continuing the Norman conquest vocabulary doubling: 'Deer' is the Old English animal word. Which Old French word for the meat completes the pair?
answer: Venison — from Old French 'venesoun,' originally meaning meat from any large hunted game.
choices: Venison — from Old French 'venesoun,' originally meaning meat from any large hunted game.
Cervina — from Latin 'cervus' meaning stag, applied to all the meat of male deer.
Hartwood — from Old English 'heorot' meaning deer-meat, the original Anglo-Saxon word.
Roebuck — from Middle English 'roo' meaning a small roe deer's meat, often the female.
context: 'Venison' comes from Old French 'venesoun,' which traces to Latin 'venatio' meaning 'hunting' (root verb 'venari,' to hunt). In medieval Norman use, 'venison' meant the meat of ANY large hunted animal — deer, but also boar, hare, even bear. It narrowed in English to mean deer meat specifically by about the 1600s. The semantic narrowing parallels the way 'deer' itself once meant 'any wild animal' in Old English ('dēor') before narrowing to the specific Cervidae family. The Norman pair cow/beef has had similar narrowing — 'beef' once meant any bovine meat regardless of age.

question: The Latin root 'manus' (hand) is one of English's most productive — manuscript, manual, manipulate, manicure, manufacture all descend from it. Which of these English words also comes from 'manus'?
answer: Emancipate — from 'ex-' (out of) + 'manus' (hand), originally 'out of the master's hand.'
choices: Emancipate — from 'ex-' (out of) + 'manus' (hand), originally 'out of the master's hand.'
Emphasize — from Greek 'en-' (in) + 'phainein' (to show), meaning to make prominent.
Emigrate — from 'ex-' (out of) + 'migrare' (to move), meaning to depart one's homeland.
Eminent — from 'ex-' (out of) + 'minere' (to project), meaning to stand out from others.
context: Latin 'manus' is one of English's most productive Latin roots. From it: MANUAL (done by hand), MANUSCRIPT ('written by hand' — manu + scriptus), MANIPULATE ('to handle skillfully'), MANICURE (manu + cura, 'care of hands'), MANUFACTURE (manu + factura, 'made by hand'), MAINTAIN ('to hold in the hand'), MANAGE (manu + agere, 'to handle'), MANDATE ('given into the hand'), EMANCIPATE ('out of the hand' — out of a master's possession), MANNER (originally 'way of handling'). Learning Latin and Greek roots multiplies English vocabulary geometrically — one root yields a dozen related words.

question: Latin 'aqua' means water and built a wide English vocabulary family. Which of these English words is NOT from 'aqua'?
answer: Equate — from Latin 'aequus' meaning equal or level, unrelated to water.
choices: Equate — from Latin 'aequus' meaning equal or level, unrelated to water.
Aquarium — from Latin 'aqua,' literally a water-tank for keeping fish and plants.
Aqueduct — from 'aqua' plus 'ductus,' an engineered channel for moving water.
Aquatic — from 'aqua,' an adjective for things that live or happen in water bodies.
context: Latin 'aqua' (water) gave English: AQUARIUM (water-tank), AQUEDUCT ('water-leading' — Roman engineering masterworks still standing in France and Spain), AQUATIC (water-dwelling), AQUAMARINE ('sea-water,' a pale blue-green gem and color), AQUIFER ('water-bearing,' an underground water layer), and the brand name AQUAFRESH. 'Equate' looks similar but comes from a different Latin root: 'aequus' (equal, level, even), which also gave English EQUATION, EQUITY, EQUIVALENT, EQUINOX ('equal night'). Latin's similar-sounding-but-unrelated roots are a constant trap for new etymologists.

question: Latin 'terra' (earth, land) is the root of a large English vocabulary family. Which of these English words descends from 'terra'?
answer: Subterranean — from 'sub-' (under) + 'terra' (earth), meaning located beneath the ground.
choices: Subterranean — from 'sub-' (under) + 'terra' (earth), meaning located beneath the ground.
Subordinate — from 'sub-' (under) + 'ordo' (rank), meaning lower in rank or position.
Submerge — from 'sub-' (under) + 'mergere' (to plunge), meaning to dip below the surface.
Submarine — from 'sub-' (under) + 'mare' (sea), meaning a vessel that travels under sea.
context: Latin 'terra' (earth, land, ground) gave English: TERRESTRIAL (of the earth), TERRITORY (originally 'land around a town'), TERRACE ('earthen platform'), TERRAIN ('lay of the land'), TERRA-COTTA ('cooked earth' — Italian for the fired clay), TERRIER (originally a dog that goes 'to earth' after burrowing prey), INTER ('put into the earth' — to bury), SUBTERRANEAN ('beneath the earth'), MEDITERRANEAN ('in the middle of the lands' — the sea between Europe, Africa, and Asia), EXTRATERRESTRIAL ('outside the earth'). The Romans saw 'terra' as opposed to 'mare' (sea); each gave its own large English word family.

question: Latin 'corpus' (body) built a wide English vocabulary family. Which of these English words is from 'corpus'?
answer: Incorporate — from 'in-' (into) + 'corpus' (body), originally meaning to form into a body.
choices: Incorporate — from 'in-' (into) + 'corpus' (body), originally meaning to form into a body.
Incorrigible — from 'in-' (not) + 'corrigere' (to correct), describing an unmanageable person.
Incomparable — from 'in-' (not) + 'comparare' (to compare), describing an unmatched quality.
Incoherent — from 'in-' (not) + 'cohaerere' (to stick together), describing disjointed speech.
context: Latin 'corpus' (body) gave English: CORPSE (a dead body), CORPORATION ('body of members' formed into one), CORPS (a military body — pronounced 'kor' in English), CORPULENT ('full-bodied' — heavyset), CORPUSCLE ('little body' — a blood cell), CORPSE (a dead body), CORPORATE, CORPOREAL ('having a body' — bodily, physical), INCORPORATE ('to form into a body' or 'to take into a body'), HABEAS CORPUS ('you shall have the body' — the legal writ requiring an arrested person to be brought before a judge). The word root sits at the foundation of English legal, business, and medical vocabulary.

question: Latin 'animus' (mind, spirit, breath) is the root of an English word family centered on mental life. Which of these English words is from 'animus'?
answer: Magnanimous — from 'magnus' (great) + 'animus' (spirit), meaning generous of spirit.
choices: Magnanimous — from 'magnus' (great) + 'animus' (spirit), meaning generous of spirit.
Magnificent — from 'magnus' (great) + 'facere' (to make), meaning made with grandeur.
Magnitude — from 'magnus' (great), meaning the great size or extent of a thing.
Magnify — from 'magnus' (great) + 'facere' (to make), meaning to enlarge in view.
context: Latin 'animus' (mind, spirit, breath, life-force) gave English: ANIMAL ('having breath' — living thing), ANIMATE ('to give life to'), ANIMATION (the art of giving the appearance of life), ANIMOSITY (hostile spirit), UNANIMOUS ('one mind' — all agreeing), MAGNANIMOUS ('great-spirited' — generous and forgiving), PUSILLANIMOUS ('small-spirited' — cowardly), EQUANIMITY ('level mind' — calm composure). The root also lies behind ANIMUS itself, used in English for hostile or aggressive feelings ('she bore him no animus'). The 'magn-' words come from a different root: 'magnus' (great).

question: Bishop Robert Lowth's 'Short Introduction to English Grammar' (1762) imposed several rules on English by analogy to Latin grammar. Which of the following 'rules' did Lowth or his contemporaries introduce that has since become controversial?
answer: Do not split infinitives — the rule that bans 'to boldly go' on the grounds that Latin infinitives are single words.
choices: Do not split infinitives — the rule that bans 'to boldly go' on the grounds that Latin infinitives are single words.
Do not double a negative — the rule, original to Old English, that two negatives cancel each other entirely.
Do not begin a sentence with 'and' — the rule, original to Anglo-Saxon, that bans coordinating conjunctions.
Do not capitalize common nouns — the rule, original to Middle English, that distinguishes the proper nouns.
context: Bishop Robert Lowth (1710-1787) wrote 'A Short Introduction to English Grammar' in 1762, applying Latin grammatical analysis to English. Several 'rules' he introduced have survived in the prescriptive tradition but have no native basis in English: no split infinitives (Latin infinitives are single words, so they can't be split — but English ones can be), no preposition at the end of a sentence (Latin doesn't strand prepositions; English does naturally), no double negatives (Old and Middle English used them for emphasis, as in 'I don't know nothing'). The double-negative ban was already declining before Lowth, but he reinforced it. Modern style guides have softened all three rules.

question: Noah Webster's 'An American Dictionary of the English Language' (1828) deliberately diverged from British spelling for nationalist reasons. Which of these spelling changes did Webster introduce as standard American?
answer: Color instead of colour — dropping the 'u' from many '-our' words that British English kept.
choices: Color instead of colour — dropping the 'u' from many '-our' words that British English kept.
Wisdom instead of wysdom — modernizing the 'y' in Old English words to the simpler 'i'.
Cheese instead of cheez — adding the silent 'e' to clarify the final consonant sound.
Light instead of lite — preserving the archaic 'gh' digraph instead of phonetic spelling.
context: Noah Webster (1758-1843) was a deliberate language reformer — a Federalist who believed a distinct American English would help unify the new nation and free it from British cultural dominance. His 1828 dictionary established American spelling conventions: drop the 'u' in -our words (color, honor, labor, favor); swap '-re' to '-er' in some words (center, theater, meter); drop the doubled 'l' in -eled/-eling words (traveled not travelled); use '-ize' for many verbs where British uses '-ise' (recognize, organize, realize). Some of his more radical proposed reforms (tung for tongue, wimmen for women, hed for head) failed to take.

question: The Oxford English Dictionary is famous for the length of time it took to compile its first complete edition. Begun in 1857, how long did the first complete edition take to publish?
answer: Seventy-one years — the first complete edition was published in 1928.
choices: Seventy-one years — the first complete edition was published in 1928.
One hundred years — the first complete edition was published in the year 1957.
Fifteen years — published quickly with a team of around 400 paid Oxford lexicographers.
Thirty-eight years — published just at the close of the Victorian era around 1895.
context: The Oxford English Dictionary was proposed by the Philological Society of London in 1857. James Murray became chief editor in 1879 and built a 'Scriptorium' (a corrugated-iron shed in his Oxford garden) where thousands of volunteer readers sent in quotation slips documenting word usage. Murray edited until his death in 1915; his successors completed the first edition in 1928. The OED's defining principle is historical: every word is illustrated by quotations showing its earliest use and changes in meaning. The original 'A Dictionary of Madness' connection: William Chester Minor, one of the most prolific contributors, was an inmate of Broadmoor Criminal Lunatic Asylum.

question: The past tense of 'go' is 'went' — completely unrelated to the verb 'go.' Linguists call this 'suppletion.' From which Old English verb did 'went' originally come?
answer: Wend — Old English 'wendan,' meaning to turn or wind one's way, surviving in 'wend my way.'
choices: Wend — Old English 'wendan,' meaning to turn or wind one's way, surviving in 'wend my way.'
Walk — Old English 'wealcan,' meaning to roll along, the original past tense of all motion verbs.
Wander — Old English 'wandrian,' meaning to roam, which donated its past form to 'go' around 1100.
Win — Old English 'winnan,' meaning to strive or labor, whose past 'wann' was reanalyzed as motion.
context: Suppletion is when unrelated word-stems share a paradigm. 'Went' is the past tense of 'wend' (Old English 'wendan,' to turn). The Old English past of 'go' was 'eode' or 'yode' — but this form sounded increasingly odd and gradually fell out of use between 1200 and 1500. English speakers grafted 'went' onto 'go' instead. 'Wend' kept the form 'wended' for itself, surviving in the formal 'I wend my way homeward.' The most extreme suppletion case in English is the verb 'be': am / is / are / was / were / been / being come from THREE different roots. English's most-used verbs are its most-irregular.

question: The English verb 'be' is the most suppletive in the language — its forms come from THREE different Proto-Indo-European roots. Which of these forms of 'be' descends from a root meaning 'to grow, to become'?
answer: 'Be' and 'been' — from the Proto-Indo-European root *bheue meaning to grow or become.
choices: 'Be' and 'been' — from the Proto-Indo-European root *bheue meaning to grow or become.
'Is' and 'are' — from the Proto-Indo-European root *bheue meaning to grow or become.
'Was' and 'were' — from the Proto-Indo-European root *bheue meaning to grow or become.
'Am' and 'art' — from the Proto-Indo-European root *bheue meaning to grow or become.
context: The verb 'be' is built from three Proto-Indo-European roots. *es- gave English 'is,' 'am,' 'are,' 'art' (and Latin 'est,' German 'ist,' Sanskrit 'asti'). *bheue- gave English 'be,' 'been,' 'being' (and Latin 'fui,' meaning 'I have been,' which is the 'f' in 'future'). *wes- gave English 'was,' 'were' (and Old English 'wesan'). When you conjugate 'I am, you are, he is, I was, we were, having been,' you're using verb-stems from three separate ancient roots — none of which mean the same thing originally. No other English verb is so thoroughly suppletive.

question: English's 'strong verbs' change tense by changing the vowel in the stem — 'sing/sang/sung,' 'drive/drove/driven.' Which of these verbs follows the same Old English strong-verb pattern?
answer: Ride / rode / ridden — the 'i / o / i' vowel shift inherited directly from Old English.
choices: Ride / rode / ridden — the 'i / o / i' vowel shift inherited directly from Old English.
Walk / walked / walked — adding the regular 'ed' ending for both past tense forms.
Watch / watched / watched — using the regular 'ed' suffix for both past tense forms.
Pull / pulled / pulled — using the regular 'ed' suffix for the past simple and participle.
context: English inherited about 200 'strong verbs' from Old English — verbs that mark tense by changing the stem vowel rather than adding -ed. The pattern groups: 'ride/rode/ridden,' 'drive/drove/driven,' 'write/wrote/written' (class I). 'Sing/sang/sung,' 'drink/drank/drunk,' 'swim/swam/swum' (class III). 'Speak/spoke/spoken,' 'break/broke/broken,' 'steal/stole/stolen' (class IV). Modern English has lost many strong verbs (chode chid chidden became chided chided; clomb climbed became climbed climbed climbed). The pressure of regularization is constant; only the most common strong verbs survive ('go,' 'do,' 'see,' 'know,' 'come' — all irregular).

question: Old English was written in two alphabets at different points. The earliest writing used runes (the futhorc), but by the time of King Alfred (around 880) most writing used a different alphabet. Which alphabet replaced the runes?
answer: The Latin alphabet — brought by Christian missionaries starting around 597 AD.
choices: The Latin alphabet — brought by Christian missionaries starting around 597 AD.
The Greek alphabet — brought by Byzantine monks in trade missions of the 8th century.
The Hebrew alphabet — brought by Jewish merchants who settled in coastal trade towns.
The Arabic alphabet — brought by Moorish scholars after the Spanish reconquest period.
context: Old English used two writing systems. The earliest was the FUTHORC — a runic alphabet inherited from Germanic peoples, used for inscriptions on stone, wood, and metal (about 29-33 runes). Christian missionaries, beginning with Augustine of Canterbury in 597 AD, brought the LATIN alphabet for book-writing. Old English scribes added a few letters the Latin alphabet lacked: 'thorn' (þ, the 'th' sound), 'eth' (ð, the voiced 'th'), 'ash' (æ, the 'a' in 'cat'), and 'wynn' (ƿ, the 'w' sound, later replaced by 'w'). The thorn survived in handwriting until the 1400s — its loss is why we have 'ye olde shoppe' (with 'y' written for thorn).

question: Old English had a letter called 'thorn' (þ) for the 'th' sound. It survived into Middle English in handwriting but disappeared from print. The thorn is the reason for an apparent oddity in modern English signage. Which oddity?
answer: 'Ye olde' signs — the 'y' is actually a misread thorn, so 'ye' was originally pronounced 'the.'
choices: 'Ye olde' signs — the 'y' is actually a misread thorn, so 'ye' was originally pronounced 'the.'
Silent 'gh' words — the 'gh' actually preserves the sound originally written with the thorn.
Double 'oo' words — the 'oo' actually preserves an early thorn-marked long vowel sound.
Capitalized 'I' — the lone capitalization in English comes from a tall variant of the thorn.
context: Old English thorn (þ) wrote the 'th' sound. When William Caxton brought the printing press from continental Europe in 1476, the type-pieces he imported had no thorn — so printers substituted 'y,' which in some handwritten styles looks similar to thorn. The 'y' wasn't pronounced as a 'y' in these contexts; it was a graphical stand-in for 'th.' The convention faded but left fossil signs: 'Ye Olde Shoppe' was pronounced 'the old shop' by everyone who could read it. The letter eth (ð) had a similar fate — both letters were unceremoniously dropped from English print, leaving the digraph 'th' to do double duty.

question: The Oxford English Dictionary contains the largest documented vocabulary of any language, but the number depends on how you count. Roughly how many distinct words does the current OED define?
answer: About 600,000 — including obsolete, dialectal, and technical terms across the language's history.
choices: About 600,000 — including obsolete, dialectal, and technical terms across the language's history.
About fifty thousand — close to the vocabulary that an average literate adult actively uses today.
About eight million — counting every recorded compound noun and proper noun ever printed.
About one hundred — counting only the very most fundamental short core words of the language.
context: The Oxford English Dictionary's second edition (1989) defined about 600,000 word-senses, with the online edition continuing to add new entries. Of these, roughly 170,000 are in current use; the rest are obsolete, archaic, dialectal, or highly technical. An educated native speaker knows about 20,000-35,000 words actively (productive vocabulary) and recognizes maybe 50,000-70,000 (receptive vocabulary). English's huge vocabulary comes from massive borrowing: Latin and Greek for science/medicine/law; Old French for governance/cuisine/military; Norse for everyday words (sky, leg, ill, take); world languages for specific items (pajamas, ketchup, robot, tycoon, algebra).

question: The word 'robot' entered English from a 1920 Czech play called 'R.U.R.' by Karel Capek. What does the Czech word 'robota' originally mean?
answer: Forced labor or drudgery — the kind of work serfs owed to their feudal lord.
choices: Forced labor or drudgery — the kind of work serfs owed to their feudal lord.
Iron servant or machine — an engineered helper made from metal and clockwork parts.
Robotic motion or pacing — a stiff, jerky way of moving like a wind-up toy soldier.
Worker bee or hive-mind — a colony member with no individual will of its own.
context: Karel Capek's 1920 play 'R.U.R.' (Rossum's Universal Robots) introduced the word 'robot' to world languages. The Czech 'robota' means hard labor — specifically the compulsory work that peasants owed to their lord under the feudal system in central Europe. Capek's robots in the play are not metal machines but artificial biological workers, mass-produced as cheap labor. Capek's brother Josef actually coined the term — Karel had been considering 'labori' from Latin 'labor.' The play was a smash hit, and 'robot' entered English by 1922. Czech also gave English 'pistol,' 'polka,' 'bohemian,' and 'howitzer.'

question: The word 'ketchup' entered English in the 1690s from a Chinese sauce-name carried through Malay traders. What did the original Chinese 'kê-tsiap' refer to?
answer: A fermented fish or shellfish sauce — the tomato version was a much later American innovation.
choices: A fermented fish or shellfish sauce — the tomato version was a much later American innovation.
A spicy pepper paste — the chili-base for many southern Chinese provincial dishes today.
A sweet plum jam — a fruit-based condiment served alongside roasted meat dishes everywhere.
A thick soy paste — the umami-rich preserve used for centuries in northern Chinese cooking.
context: 'Ketchup' is one of English's most surprising etymologies. The word came from southeast-Chinese 'kê-tsiap' (sometimes spelled 'kôe-chiap' in older sources) — a fermented fish sauce similar to Vietnamese 'nuoc mam' or Roman 'garum.' British traders encountered the sauce in Asia in the 1600s and brought the word home. English versions of 'ketchup' included walnut ketchup, mushroom ketchup, oyster ketchup, and lemon ketchup before tomato ketchup became dominant in the early 1800s. The Heinz Company's 1876 ketchup made the tomato version internationally famous. Today most English speakers don't know the word ever applied to anything but tomato sauce.

question: The word 'algebra' comes from a 9th-century Arabic mathematics treatise. What does the Arabic 'al-jabr' literally mean?
answer: The reunion of broken parts — a metaphor for restoring an equation by moving its terms.
choices: The reunion of broken parts — a metaphor for restoring an equation by moving its terms.
The arithmetic of numbers — the basic study of counting and ordering whole quantities.
The wisdom of letters — the symbolic representation of unknown values by letter codes.
The mathematics of triangles — the geometric study of figures with three sides equally.
context: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780-850) of Baghdad wrote 'Kitab al-Jabr wa-l-Muqabala' (The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing) around 820 AD. The term 'al-jabr' literally means 'reunion of broken parts' — al-Khwarizmi used it to describe his technique of moving a subtracted term from one side of an equation to the other, restoring the equation's balance. The word entered medieval Latin as 'algebra' and reached English by the 1500s. Al-Khwarizmi's own name, Latinized, gave English 'algorithm.' Arabic also gave English: alcohol, alchemy, alkali, almanac, azimuth, zenith, nadir, cipher, zero.

question: The word 'zero' entered English from Arabic via Italian, but the Arabic word itself meant something physically concrete. What did 'sifr' originally mean in Arabic?
answer: Empty — a translation of the Sanskrit 'shunya,' meaning emptiness or the absence of value.
choices: Empty — a translation of the Sanskrit 'shunya,' meaning emptiness or the absence of value.
Number — a generic term for any quantity used in the calculations of Arabic mathematics.
Beginning — the starting position from which all the higher numbers are counted forward.
Round — a description of the visual shape of the digit, distinct from other letters.
context: The concept of zero as a number — distinct from the absence of a number — was developed in India by mathematicians like Brahmagupta (628 AD). The Sanskrit word for it was 'shunya' (emptiness). Arabic mathematicians borrowed both the concept and translated the word as 'sifr' (empty). 'Sifr' entered Latin as 'cifra' and Italian as 'zefiro' or 'zero,' arriving in English by the 1600s. The same Arabic word 'sifr' also gave English 'cipher,' which originally meant zero, then a generic numeral, then a coded message. The two English descendants of the same Arabic word now mean very different things.

question: The English word 'tycoon' (a powerful businessman) came from Japanese in the 1850s. What did the Japanese 'taikun' originally mean?
answer: Great lord — a title used by foreign envoys for the Japanese military ruler, the shogun.
choices: Great lord — a title used by foreign envoys for the Japanese military ruler, the shogun.
Great merchant — the head of a major trading house in the Edo period commercial cities.
Great warrior — a samurai of the highest rank who led private armies for landed lords.
Great teacher — a master of philosophy whose disciples spread his school across Japan.
context: 'Tycoon' came into English from Japanese 'taikun' (大君) — literally 'great lord' or 'great prince.' Foreign envoys used the title for the SHOGUN (the military ruler of Japan) during negotiations in the 1850s, since calling him 'king' would imply equality with their own monarchs. Matthew Perry's expedition (1853-54) brought the word to American attention. By the 1860s 'tycoon' was a nickname for Abraham Lincoln among his cabinet ('the Tycoon'), used affectionately for a strong leader. It shifted to mean 'powerful businessman' in the early 1900s and stuck there. Japanese also gave English: tsunami, karaoke, sushi, emoji, honcho.

question: The Great Vowel Shift (1400-1700) moved English long vowels upward in the mouth. Geoffrey Chaucer pronounced his word 'time' to rhyme with the modern English word for which beverage?
answer: Team — Middle English 'time' had a long-e sound that rhymed with what we now spell 'team.'
choices: Team — Middle English 'time' had a long-e sound that rhymed with what we now spell 'team.'
Tame — Middle English 'time' had a long-a sound that rhymed with what we now spell 'tame.'
Tame — Middle English 'time' had a long-a sound that rhymed with what we now spell 'name.'
Tomb — Middle English 'time' had a long-o sound that rhymed with what we now spell 'tomb.'
context: Middle English 'time' was pronounced something like 'teem' /tiːm/ — the long-i vowel was a high front /iː/, the same sound modern English spells 'ee.' During the Great Vowel Shift, this /iː/ moved up and could not rise further, so it 'broke' into the diphthong /aɪ/ that modern English spells with the letter 'i.' Similarly, Middle English 'house' /huːs/ (rhyming with modern 'hoose') became /haʊs/. The pattern: long-e moved to long-i; long-i diphthongized to /aɪ/; long-a moved to long-e; long-u diphthongized to /aʊ/. Reading Chaucer aloud properly requires un-doing the Great Vowel Shift.

question: Linguists divide the history of English into three main periods: Old English, Middle English, and Modern English. Roughly what time spans do these cover?
answer: Old English 450-1100, Middle English 1100-1500, Modern English 1500 to today.
choices: Old English 450-1100, Middle English 1100-1500, Modern English 1500 to today.
Old English 0-500, Middle English 500-1000, Modern English 1000 to today (the past millennium).
Old English 800-1200, Middle English 1200-1700, Modern English 1700 to today (since Lowth).
Old English 1066-1500, Middle English 1500-1800, Modern English 1800 to today (since Webster).
context: The three traditional periods of English: OLD ENGLISH (Anglo-Saxon, c. 450-1100) — Germanic base, brought by Angles, Saxons, and Jutes from continental Europe; mostly unreadable today without training; Beowulf is the canonical text. MIDDLE ENGLISH (c. 1100-1500) — heavy Norman French influence after 1066; Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (1387) is the canonical text; readable with effort. MODERN ENGLISH (c. 1500-present) — sometimes split into Early Modern (1500-1700, Shakespeare and the King James Bible) and Late Modern (1700-present). The boundaries are gradual; each is a convenience for historical study, not a sharp linguistic break.

question: The English word 'decimate' originally had a precise mathematical meaning from Roman military discipline. What fraction did it originally signify?
answer: One in ten — the Roman punishment killed exactly one tenth of a mutinous legion by lot.
choices: One in ten — the Roman punishment killed exactly one tenth of a mutinous legion by lot.
One in fifty — the Roman punishment killed roughly one fiftieth of a mutinous legion by lot.
One in two — the Roman punishment killed exactly half of a mutinous legion by random lot.
One in twenty — the Roman punishment killed exactly one twentieth of a mutinous legion by lot.
context: 'Decimate' comes from Latin 'decimus' (tenth) — the Roman military punishment killed exactly one in ten soldiers, chosen by lot, with the surviving nine forced to carry out the executions. It was rare, reserved for grave offenses like cowardice or mutiny. The most famous historical instance: Marcus Licinius Crassus decimated his troops after their defeat by Spartacus's army (71 BC). Modern English has broadened 'decimate' to mean 'destroy a large portion of,' which usage purists object to but most style guides now accept. The semantic shift from 'exactly 10%' to 'a large amount' shows how a precise technical term can drift into a vague intensifier.

question: The English word 'awful' has shifted meaning entirely over the centuries. What did 'awful' mean in early Bible translations (1500s-1600s)?
answer: Inspiring awe or reverence — full of the kind of dread one feels before God.
choices: Inspiring awe or reverence — full of the kind of dread one feels before God.
Inspiring laughter or mirth — full of the kind of joy one shares with children.
Inspiring sleep or boredom — full of the kind of dullness one finds in a long sermon.
Inspiring hunger or appetite — full of the kind of pleasure one finds in a feast.
context: 'Awful' is the classic pejoration example — a word whose meaning slid from positive to negative over centuries. In Middle English and Early Modern English, 'awful' meant 'inspiring awe' — full of awe, in the same way 'powerful' means full of power. The King James Bible used it of God; sunsets and mountains were 'awful' in admiring poetry. By the 1800s the negative sense ('terrible, bad') had taken over. The same pattern produced 'terrific' (originally 'causing terror'; now 'wonderful' — amelioration in the opposite direction), 'awesome' (which has been making the inverse trip from 'inspiring fear' to 'great' in modern slang).

question: The English word 'silly' has flipped meaning to nearly the opposite of where it started. What did 'silly' mean in Old English ('sælig')?
answer: Blessed, holy, or innocent — the word that gave us 'sælig' originally meant blessed by God.
choices: Blessed, holy, or innocent — the word that gave us 'sælig' originally meant blessed by God.
Wealthy, powerful, or proud — the word originally described the lord of a wealthy estate.
Strong, sturdy, or unwavering — the word originally described a healthy and hardy person.
Loud, boisterous, or rowdy — the word originally described a noisy and unruly behavior.
context: 'Silly' is one of the most dramatic semantic shifts in English. The Old English ancestor 'sælig' meant 'blessed, happy, fortunate, holy.' Through Middle English it shifted: 'blessed' became 'innocent' (since the blessed are innocent), 'innocent' became 'simple,' 'simple' became 'foolish,' and 'foolish' became the modern 'silly.' The whole journey took about six centuries and produced one of the most extreme pejorations in English. Other words that traveled the same downhill path: 'fond' (originally 'foolish,' now 'loving'); 'crazy' (originally 'cracked' as of pottery, then 'mentally unstable'). The reverse path is rarer.

question: The English word 'nice' has shifted meaning four or five times in its journey from Latin to modern English. What did 'nice' mean when first borrowed into Middle English (1200s)?
answer: Foolish or silly — from Latin 'nescius' meaning 'not-knowing,' ignorant.
choices: Foolish or silly — from Latin 'nescius' meaning 'not-knowing,' ignorant.
Kind or pleasant — from Latin 'nitidus' meaning shining, polished, refined.
Beautiful or pretty — from Latin 'nivea' meaning snow-white and clean.
Friendly or warm — from Latin 'nicere' meaning to nod or wink in greeting.
context: 'Nice' comes from Latin 'nescius' (literally 'not-knowing,' from 'ne-' + 'scire' to know). In Middle English (1200s-1400s), 'nice' meant foolish, simple-minded, or silly. By the 1500s the meaning shifted toward 'careful' or 'precise' (as in 'a nice distinction' — still surviving in formal writing). By the 1700s it had moved to 'agreeable, pleasant.' By the 1800s it landed on its modern meaning: kind and friendly. The amelioration journey — from insult to compliment — took six centuries. 'Nice' is the canonical example of a word whose modern meaning would baffle its medieval users.

question: The English word 'terrific' has shifted meaning over the centuries. What did 'terrific' originally mean when it entered English in the 1600s?
answer: Causing terror or fear — frightening, dreadful, the way 'horrific' still means today.
choices: Causing terror or fear — frightening, dreadful, the way 'horrific' still means today.
Causing thirst or hunger — describing food that excites strong appetite of the eater.
Causing temperature change — describing cold winters or hot summers in equal measure.
Causing thought or wonder — describing puzzles that demanded careful study to resolve.
context: 'Terrific' descends from Latin 'terrere' (to frighten) — the same root that gave English 'terror' and 'terrify.' In its 1660s English debut, 'terrific' meant 'causing terror' — a sublimely scary kind of awe. Over the 1800s it weakened to 'great in size or intensity' (a terrific storm) and then shifted to 'wonderful, excellent' in the early 1900s. The amelioration is parallel to 'awesome' (which is still completing the same journey). The reverse path was traveled by 'awful' (once 'inspiring awe,' now 'bad'). English speakers casually use both endpoints of these shifts without noticing the contradiction.

question: The English word 'literally' has expanded to mean its own opposite — a shift that enrages usage purists. What is the older, traditional meaning of 'literally'?
answer: Word for word, in the strictest exact sense — meaning to the letter.
choices: Word for word, in the strictest exact sense — meaning to the letter.
Quickly and decisively, without delay — meaning to act in the moment.
Quietly and respectfully, with dignity — meaning to speak with restraint.
Privately and confidentially, behind closed doors — meaning to keep a secret.
context: 'Literally' comes from Latin 'litera' (letter). Its original strict meaning is 'word for word' or 'to the letter' — the opposite of 'figuratively.' Since at least the 1700s, English speakers have used 'literally' as an intensifier, often in figurative statements ('I was literally dying of laughter'). Authors including Mark Twain, James Joyce, and F. Scott Fitzgerald used 'literally' this way. The OED added the intensifier sense in 2011, causing prescriptivist outcry. The figurative use is now centuries old and increasingly unstoppable — though careful writing still distinguishes literal from figurative.

question: The English word 'fond' meant something quite different in Middle English than in modern usage. What did 'fond' originally mean?
answer: Foolish or naive — the same root as 'fonne,' a Middle English word for a fool.
choices: Foolish or naive — the same root as 'fonne,' a Middle English word for a fool.
Distant or estranged — the opposite of close, describing a once-warm relationship now cold.
Doubtful or hesitant — the opposite of confident, describing tentative emotional commitment.
Hopeful or wishful — close to the modern sense but without the affectionate connection.
context: 'Fond' comes from Middle English 'fonned' — the past participle of 'fonnen' meaning 'to be foolish.' The semantic journey: 'foolish' became 'foolishly affectionate' (the foolish doter doting on the object of affection) then narrowed to plain 'affectionate.' The shift is mostly complete by Shakespeare's time, though traces of the older sense linger: 'a fond hope' still means a hope held with foolish confidence; 'fondle' (to handle affectionately) carries a hint of the original silliness. The pattern matches 'silly' (blessed -> foolish) and 'nice' (foolish -> pleasant). Each is a journey of centuries.

question: The English word 'pajamas' came from Hindi-Urdu via British India in the 1800s. What is the literal meaning of the Persian-rooted original?
answer: Leg-garment — from Persian 'pay' (leg) plus 'jama' (garment), describing loose trousers.
choices: Leg-garment — from Persian 'pay' (leg) plus 'jama' (garment), describing loose trousers.
Night-shirt — from Persian 'shab' (night) plus 'jama' (garment), worn for sleeping.
Soft-cloth — from Persian 'narm' (soft) plus 'jama' (garment), describing comfortable wear.
Sleep-cover — from Persian 'khwab' (sleep) plus 'jama' (garment), worn only in bed.
context: British colonial officials and soldiers in India encountered loose drawstring trousers called 'pay-jama' (Persian roots 'pay' = leg, 'jama' = garment). They borrowed both the trousers and the word; by 1800, 'pajamas' (American spelling) or 'pyjamas' (British) had entered English, originally meaning the loose Indian trousers worn around the house. The meaning extended to a matching nightshirt-and-trouser sleep outfit by the late 1800s. Other words English took from Hindi-Urdu: shampoo (from 'champo,' a massage), bungalow (from 'bangla,' a house in the Bengali style), jungle, loot, thug, guru, bandana, dungaree, juggernaut.

question: The English word 'assassin' comes from a 13th-century Arabic name for a Shia Islamic sect. What does the Arabic 'hashishin' literally mean?
answer: Hashish-users — a term applied to a militant sect by their enemies, though it may be a slur.
choices: Hashish-users — a term applied to a militant sect by their enemies, though it may be a slur.
Mountain-dwellers — describing the high fortress monasteries from which the sect operated.
Faithful-servants — describing the sect's religious devotion to their hidden imam leader.
Sword-bearers — describing the curved blades typically carried by the sect's warriors.
context: The Order of Assassins (the Nizari Isma'ilis) was a Shia Islamic sect operating in mountain fortresses in Persia and Syria from about 1090 to 1273. Their most famous tactic was infiltration and targeted killing of political and religious enemies — Sunni viziers, Crusader leaders. European Crusaders called them 'Assassini' from Arabic 'hashishin,' a term used by hostile contemporaries. Whether they actually used hashish is disputed; the name may be a slur. Marco Polo's 'Travels' (c. 1300) spread the story to medieval Europe. The word 'assassin' meaning 'political murderer' was widespread in English by the 1500s. It is one of many Arabic words that entered English through the Crusades.

question: The English word 'loot' (stolen goods) entered English in the 1700s from Hindi via British soldiers. What did the Hindi 'lut' originally signify?
answer: Plunder or stolen goods — the wartime booty taken by victors from the defeated.
choices: Plunder or stolen goods — the wartime booty taken by victors from the defeated.
Treasure or gold coin — the wealth stored by Indian rulers in temple vaults.
Heavy cargo — the trade goods carried in the holds of merchant ships at sea.
Family inheritance — the property a man left to his sons after his death.
context: 'Loot' is one of dozens of words English took from Hindi during British colonial rule in India. The Hindi 'lut' (plunder, spoils) came from Sanskrit 'lotra,' meaning the same. British soldiers picked up the term in the 1700s and brought it home; it appeared in English print by 1788. The verb 'to loot' (to plunder, especially in war or civil unrest) followed by 1840. Other Hindi-origin words in English: jungle, bungalow, pajamas, shampoo, thug, guru, bandana, dungaree, juggernaut, cushy, pucker, pukka. The vocabulary doubling parallels the older Norman-French doubling of 1066 — colonial contact moves words across languages in volume.

question: The English word 'thug' came from Hindi in the early 1800s. What was a 'thugee' in 19th-century India?
answer: A member of a network of ritual highway-robbers and murderers operating across India.
choices: A member of a network of ritual highway-robbers and murderers operating across India.
A wealthy merchant who controlled the spice trade routes in northern Indian provinces.
A peasant farmer who paid annual tribute to the local British colonial administrators.
A spiritual teacher who collected donations from devotees at major Hindu temple sites.
context: 'Thug' comes from Hindi 'thag' (a deceiver, swindler) and entered English through the British colonial campaign against 'Thuggee' — networks of ritual highway-robbers who strangled travelers on Indian roads from the 1300s to the early 1800s. The British colonial administrator William Sleeman led the suppression campaign (1830-1840), and reports of the Thuggee networks were widely read in Britain. By 1839 'thug' was being used in English for any violent criminal. The word's path: from Sanskrit 'sthaga' (cunning) to Hindi 'thag' to English 'thug,' carrying its meaning of dangerous deceiver intact across three languages and two thousand years.

question: The English word 'shampoo' comes from Hindi and originally had nothing to do with hair washing. What did the Hindi 'champo' originally mean?
answer: To press or massage — a vigorous head massage was the original Indian custom borrowed.
choices: To press or massage — a vigorous head massage was the original Indian custom borrowed.
To rinse or splash — describing the bathing rituals of Hindu temples in northern India.
To color or dye — describing the henna-and-oil hair treatments of Mughal noblewomen.
To plait or braid — describing the hair styling of Indian courtesans of the period.
context: 'Shampoo' comes from Hindi 'champo' — the imperative of 'champna,' to press or knead. The word originally referred to a vigorous head and body massage with herbal oils, common in Indian bathing rituals. Sake Dean Mahomed opened a 'shampooing surgery' (massage parlor) in Brighton, England in 1814, marketing the treatment to British patrons. By the late 1800s, 'shampoo' had narrowed to mean the hair-washing soap-and-water treatment that often accompanied the massage. The original massage meaning is gone from English. The product name now means only the cleaning agent, not the massage that gave it its name.

question: English's everyday vocabulary — the words we use most often — is overwhelmingly Germanic in origin. Which of the following English words came from Old English (Anglo-Saxon)?
answer: Water — from Old English 'wæter,' inherited from Proto-Germanic and used continuously.
choices: Water — from Old English 'wæter,' inherited from Proto-Germanic and used continuously.
Liquid — from Old English 'liquidus,' inherited from Proto-Germanic and used continuously.
Aqua — from Old English 'aqua,' inherited from Proto-Germanic and used continuously.
Ocean — from Old English 'oceanus,' inherited from Proto-Germanic and used continuously.
context: English's everyday vocabulary is overwhelmingly Germanic — the short, common words for human life. Old English roots: house, home, hand, foot, eye, ear, water, fire, sun, moon, day, night, food, eat, drink, sleep, walk, speak, think, know, man, woman, child, father, mother. Latin and Greek words (liquid, aqua, ocean, illuminate) tend to be longer and more formal. The pattern in English: short Germanic word + longer Latin synonym = different register (kingly/royal, brotherly/fraternal, motherly/maternal). Writers use the Germanic for warmth and directness; the Latin for formality and abstraction.

question: English often has two words for the same concept — one Germanic (everyday) and one Latin/French (formal). Which Germanic-Latin pair shows this pattern correctly?
answer: Kingly (Germanic) and royal (Latin via French) — both meaning 'pertaining to a king.'
choices: Kingly (Germanic) and royal (Latin via French) — both meaning 'pertaining to a king.'
Reading (Germanic) and writing (Latin via French) — both meaning 'involving text.'
Walking (Germanic) and running (Latin via French) — both meaning 'moving on foot.'
Sleeping (Germanic) and dreaming (Latin via French) — both meaning 'resting at night.'
context: English has many doublets — synonym pairs from different historical sources, often with different registers. Germanic-Latin/French pairs: kingly/royal, motherly/maternal, brotherly/fraternal, fatherly/paternal, fishy/piscine, deep/profound, hearty/cordial, hidden/concealed, freedom/liberty, friend/companion, room/chamber, ask/inquire, end/conclude, begin/commence. The Germanic words feel warmer and more direct; the Latin/French words feel more formal and abstract. Writers exploit this for tone — 'kingly bearing' has a different register than 'royal dignity.' The doubling is the legacy of 1066 — the Norman vocabulary layered onto the Anglo-Saxon foundation without erasing it.

question: Samuel Johnson's 'Dictionary of the English Language' (1755) was the first major English dictionary aimed at usage. How long did Johnson spend compiling it, working largely alone?
answer: Nine years — Johnson had estimated three but the work expanded as it went.
choices: Nine years — Johnson had estimated three but the work expanded as it went.
Forty years — Johnson devoted most of his adult life to this single magnum opus.
One year — Johnson worked rapidly with a small team to complete it on commission.
Twenty-five years — Johnson took on the project as a young man and finished it middle-aged.
context: Samuel Johnson (1709-1784) accepted a contract in 1746 to compile a dictionary of English. He estimated three years; the job took nine. His 'A Dictionary of the English Language' (1755) defined about 40,000 words, with usage illustrated by quotations from English literature — a method that the OED would later adopt at scale. Johnson worked with six assistants in a London garret. His definitions are famously opinionated ('oats: a grain which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people'). Johnson's dictionary was the English standard until the OED began publication in 1884.

question: Many English words came from Yiddish, mostly through Jewish immigrants to America in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Which of these English words is Yiddish in origin?
answer: Klutz — from Yiddish 'klots,' meaning a clumsy person, literally 'a wooden block.'
choices: Klutz — from Yiddish 'klots,' meaning a clumsy person, literally 'a wooden block.'
Klatch — from Yiddish 'klatzch,' meaning a public square or village gathering place.
Knapsack — from Yiddish 'knappel,' meaning a small leather bag worn over the shoulder.
Knish — from Yiddish 'knesset,' meaning a council or assembly of community elders.
context: Yiddish (the Jewish language of central and eastern Europe, German-based with Hebrew, Slavic, and Aramaic elements) gave English many words through immigration to America. Examples: chutzpah (audacity), schmooze (chat intimately), schlep (drag, lug), schmaltz (sentimentality, literally chicken fat), klutz (clumsy person), bagel, blintz, knish, kvetch (complain), kosher, mensch (a person of integrity), nosh (snack), shmear, schtick, tchotchke (trinket), maven (expert). Many Yiddish words add an irreverent or affectionate tone to English unavailable from native vocabulary. New York Jewish English carried most into general use.

question: The phrase 'apple of his eye' (meaning a treasured person) is one of many idioms the King James Bible (1611) made standard in English. Which book of the Bible does the phrase come from?
answer: Deuteronomy — 'He kept him as the apple of his eye' (Deuteronomy 32:10).
choices: Deuteronomy — 'He kept him as the apple of his eye' (Deuteronomy 32:10).
Revelation — 'A new heaven and a new earth' (Revelation 21:1), the closing book.
Matthew — 'Blessed are the meek' (Matthew 5:5), part of the Sermon on the Mount.
Genesis — 'And God said, Let there be light' (Genesis 1:3), the very opening.
context: The KJV (1611) shaped English idiom more than any other single book except Shakespeare. The 'apple of the eye' was an ancient Hebrew metaphor for the pupil — the most carefully guarded part of the body — and meant something precious. From the KJV: 'salt of the earth' (Matthew 5:13), 'cast pearls before swine' (Matthew 7:6), 'fly in the ointment' (Ecclesiastes 10:1), 'a thorn in the flesh' (2 Corinthians 12:7), 'wolf in sheep's clothing' (Matthew 7:15), 'powers that be' (Romans 13:1), 'beat their swords into ploughshares' (Isaiah 2:4), 'writing on the wall' (Daniel 5:5). English speakers use these constantly without knowing their source.

question: The word 'scapegoat' (a person blamed for the failings of others) entered English from the King James Bible (1611). What was the original ritual it described in Leviticus?
answer: A goat sent into the wilderness on Yom Kippur, symbolically carrying the people's sins away.
choices: A goat sent into the wilderness on Yom Kippur, symbolically carrying the people's sins away.
A goat sacrificed at the entrance to the temple, blood used to mark the doorposts.
A goat kept tethered outside a city gate, marking the boundary of the holy ground.
A goat bought from a foreign merchant, used to test the honesty of the marketplace.
context: 'Scapegoat' was coined by William Tyndale in his 1530 English translation of the Pentateuch, used by the KJV in Leviticus 16. The Hebrew text describes the Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement) ritual: two goats are chosen; one is sacrificed; the other has the people's sins symbolically transferred to it by the high priest, then is driven into the wilderness, carrying the sins away. Tyndale rendered the Hebrew 'azazel' (the destination or recipient) as 'scape-goat' (escape-goat). The figurative sense — 'someone blamed for others' wrongs' — is in English by the 1820s. The Bible is full of words coined by Tyndale and inherited from him by the KJV.

question: The phrase 'the powers that be' (the people in authority) comes from a specific verse of the King James Bible. Which apostle wrote the relevant verse?
answer: Paul — 'the powers that be are ordained of God' (Romans 13:1), a much-debated political verse.
choices: Paul — 'the powers that be are ordained of God' (Romans 13:1), a much-debated political verse.
Peter — 'fear God and honor the king' (1 Peter 2:17), the apostolic command to civic respect.
John — 'render unto Caesar' (Revelation 13:7), a vision of authority over the nations.
Matthew — 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (Matthew 14:6), a teaching of Christ.
context: Romans 13:1 — 'Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God' — is one of the New Testament's most politically debated verses. Paul wrote it from Corinth around 56 AD, addressing Christians in Rome about civic obligation under the Roman empire. The KJV's translation (1611) put 'the powers that be' into common English; the phrase has remained a fixed idiom for 'those in authority,' often used skeptically or wryly. The verse itself has been cited by political authorities of every kind defending themselves, and by Christians grappling with whether obedience extends to unjust rulers.

question: English has the doublet 'freedom' and 'liberty,' which mean nearly the same thing but feel different. Which language gave English which word?
answer: Freedom is Old English (freodom); liberty is Latin via French (libertas, liberte).
choices: Freedom is Old English (freodom); liberty is Latin via French (libertas, liberte).
Both words came from Old English (freodom and libertus), one preserved by ecclesiastics.
Both words came from Latin (libertas and libratus), arriving in two waves of borrowing.
Freedom is Latin via French (freedomus); liberty is Old English (libertyge), restored later.
context: 'Freedom' is from Old English 'freodom' (free + suffix -dom, like 'kingdom' or 'wisdom'). 'Liberty' is from Latin 'libertas' via Old French 'liberte.' The doublet is one of many such pairs in English — same concept, different registers. The Germanic word feels warmer and more personal ('freedom of speech,' 'set me free'); the Latin word feels more formal and political ('the Statue of Liberty,' 'civil liberties'). Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty or give me death' uses the formal register; the abolitionist hymn 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee' uses the warmer 'sweet land of liberty.' Same meaning, different rhetorical effect.

question: Estimates vary, but how many words does the average English-speaking adult know actively (productively use in speech and writing)?
answer: About twenty to thirty-five thousand words — though estimates depend on counting method.
choices: About twenty to thirty-five thousand words — though estimates depend on counting method.
About one to two thousand words — most adult speech draws on a fairly compact core.
About one hundred to two hundred thousand words — comparable to the OED current-use entries.
About six hundred thousand words — equal to the total entries in the Oxford English Dictionary.
context: Vocabulary estimates vary because 'knowing a word' is hard to define. An educated adult native speaker actively uses about 20,000-35,000 words (productive vocabulary — used in speech and writing) and recognizes 50,000-75,000 (receptive vocabulary — understood when heard or read). The OED's 170,000 current-use entries include technical, dialectal, and obsolete words most speakers never encounter. A toddler might know 200 words at 18 months; a five-year-old might know 5,000. Reading is the strongest predictor of vocabulary growth across childhood. The advantage in vocabulary between the most and least readers grows continuously through life.

question: A 'false friend' (faux ami) is a word that looks the same in two languages but means different things. Which of these French words is a classic false friend for English speakers?
answer: Library in French is 'librairie,' but it actually means a bookstore, not a lending library.
choices: Library in French is 'librairie,' but it actually means a bookstore, not a lending library.
Restaurant in French is 'restaurant,' but it actually means only a fast-food eatery.
Hotel in French is 'hotel,' but it actually means a roadside motel for car travelers.
Garage in French is 'garage,' but it actually means a public market for fresh produce.
context: False friends (faux amis) are pairs of words that look identical across languages but have diverged in meaning. French-English examples: 'librairie' (bookstore, not library — French for library is 'bibliotheque'); 'sympathique' (likeable, not sympathetic); 'eventuellement' (possibly, not eventually); 'demander' (to ask, not to demand); 'assister a' (to attend, not to assist); 'actuellement' (currently, not actually); 'sensible' (sensitive, not sensible). False friends often arise when shared Latin or French roots take different semantic paths in each language. They trip up learners — and confident polyglots — constantly.

question: The Viking invasions of the 9th and 10th centuries left English with many common Old Norse words. Which everyday English verb came from Old Norse?
answer: Take — from Old Norse 'taka,' which replaced the Old English 'niman' between 1100 and 1300.
choices: Take — from Old Norse 'taka,' which replaced the Old English 'niman' between 1100 and 1300.
Eat — from Old Norse 'ata,' which replaced the Old English 'etan' in the 9th century.
Walk — from Old Norse 'gangr,' which replaced the Old English 'wealcan' after Norse contact.
Live — from Old Norse 'lifa,' which replaced the Old English 'libban' after the Conquest.
context: The Viking Age (8th-11th centuries) brought Scandinavian settlers to large parts of northern and eastern England. Old Norse words entered English in large numbers — many displacing native Old English equivalents. Norse-origin words in modern English: take (replaced 'niman'), get, give, both, same, want, call, die, leg, skin, sky, egg, knife, husband, wife, anger, raise, root, window. The Norse 'sk-' words (sky, skill, skin, skirt) often have Old English 'sh-' cognates (sheen, shirt). The Norse words tend to be short and everyday — they integrated into the most basic vocabulary. They're invisible because they don't 'feel' foreign.

question: The English pronouns 'they,' 'them,' and 'their' came from Old Norse. Why did English speakers borrow even basic pronouns from the Vikings?
answer: The native Old English pronouns sounded similar to other pronouns, causing confusion.
choices: The native Old English pronouns sounded similar to other pronouns, causing confusion.
The Vikings outlawed the use of native English pronouns under their political occupation.
Old English had no plural pronouns at all, so the Norse forms filled an empty grammar slot.
Christian missionaries imposed the Norse pronouns to standardize Bible translation work.
context: Old English had its own third-person plural pronouns ('hie,' 'hira,' 'him') which sounded confusingly similar to the singular pronouns ('he,' 'her,' 'him' — and yes, Old English already had 'him'). Contact with Old Norse speakers in the Danelaw (northern and eastern England, c. 9th-11th centuries) introduced the Norse forms 'they' (þeir), 'them' (þeim), 'their' (þeira). The Norse pronouns were phonetically distinct from the singular ones and gradually replaced the Old English plurals between 1200 and 1500. Borrowing CORE grammatical words like pronouns is rare across languages — it took centuries of intimate bilingual contact for this to happen.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.'
answer: Chiasmus — mirror-image inversion of paired terms (A-B then B-A).
choices: Chiasmus — mirror-image inversion of paired terms (A-B then B-A).
Anaphora — repetition of an opening word across successive clauses.
Epistrophe — repetition of an ending word across successive clauses.
Antithesis — sharp contrast within an otherwise parallel structure.
context: Chiasmus reverses the order of paired elements between two clauses: A (country-you) then B (you-country). Kennedy's 1961 inaugural line is the most famous American example. The name comes from the Greek letter chi (X), shaped to map the criss-cross of the figure. Other chiasmus examples: 'When the going gets tough, the tough get going'; 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' (Macbeth); 'The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath' (Mark 2:27); 'It is not the years in your life that count, it is the life in your years.' Chiasmus is one of rhetoric's most memorable patterns.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'He ran and jumped and laughed and shouted and danced for joy.'
answer: Polysyndeton — deliberately using many conjunctions where one would do for rhythm.
choices: Polysyndeton — deliberately using many conjunctions where one would do for rhythm.
Asyndeton — deliberately omitting conjunctions to produce a compact rapid force.
Anaphora — repeating the same opening word across multiple successive clauses.
Polyptoton — repeating the same root in different grammatical forms throughout.
context: Polysyndeton piles on conjunctions ('and ... and ... and') where standard usage would drop them. The effect is cumulative weight or breathless excitement. Ernest Hemingway used polysyndeton constantly — his prose strings clauses with 'and' instead of subordinating them ('The Old Man and the Sea' opens with such a sentence). The King James Bible uses it heavily too: 'And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house' (Matthew 7:25). The opposite figure is asyndeton (Caesar's 'Veni, vidi, vici' — no 'and'). Both are choices about rhythm, not grammar.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in Caesar's famous: 'Veni, vidi, vici' — 'I came, I saw, I conquered.'
answer: Asyndeton — deliberately omitting conjunctions to produce compact rapid force.
choices: Asyndeton — deliberately omitting conjunctions to produce compact rapid force.
Polysyndeton — deliberately using many conjunctions where one would do for rhythm.
Anaphora — repeating the same opening word across multiple successive clauses.
Tricolon — arranging the same idea in three parallel clauses of similar length.
context: Asyndeton (Greek 'unconnected') omits conjunctions where standard usage would put them. 'I came, I saw, I conquered' has no 'and' — the bare verbs hit harder. Julius Caesar reportedly said this after his lightning victory over Pharnaces II at Zela (47 BC). Lincoln used asyndeton in the Gettysburg Address: 'we cannot dedicate, we cannot consecrate, we cannot hallow this ground.' Modern advertising loves it: 'Eat. Sleep. Repeat.' The opposite figure is polysyndeton (piling on conjunctions). Both are rhetorical choices about pacing.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in Churchill's June 1940 speech: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets.'
answer: Anaphora — repeating the same opening words across successive clauses.
choices: Anaphora — repeating the same opening words across successive clauses.
Epistrophe — repeating the same ending words across successive clauses.
Chiasmus — mirror-image inversion of paired terms across a sentence.
Asyndeton — omitting conjunctions to produce compact rapid force.
context: Anaphora repeats opening words across successive clauses ('We shall fight ... we shall fight ... we shall fight'). Churchill's speech to Parliament on June 4, 1940 — three weeks after the Dunkirk evacuation, while Britain stood alone against Nazi Germany — used anaphora to build defiant momentum, culminating in the most famous resolve in 20th-century rhetoric. Other anaphora: Martin Luther King's 'I have a dream' (repeated eight times in the August 1963 speech); Dickens's 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' (start of A Tale of Two Cities). The opposite figure is epistrophe (repetition at the END of clauses).

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in Lincoln's closing line of the Gettysburg Address: 'government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.'
answer: Epistrophe — repeating the same ending words across successive clauses.
choices: Epistrophe — repeating the same ending words across successive clauses.
Anaphora — repeating the same opening words across successive clauses.
Polysyndeton — piling on conjunctions where one or none would do.
Hyperbaton — inverting the standard subject-verb-object word order.
context: Epistrophe repeats words at the END of successive clauses ('of the people, by the people, for the people'). Lincoln's Gettysburg Address (November 19, 1863) ended with this triplet, condensing the principle of democratic government into nine words. Other famous epistrophe: Paul's 1 Corinthians 13:11 — 'When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child'; Sojourner Truth's 1851 speech — 'Ain't I a woman?' (repeated four times). Epistrophe is the opposite of anaphora; both rely on repetition for emphasis. Together they can frame a single sentence: 'In her was found life, by her was found peace, through her was found joy.'

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'She is not unintelligent' or 'That was no small feat.'
answer: Litotes — affirmation by denying the contrary, a deliberate understatement.
choices: Litotes — affirmation by denying the contrary, a deliberate understatement.
Hyperbole — extreme exaggeration of a quality for rhetorical effect.
Metonymy — substituting a closely associated term for the actual subject.
Synecdoche — using a part of something to represent the whole thing.
context: Litotes (Greek 'simplicity') affirms by denying the opposite — 'not unintelligent' means 'intelligent,' but with cooler restraint. The figure is associated with Old English and Norse understatement: Beowulf is full of it. Modern English examples: 'not bad' (good); 'no small feat' (a big achievement); 'I am not unhappy' (I'm content); 'It's no small matter' (it's serious); 'She is not without ambition' (she's ambitious). The figure works because the denial pretends to be less assertive than direct affirmation — but the listener parses the double negative and arrives at a meaning that often feels stronger for being indirect.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in Dickens's opening of A Tale of Two Cities: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.'
answer: Antithesis — contrast within a parallel grammatical structure.
choices: Antithesis — contrast within a parallel grammatical structure.
Chiasmus — mirror-image inversion of paired terms across a sentence.
Oxymoron — a single compact pairing of two contradictory words.
Asyndeton — omitting conjunctions to produce compact rapid force.
context: Antithesis sets contrasting ideas in parallel grammatical structures — 'best of times, worst of times.' The figure is older than Greek rhetoric (it appears in Hebrew Psalms and Sumerian poetry). Dickens's 1859 opening continues the pattern through ten parallel pairings ('it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness; it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity'). Other antithesis: 'Many are called, but few are chosen' (Matthew 22:14); 'To err is human, to forgive divine' (Pope); 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind' (Armstrong). Antithesis is grammatically loose chiasmus — paired contrast without the criss-cross inversion.

question: Yoda from Star Wars is famous for sentences like 'Powerful you have become.' What rhetorical figure does Yoda employ?
answer: Hyperbaton — inverting the standard word order for stylistic or rhetorical effect.
choices: Hyperbaton — inverting the standard word order for stylistic or rhetorical effect.
Anaphora — repeating the same opening word across successive clauses.
Antithesis — placing contrasting ideas in a parallel grammatical structure.
Litotes — affirming by denying the contrary for understated effect.
context: Hyperbaton inverts standard English word order — 'Powerful you have become' instead of 'You have become powerful.' Yoda speaks in Object-Subject-Verb order (OSV), one of the rarest patterns in world languages. The effect is alien and emphatic. English uses hyperbaton occasionally for emphasis: 'Brave he was, and quick'; 'Beautiful was the morning.' Latin and Old English used it freely because their grammar relied on inflectional endings rather than word order, so the order could shift for rhythm or focus. The Yoda speech pattern works because the listener can still parse the sentence — it's just unmistakably marked as non-standard.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'Easy come, easy go.'
answer: Isocolon — clauses of equal length and parallel grammatical structure.
choices: Isocolon — clauses of equal length and parallel grammatical structure.
Tricolon — clauses or items arranged in groups of three of similar length.
Anaphora — repeating the same opening words across successive clauses.
Litotes — affirming by denying the contrary for understated effect.
context: Isocolon (Greek 'equal limb') uses clauses of approximately equal length and parallel grammar. 'Easy come, easy go' — two two-word clauses, same shape. The pleasure of isocolon is its balance, and it's a workhorse of advertising, proverbs, and aphorism. Other examples: 'No pain, no gain'; 'Like father, like son'; 'Out of sight, out of mind'; 'First come, first served'; 'Live and let live.' When isocolon produces three parallel clauses, it becomes TRICOLON. The figure depends on rhythm — the listener feels the balance. Even slight changes in length break the effect.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in Jefferson's phrase from the Declaration of Independence: 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.'
answer: Tricolon — three parallel words or clauses arranged in a triple of similar weight.
choices: Tricolon — three parallel words or clauses arranged in a triple of similar weight.
Isocolon — two parallel clauses of approximately equal length and shape.
Anaphora — repeating the same opening words across successive clauses.
Polysyndeton — piling on conjunctions to slow the rhythm of speech.
context: Tricolon arranges words or clauses in threes — a structure the ear finds satisfying. Jefferson's 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness' (Declaration of Independence, 1776) is the most famous American example. Caesar's 'Veni, vidi, vici' is also a tricolon (the three verbs also forming an asyndeton). Lincoln's 'of the people, by the people, for the people' is a tricolon AND an epistrophe. Other tricolons: 'wine, women, and song'; 'father, son, and holy spirit'; 'reading, writing, and arithmetic'; 'sun, sea, and sand'; 'mind, body, and soul.' The pattern is so deep-rooted that listeners notice when a rhetorical climb stops at two or runs to four.

question: Identify the syntactic style in: 'I came home. I ate dinner. I went to bed. I slept badly.'
answer: Parataxis — short coordinate clauses placed side by side, with little subordination.
choices: Parataxis — short coordinate clauses placed side by side, with little subordination.
Hypotaxis — clauses arranged with extensive subordination and embedded structure.
Anaphora — the same opening word repeated across each successive clause.
Polysyndeton — piling on conjunctions between every clause to slow the rhythm.
context: Parataxis (Greek 'placing side by side') strings coordinate clauses without subordinating one to another. 'I came home. I ate dinner. I went to bed.' is parataxis; 'After coming home and eating dinner, I went to bed, having found the meal unsatisfactory' is hypotaxis. Hemingway's prose is famously paratactic, as is the King James Bible and most folk-tale narration. Hypotaxis (with its embedded clauses) is the style of Cicero, Henry James, and academic English. The choice is rhetorical: parataxis feels brisk and direct; hypotaxis feels complex and reflective. Both styles have produced great prose.

question: Identify the syntactic style in: 'After he had finished his work, which had taken him several hours longer than expected because of the unforeseen complications, he went to bed.'
answer: Hypotaxis — clauses arranged with extensive subordination and embedded structure.
choices: Hypotaxis — clauses arranged with extensive subordination and embedded structure.
Parataxis — short coordinate clauses placed side by side without subordination.
Polysyndeton — piling on conjunctions across coordinate clauses for slow rhythm.
Asyndeton — dropping conjunctions across coordinate clauses for fast rhythm.
context: Hypotaxis (Greek 'arrangement under') subordinates clauses to one another — a main clause with multiple dependent clauses embedded inside it. Latin prose (Cicero, Caesar) is heavily hypotactic; classical English prose (Edward Gibbon, Henry James) imitates it. The example sentence has a main clause ('he went to bed') buried under three dependents. Hypotaxis can carry complex argument and qualification but slows the pace. Parataxis is the opposite — fast, simple, side-by-side. Both styles have prestige eras: Latin schools taught hypotaxis; 20th-century American minimalism (Hemingway, Carver) revived parataxis. Most prose mixes both.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'He stole my heart and my wallet.'
answer: Zeugma — one verb governs two nouns in different senses (literal and figurative here).
choices: Zeugma — one verb governs two nouns in different senses (literal and figurative here).
Hyperbole — extreme exaggeration of a quality for rhetorical effect.
Metonymy — substituting an associated word for the actual subject.
Personification — attributing human qualities to a non-human noun.
context: Zeugma (Greek 'yoke') joins two nouns under one verb where the verb operates differently on each — usually one literally, the other figuratively. 'He stole my heart and my wallet' — stole literally (the wallet) and figuratively (the heart). Other classic zeugma: 'She broke his car and his heart'; 'He took his hat and his leave'; 'You are free to execute your laws and your citizens as you see fit' (Star Trek's Captain Kirk). Charles Dickens loved zeugma: 'Miss Bolo went home in a flood of tears and a sedan chair.' The figure is closely related to syllepsis — both depend on a single word doing double duty in different senses.

question: Identify the rhetorical device in: 'Marriage is his Achilles' heel.'
answer: Allusion — a brief indirect reference to a person, place, event, or work known to the audience.
choices: Allusion — a brief indirect reference to a person, place, event, or work known to the audience.
Metaphor — a direct comparison stating one thing is another, without 'like' or 'as.'
Hyperbole — an extreme exaggeration of a quality for rhetorical effect.
Personification — attributing human qualities to non-human nouns or objects.
context: Allusion is a glancing reference to a person, event, or work the audience is expected to recognize without explanation. 'His Achilles heel' alludes to Homer's Iliad — Achilles, dipped in the river Styx by his mother, was invulnerable everywhere except the heel she held him by. 'Achilles' heel' now means 'a critical weakness' in someone otherwise strong. Other common English allusions: 'Catch-22' (Joseph Heller's novel); 'good Samaritan' (Luke 10); 'opening Pandora's box' (Greek myth); 'the Midas touch' (Greek myth); 'a Solomon's choice' (1 Kings 3); 'Big Brother is watching' (Orwell's 1984); 'a Pyrrhic victory' (King Pyrrhus's costly wins). Allusion is the rhetoric of shared cultural memory.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'All hands on deck!'
answer: Synecdoche — a part stands for the whole (hands stand for the sailors as a whole).
choices: Synecdoche — a part stands for the whole (hands stand for the sailors as a whole).
Metonymy — substituting an associated thing for the actual subject (crown for king).
Hyperbole — exaggeration of a quality for rhetorical or emotional effect.
Litotes — affirming by denying the contrary for understated emphasis.
context: Synecdoche (Greek 'taking together') uses a part to stand for the whole, or the whole for a part. 'All hands on deck' uses 'hands' for the sailors who possess them. Other part-for-whole synecdoche: 'a fleet of fifty SAILS' (ships); 'count NOSES' (people); 'give him a HAND' (applause); 'wheels' (a car); 'boots on the ground' (soldiers). Whole-for-part also exists: 'AMERICA won the gold medal' (the American athlete, not the whole country). Synecdoche is often confused with metonymy, but synecdoche specifically involves part-whole relationships; metonymy uses any associated word ('the CROWN' for monarchy).

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'The White House announced new sanctions.'
answer: Metonymy — substituting an associated thing for the subject (White House for the administration).
choices: Metonymy — substituting an associated thing for the subject (White House for the administration).
Synecdoche — using a part of something to stand for the whole thing it belongs to.
Personification — attributing human action to a non-human building or place.
Hyperbole — exaggeration of a quality for rhetorical or emotional effect.
context: Metonymy (Greek 'change of name') substitutes a closely associated thing for the subject itself. 'The White House' doesn't literally announce sanctions — the executive branch's officials do; but the building is so closely associated with the office that the building's name stands in. Other metonymy: 'the CROWN' (monarchy); 'WALL STREET' (American finance); 'the PENTAGON' (US military); 'HOLLYWOOD' (the American film industry); 'the SUITS' (corporate executives); 'the BENCH' (judges); 'the PRESS' (journalists); 'the CHURCH' (the institution). Metonymy differs from synecdoche: synecdoche is part-whole specifically; metonymy is any associative substitution.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'deafening silence' or 'bittersweet.'
answer: Oxymoron — a compact pairing of two seemingly contradictory terms.
choices: Oxymoron — a compact pairing of two seemingly contradictory terms.
Paradox — a longer statement that seems self-contradictory but reveals a truth.
Antithesis — contrast within an otherwise parallel grammatical structure.
Hyperbole — exaggeration of a quality for rhetorical or emotional effect.
context: Oxymoron (Greek 'pointedly foolish') pairs two terms that seem to contradict — and yet together capture a real experience. 'Deafening silence' (so total it feels physical); 'bittersweet' (mixed pleasure and sorrow); 'jumbo shrimp' (large among small); 'pretty ugly'; 'living dead'; 'cruel kindness'; 'civil war'; 'open secret'; 'organized chaos'; 'controlled chaos'; 'serious joke.' Shakespeare loved oxymorons; Romeo's speech on love runs through dozens. The longer figure 'paradox' makes a whole statement contradict itself ('I always lie'; 'this sentence is false') — an oxymoron is the compact two-word version.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'Less is more' (the architect Mies van der Rohe).
answer: Paradox — a statement that seems self-contradictory but reveals a deeper truth.
choices: Paradox — a statement that seems self-contradictory but reveals a deeper truth.
Oxymoron — a compact two-word pairing of contradictory terms in juxtaposition.
Antithesis — contrast within a parallel grammatical structure between two clauses.
Hyperbole — extreme exaggeration of a quality for rhetorical or emotional effect.
context: Paradox is a statement that contradicts itself on the surface but reveals a deeper truth. Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's 'less is more' (popularized in 1947 about architectural design) means restraint produces stronger results than embellishment. Other paradox: 'I know that I know nothing' (Socrates); 'The first shall be last' (Matthew 19:30); 'I must be cruel to be kind' (Hamlet); 'Standing is more tiring than walking' (a physiological fact). Paradox differs from oxymoron in length: oxymoron is compact ('deafening silence'); paradox is a full proposition. Both depend on apparent contradiction yielding to insight.

question: Identify the rhetorical figure in: 'The wind whispered through the trees.'
answer: Personification — attributing human qualities or actions to non-human things.
choices: Personification — attributing human qualities or actions to non-human things.
