question: Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg published 'Higher Lessons in English' in 1877. Their grammar textbook introduced a visual technique that became standard in American schools through the 20th century. Their diagrams used what visual logic?
answer: A horizontal baseline carrying subject and verb; verticals and slants attaching modifiers and dependent elements.
choices: A horizontal baseline carrying subject and verb; verticals and slants attaching modifiers and dependent elements.
Concentric circles, with each ring representing a deeper level of grammatical complexity in the sentence.
Branching trees, analogous to modern syntactic trees with nodes for every word in the sentence.
Numbered lists, with each sentence rewritten as a stack of grammatical roles from top to bottom.
context: Reed-Kellogg diagrams put the subject and verb on a horizontal baseline, separated by a vertical line. Modifiers attached on diagonal lines below the words they modified. Direct objects sat on the baseline to the right of the verb, separated by a short vertical. Prepositional phrases dangled on diagonals. Dependent clauses sat on their own baselines beneath the main one. The system gave students a visual way to see how sentences hang together — and a quick way to spot dangling modifiers and unclear references. Sentence diagramming was a staple of American English instruction from the 1880s through the 1970s; it has faded from many curricula but is enjoying a revival in homeschooling and classical-education programs.

question: Noah Webster's 'American Dictionary of the English Language' (1828) was a deliberately nationalist project — distinguishing American English from British English. Which of Webster's spelling reforms succeeded and remain American standard today?
answer: Dropping 'u' in -our words (color, labor, honor) and reversing -re to -er (center, theater).
choices: Dropping 'u' in -our words (color, labor, honor) and reversing -re to -er (center, theater).
Replacing every 'c' with 'k' (kreate, klock, klimb) and dropping all silent letters.
Removing all double letters wholesale (mising for missing, butter for butter, etc.).
Spelling all words exactly as pronounced, eliminating English spelling's historical layers.
context: Webster proposed many spelling reforms in his 1828 dictionary; most failed. The ones that stuck: -or for -our (color, labor, honor, neighbor); -er for -re (center, theater, fiber); -ize for -ise in many verbs (organize, realize); dropping final 'e' on some words (axe → ax); -se for -ce (defense, offense, license). Webster also proposed 'wimmen' for 'women,' 'tung' for 'tongue,' 'iz' for 'is,' and 'fether' for 'feather' — none of these took. American spelling is a partial Webster project — bold enough to mark identity but conservative enough not to break readability with older texts.

question: James Murray became the editor of the Oxford English Dictionary in 1879. He worked in a corrugated-iron shed at his home — known as the Scriptorium — for over 40 years. How did Murray collect the millions of quotations needed to define every English word historically?
answer: Through a worldwide army of volunteer readers who mailed slips with cited usages from old and new texts.
choices: Through a worldwide army of volunteer readers who mailed slips with cited usages from old and new texts.
Through a paid staff of researchers based at Oxford working on commercial salaries throughout the project.
Through the British Library's holdings alone, using only books in the central Oxford collection of texts.
Through computer-aided scanning of Victorian-era newspapers using punch-card analysis systems for parsing.
context: Murray's Scriptorium received millions of paper slips, each carrying a single dated quotation that illustrated a word's use. Volunteers — anyone who answered Murray's call for readers — were assigned books to read, copying out interesting words and their contexts onto slips and mailing them in. At its peak the OED had hundreds of contributors worldwide. Murray's filing system organized the slips alphabetically and by word; the lexicographers worked from these to write entries that traced each word's history with attestations across centuries. The first edition was completed in 1928, fifty years after Murray began, three years after his death.

question: One of the OED's most prolific volunteer contributors was Dr. William Chester Minor — an American Civil War veteran who sent in tens of thousands of slips over 20 years. Where was Minor living when he made his contributions?
answer: Broadmoor Criminal Lunatic Asylum, where he had been confined after killing a man in a paranoid delusion in London in 1872.
choices: Broadmoor Criminal Lunatic Asylum, where he had been confined after killing a man in a paranoid delusion in London in 1872.
Oxford University, where he held a quiet lectureship in classics after immigrating from Connecticut.
A Yorkshire farmhouse, where he had retired from medicine after distinguished Civil War service.
The British Museum's reading room, where he held a paid researcher post for over twenty years.
context: William Chester Minor (1834-1920) was a Yale-trained American surgeon who had served in the Civil War, where he was traumatized by his battlefield experiences. After moving to London in 1871, his deepening paranoia led him to shoot a stranger he believed was tormenting him. Found not guilty by reason of insanity, he was confined to Broadmoor Asylum. There, with access to books bought through the asylum's library system and his own pension, Minor began contributing to the OED. Murray and Minor corresponded for years before Murray learned where his most prolific contributor was actually living. Their story is told in Simon Winchester's 'The Professor and the Madman' (1998).

question: Bishop Robert Lowth's 'Short Introduction to English Grammar' (1762) sold tens of thousands of copies. What did Lowth believe was the proper purpose of an English grammar?
answer: To teach correct usage to readers — explicitly prescriptive: telling them how they should speak and write.
choices: To teach correct usage to readers — explicitly prescriptive: telling them how they should speak and write.
To record how educated speakers actually spoke — a descriptive enterprise based on observation.
To preserve Old English forms — a backward-looking project of grammatical archaeology.
To compare English systematically with French — a comparative project for translators only.
context: Lowth was explicit about his prescriptive purpose. He thought English needed correction: writers were prone to errors that Latin and Greek would have prevented. His 'Short Introduction' opens by stating its goal is to teach 'what is right' by 'showing what is wrong.' He drew on classical grammar's authority and applied its categories to English wherever he could — sometimes producing artificial rules (split-infinitive ban, preposition-stranding ban) but also genuinely useful guidance (subject-verb agreement, pronoun case). His book was the standard English grammar textbook for over a century, shaping every subsequent prescriptive grammar.

question: Lindley Murray's 'English Grammar' (1795) sold over 20 million copies in the 19th century — likely the most-printed English grammar of all time. What was Murray's relationship to Robert Lowth?
answer: Murray adapted and expanded Lowth's grammar for a wider audience; his book became the standard schoolroom text.
choices: Murray adapted and expanded Lowth's grammar for a wider audience; his book became the standard schoolroom text.
Murray rejected Lowth's prescriptive approach in favor of a Webster-style descriptivist account of usage.
Murray and Lowth were rivals, and Murray's grammar deliberately contradicted Lowth's at every single point.
Murray taught Lowth at Oxford; Murray's grammar was the original Lowth based his entire later work on.
context: Lindley Murray (1745-1826) was an American-born Quaker lawyer who moved to England for his health and turned to writing grammars. His 'English Grammar' (1795) borrowed heavily from Lowth (whom Murray credited) but presented the material more accessibly, with exercises and examples geared to school use. Murray's book was the schoolroom standard for the entire 19th century — over 20 million copies sold, in the US and Britain. Through Murray's textbook, Lowth's prescriptive rules became the rules every American and British schoolchild learned. The 'Murrayan tradition' shaped English-language education well into the 20th century.

question: Samuel Johnson's 'Dictionary of the English Language' (1755) preceded Webster's American Dictionary by 73 years and was the most influential English dictionary of its time. Johnson's definition of 'oats' has become famous. What did he write?
answer: 'A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people.'
choices: 'A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people.'
'A common cereal of the genus Avena cultivated in temperate climates for fodder use.'
'A foodstuff suitable for breakfast preparation when boiled in water with sugar and milk.'
'A cheap grain unworthy of human consumption in any nation except as a last resort.'
context: Johnson's dictionary is full of voice — sometimes acerbic, often opinionated, occasionally affectionate. His definition of 'oats' jabs the English-Scottish relationship of his era. 'Lexicographer' he famously defined as 'A writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge.' 'Excise' he called 'a hateful tax levied upon commodities, and adjudged not by the common judges of property, but wretches hired by those to whom excise is paid.' These editorial flashes are part of what made the book a literary as well as a reference work. Johnson worked alone with six clerks for nine years to produce it — a feat the French Academy had attempted with 40 lexicographers and given up.

question: Careful writers distinguish 'imply' from 'infer.' Which sentence pair uses both words correctly?
answer: The senator implied that the deal had collapsed; from her tone, the reporter inferred a leadership crisis.
choices: The senator implied that the deal had collapsed; from her tone, the reporter inferred a leadership crisis.
The senator inferred that the deal had collapsed; from her tone, the reporter implied a leadership crisis.
The senator inferred that the deal had collapsed; the reporter inferred a leadership crisis from this.
The senator implied that the deal had collapsed; the reporter implied a leadership crisis from this.
context: Speakers and writers IMPLY (suggest without saying directly); listeners and readers INFER (draw a conclusion from what they hear or read). The senator hints; the reporter deduces. The confusion is so frequent that 'infer' meaning 'imply' is now Stage 3 in Garner's Language-Change Index — widespread but resisted by careful writers. The distinction is worth keeping because it tracks an important asymmetry — between what's communicated by a speaker and what's reconstructed by a listener. Reverse the words and the sentence becomes nonsense.

question: Pick the sentence using 'principal' and 'principle' correctly in academic context.
answer: The school principal cited a fundamental principle of fairness in her ruling.
choices: The school principal cited a fundamental principle of fairness in her ruling.
The school principle cited a fundamental principal of fairness in her ruling.
The school principal cited a fundamental principal of fairness in her ruling.
The school principle cited a fundamental principle of fairness in her ruling.
context: Mnemonic: the principal is your 'pal' (ends in -PAL); a principle is a rule (ends in -LE). 'Principal' is also an adjective meaning 'main' or 'chief' ('the principal reason'), and a noun for the lead in a financial transaction ('paying down principal vs interest'). 'Principle' is always a noun meaning a fundamental rule or law. The confusion is one of the most common educated-writer typos — the two words sound identical and overlap conceptually (both come from Latin 'princip-' meaning 'first'). Careful writers double-check.

question: An academic writer drafts: 'Whose responsible for this committee report?' What's wrong, and how do you fix it?
answer: It should be 'Who's' — a contraction of 'who is.' 'Whose' is the possessive ('Whose pen is this?').
choices: It should be 'Who's' — a contraction of 'who is.' 'Whose' is the possessive ('Whose pen is this?').
It should be 'Who' — neither possessive nor contracted form is correct in the subject role here.
It should be 'Whom' — the object form is required after an interrogative pronoun like that.
It should remain 'Whose' — the possessive form is actually correct in the subject position here.
context: 'Who's' = 'who is' or 'who has' (contraction, apostrophe stands in for missing letters). 'Whose' = possessive form of 'who' (no apostrophe, like 'his,' 'her'). 'Who's responsible?' = 'Who is responsible?' (Path the substitution test: 'Who is responsible for this?' — yes, makes sense.) 'Whose pen is this?' = 'Pen belongs to whom?' (Substitution test: 'Who is pen is this?' — nonsense; so the possessive is right.) The trap is identical to its/it's and your/you're — the apostrophe ALWAYS signals a contraction in English pronouns, never the possessive.

question: The verbs 'lie' (recline) and 'lay' (place) are notoriously confused. In formal writing, which sentence uses the past-participle form of 'lie' correctly?
answer: The map has lain on my desk for three weeks, untouched.
choices: The map has lain on my desk for three weeks, untouched.
The map has laid on my desk for three weeks, untouched.
The map has lay on my desk for three weeks, untouched.
The map has layed on my desk for three weeks, untouched.
context: The full paradigms: LIE (recline, no object) — lie / lay / lain / lying. LAY (place, takes an object) — lay / laid / laid / laying. The trap: 'lay' is the SIMPLE PAST of 'lie' AND the present of 'lay.' 'I lie down now; I lay down yesterday; I have lain there for hours.' Vs: 'I lay the book down now; I laid the book down yesterday; I have laid the book down many times.' A map LIES on a desk (nobody is currently placing it). For the perfect tense, the participle of 'lie' is 'lain' — 'has lain' — a form that sounds archaic but remains the standard in formal writing.

question: The 'fewer vs less' rule has played a role in actual legal cases. In Oakhurst Dairy v. O'Connor (Maine, 2017), the absence of a single Oxford comma in a state labor law cost the company about $5 million. What did the missing comma create ambiguity about?
answer: Whether 'packing for shipment or distribution' was one activity or two activities, affecting overtime pay.
choices: Whether 'packing for shipment or distribution' was one activity or two activities, affecting overtime pay.
Whether dairy products counted as 'agricultural' or 'manufactured' goods under Maine state labor law.
Whether the workers were 'employees' or 'independent contractors' under their original work contract.
Whether the company's main office was in Portland or in Boston for tax-jurisdiction filing purposes.
context: Maine's overtime law exempted 'the canning, processing, preserving, freezing, drying, marketing, storing, packing for shipment or distribution of' certain agricultural products. The drivers argued: with no Oxford comma between 'shipment' and 'or distribution,' 'packing for shipment or distribution' was a single combined activity (packing) — and DISTRIBUTION standing alone was NOT in the exempt list. So drivers (who distributed but didn't pack) were entitled to overtime. The First Circuit Court of Appeals agreed in 2017. Maine paid out about $5 million. Maine subsequently revised its drafting style — they now use semicolons between list items to avoid future ambiguity. The Oxford comma's most expensive omission.

question: In formal English typography, the em-dash, the en-dash, and the hyphen are three different marks with three different uses. Which usage is correct?
answer: Em-dash for breaks in thought; en-dash for ranges (1995-2025); hyphen for compounds (well-known).
choices: Em-dash for breaks in thought; en-dash for ranges (1995-2025); hyphen for compounds (well-known).
All three marks are interchangeable in any context; the distinctions are typographic convention only.
Em-dash for ranges only; en-dash for breaks only; hyphen for everything else in standard writing.
Em-dash for compounds; en-dash for emphasis; hyphen for ranges in dates and times always.
context: Three marks, three uses. EM-DASH (—, the longest): strong breaks, interruption, emphasis, attribution — 'She ran — and ran — until she could go no further.' Some style guides set it close (no space); others (Oxford, AP) use thin spaces around it. EN-DASH (–, medium length): ranges and connections — '1995–2025,' 'New York–London flight,' '4–2 score.' HYPHEN (-, shortest): compound words and modifiers — 'well-known,' 'mother-in-law,' '21-year-old.' Most word processors auto-convert hyphens to em-dashes; careful typesetting respects the three-mark distinction.

question: The ellipsis (three dots) has three legitimate uses in careful writing. Which sentence uses it incorrectly?
answer: The package arrived . . . on time . . . exactly as promised by the shipper.
choices: The package arrived . . . on time . . . exactly as promised by the shipper.
Lincoln wrote: 'Four score and seven years ago . . . a new nation, conceived in liberty.'
She paused, then murmured, 'I'm not sure how to say this . . .' and let the words trail.
'Did you hear what she . . .' He stopped, suddenly aware that everyone was listening.
context: Three legitimate ellipsis uses: (1) OMISSION FROM QUOTATION — three dots show that text was cut from a quote ('Four score and seven years ago . . . a new nation'). (2) TRAILING-OFF THOUGHT — three dots end a sentence the speaker doesn't finish ('I'm not sure how to say this . . .'). (3) INTERRUPTION — three dots show a sentence cut off mid-thought, often by another speaker ('Did you hear what she . . .'). What ellipses should NOT do is interrupt prose to mark pauses for dramatic effect (the first choice). That use is journalistic and casual; in formal writing it's regarded as ungrammatical. Use commas or em-dashes for emphasis pauses; reserve ellipsis for genuine omission or trailing-off.

question: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma. Which sentence shows a comma splice?
answer: She finished her research, the deadline was tomorrow.
choices: She finished her research, the deadline was tomorrow.
She finished her research; the deadline was tomorrow.
She finished her research because the deadline was tomorrow.
She finished her research. The deadline was tomorrow.
context: A comma splice glues two complete sentences together with only a comma — and that's not enough. Fixes: (1) Replace the comma with a SEMICOLON ('She finished her research; the deadline was tomorrow') — works when the two clauses are closely related. (2) Replace the comma with a PERIOD ('She finished her research. The deadline was tomorrow') — works always. (3) Add a CONJUNCTION after the comma ('She finished her research, because the deadline was tomorrow') — subordinates one clause. (4) Use a COORDINATING CONJUNCTION ('She finished her research, and the deadline was tomorrow'). Comma splices are common in casual writing; in formal prose they're regarded as a defect.

question: A run-on sentence joins two independent clauses with no punctuation at all. Which sentence is a run-on (not a comma splice — no punctuation)?
answer: She finished her research the deadline was tomorrow.
choices: She finished her research the deadline was tomorrow.
She finished her research, the deadline was tomorrow.
She finished her research; the deadline was tomorrow.
She finished her research because the deadline was tomorrow.
context: RUN-ON (fused sentence): two independent clauses with no punctuation — 'She finished her research the deadline was tomorrow.' Reads as a single garbled sentence. COMMA SPLICE: two independent clauses with only a comma — 'She finished her research, the deadline was tomorrow.' Less wrong than a run-on but still a defect in formal writing. Fix either with a period, a semicolon, a conjunction, or by subordinating one clause. The distinction matters because the errors have slightly different reading experiences — run-ons feel like the writer rushed through; comma splices feel like the writer paused but didn't commit to ending the sentence. Both signal the same underlying issue: the writer hasn't decided whether these are two sentences or one.

question: Correlative conjunctions ('both . . . and,' 'either . . . or,' 'neither . . . nor,' 'not only . . . but also') require parallel structure. Which sentence is parallel?
answer: She enjoys not only reading novels but also writing poetry.
choices: She enjoys not only reading novels but also writing poetry.
She not only enjoys reading novels but also to write poetry.
She enjoys not only reading novels but also poetry to write.
She not only enjoys novels but also writes poetry on weekends.
context: Correlative conjunctions act as a matched pair. Whatever follows the first half should match in form (noun phrase, verb phrase, clause) whatever follows the second half. 'Not only READING novels but also WRITING poetry' — both halves are -ing verb phrases acting as direct objects of 'enjoys.' Match. The other options scramble the parallelism: putting different parts of speech or different grammatical roles on each side of the correlative breaks the rhythm and signals careless construction. Parallel structure is one of the highest-leverage tools in formal writing — it makes sentences clearer, more rhythmic, and faster to read.

question: American usage distinguishes restrictive 'that' from non-restrictive 'which' — but this is not a universal English rule. Which sentence uses the American convention correctly?
answer: The book that I read last summer is on the shelf; the book, which I bought used, was a bargain.
choices: The book that I read last summer is on the shelf; the book, which I bought used, was a bargain.
The book which I read last summer is on the shelf; the book, that I bought used, was a bargain.
The book that I read last summer is on the shelf; the book that I bought used was a bargain.
The book which I read last summer is on the shelf; the book which I bought used was a bargain.
context: American convention (Fowler, Strunk, Chicago, AP): use THAT for restrictive clauses (no commas, essential to meaning — 'the book THAT I read last summer' identifies WHICH book); use WHICH for non-restrictive clauses (with commas, extra information — 'the book, WHICH I bought used, was a bargain' adds a fact about an already-identified book). British usage is more relaxed — both can introduce restrictive clauses; the comma alone signals the restrictive/non-restrictive distinction. Garner's index puts the American distinction at Stage 4 (widely observed in formal writing but increasingly contested). The COMMA is doing most of the semantic work; the that/which is the secondary signal.

question: Semicolons join two independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction. But they have a second, less-known use. Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly in its second function?
answer: Conference attendees came from Boston, Massachusetts; Lima, Peru; and Kyoto, Japan.
choices: Conference attendees came from Boston, Massachusetts; Lima, Peru; and Kyoto, Japan.
Conference attendees came; from Boston, Lima, and Kyoto; representing three continents.
Conference attendees came from Boston; Lima; Kyoto; and many other cities worldwide.
Conference attendees; from Boston, Lima, and Kyoto; represented many time zones.
context: The semicolon's main job is joining two independent clauses without a conjunction — 'She finished her research; the deadline was tomorrow.' Its second job: separating items in a list when the items themselves contain commas. 'Boston, Massachusetts; Lima, Peru; and Kyoto, Japan' — three city-country items, each containing an internal comma; semicolons let the reader see where each item begins and ends. Without them: 'Boston, Massachusetts, Lima, Peru, and Kyoto, Japan' — five items? Three? The semicolons rescue the list's structure. This use is common in legal writing, academic citations, and technical prose.

question: The 'fewer vs less' distinction has cultural traction. In 2008, a major British grocery chain changed its express checkout signs from 'Ten items or less' to 'Up to ten items' after sustained customer pressure. Which choice describes that change accurately?
answer: The chain (Tesco) avoided the fewer/less debate by rewording the sign to skip the contested word entirely.
choices: The chain (Tesco) avoided the fewer/less debate by rewording the sign to skip the contested word entirely.
The chain (Tesco) changed the sign to 'Ten items or fewer' to match careful-writing conventions exactly.
The chain (Tesco) declared 'less' fully correct and refused to make any change to its signs.
The chain (Tesco) wrote 'Less items, please' as a deliberate provocation to its grammarian critics.
context: Tesco's sign rewrite is a real episode often cited in usage commentary. The chain had used 'Ten items or less' (the colloquial form) on express-lane signs for years; pressure from customers who pointed out that 'fewer' was the prescribed form for countable items led to a change. Tesco chose neither to capitulate to the prescriptivist 'fewer' nor to defend 'less' but to reword the sign to 'Up to ten items' — sidestepping the debate. The episode illustrates how usage controversies can become commercial irritants and how clever editors find third-way solutions. The fewer/less rule itself, as noted, traces to Robert Baker's 1770 grammar — but Tesco wasn't fighting that battle.

question: 'Affect' and 'effect' are confused so frequently that careful writers memorize the basic forms. Which sentence uses both correctly?
answer: The new policy will affect attendance; its likely effect is a 10% drop in absences.
choices: The new policy will affect attendance; its likely effect is a 10% drop in absences.
The new policy will effect attendance; its likely affect is a 10% drop in absences.
The new policy will affect attendance; its likely affect is a 10% drop in absences.
The new policy will effect attendance; its likely effect is a 10% drop in absences.
context: Default: AFFECT is the VERB ('to influence'); EFFECT is the NOUN ('the result'). 'The policy AFFECTS the schedule' (verb); 'the EFFECT of the policy' (noun). Trap: both have rare alternative parts of speech. 'Effect' as a verb means 'to bring about' ('to effect change' = to cause change). 'Affect' as a noun, mostly in psychology, means an outwardly displayed emotion ('flat affect'). For 95% of everyday writing, AFFECT/influence (verb) and EFFECT/result (noun) is the rule that holds. The other 5% — verb-effect, noun-affect — should be used only when you mean those specific things and are sure of the construction.

question: The Oxford comma has a comic exemplar: the sentence about three guests with and without the comma producing dramatically different meanings. Which version, with proper Oxford-comma punctuation, lists three separate guests?
answer: I'd like to thank my parents, Ayn Rand, and God.
choices: I'd like to thank my parents, Ayn Rand, and God.
I'd like to thank my parents, Ayn Rand and God.
I'd like to thank my parents Ayn Rand and God.
I'd like to thank my parents, namely Ayn Rand and God.
context: Without the Oxford comma — 'my parents, Ayn Rand and God' — the second and third items can read as appositives renaming 'my parents.' The reader gets: my parents (who are, namely, Ayn Rand and God). With the Oxford comma — 'my parents, Ayn Rand, and God' — the three items sit clearly in a list. AP style nonetheless omits the Oxford comma where no ambiguity results, on space-saving grounds. Chicago, MLA, APA, and Strunk all keep it on the grounds that the cost (one character) is dwarfed by the benefit (eliminating ambiguity). The dedication-line example is a perennial favorite in style-guide debates.

question: The phrase 'beg the question' is one of the most-corrected misuses in English. Its older logical meaning is being displaced by a newer everyday meaning. What is the original logical meaning?
answer: To assume the conclusion as a premise — the logical fallacy of circular reasoning.
choices: To assume the conclusion as a premise — the logical fallacy of circular reasoning.
To raise a follow-up question — naturally inviting further inquiry in the listener.
To plead for an answer — earnestly requesting that someone respond to the original question.
To deflect a question — sidestepping it by asking an unrelated question in response.
context: 'Beg the question' translates Latin 'petitio principii' — a logical fallacy in which the argument assumes what it's trying to prove. 'God exists because the Bible says so, and the Bible is true because God wrote it' begs the question. The phrase is a technical philosophy term mistranslated centuries ago — 'beg' here means 'demand' (as in 'I beg leave'), not 'request.' The newer meaning, 'raises the question,' has taken over in casual use ('the rising cost begs the question — can we afford it?'). Garner's index puts the new meaning at Stage 4 — widespread but resisted by careful writers. The original meaning survives in logic, philosophy, and formal argument.

question: An academic paper draft contains: 'The findings were significant.' A careful reader asks: 'significant' in what sense? Why?
answer: 'Significant' has both a colloquial meaning ('important') and a statistical meaning ('p < 0.05'). The sentence is ambiguous.
choices: 'Significant' has both a colloquial meaning ('important') and a statistical meaning ('p < 0.05'). The sentence is ambiguous.
'Significant' is too formal a word for academic writing, and should be replaced with 'big' here always.
'Significant' is grammatically incorrect; only the form 'significantly' can be used to describe findings.
'Significant' carries connotations of magic or supernatural meaning in this scientific writing context.
context: Academic writing has many words with technical-vs-everyday meanings that careful readers track. 'Significant' in statistics means a finding hit a p-value threshold (typically p < 0.05) — and a p < 0.05 finding can be substantively trivial (a tiny effect size with a large sample). 'Substantial' or 'meaningful' or 'important' describe magnitude; 'significant' describes statistical reliability. Careful academic style separates the two: 'The effect was statistically significant but small' (or 'large'). Sloppy use makes 'significant' do double duty and lets readers misinterpret. Other words with this trap: 'theory' (everyday: guess; scientific: well-tested explanation), 'subjective' (everyday: based on opinion; philosophical: residing in the subject), 'mean' (everyday: nasty; statistical: average).

question: Quotation marks differ between American and British conventions. Which sentence shows American convention correctly?
answer: The boy said, "Come back!" Then he ran.
choices: The boy said, "Come back!" Then he ran.
The boy said, 'Come back!' Then he ran.
The boy said, «Come back!» Then he ran.
The boy said, „Come back!" Then he ran.
context: American convention uses double quotes ("") for primary speech and single quotes ('') for nested quotes. British convention reverses this — single quotes for primary speech, double quotes for nested. American also conventionally places periods and commas INSIDE closing quotation marks regardless of logic ('She said "hello."'); British style places them outside when not part of the quoted material ('She said "hello".'). The American 'inside the quotes' rule is one of the most artificial in English style — it was inherited from 19th-century typesetting practice (the small comma or period was visually fragile when set after the larger quote mark) and has survived purely by convention. Both forms communicate equally well; pick one and stay consistent.

question: 'Compose' and 'comprise' are confused so often that careful writers double-check. Which sentence is correct?
answer: The committee comprises seven members; seven members compose the committee.
choices: The committee comprises seven members; seven members compose the committee.
The committee composes seven members; seven members comprise the committee.
The committee is comprised of seven members; seven members compose the committee.
The committee is composed of seven members; seven members comprise the committee.
context: Default rule: THE WHOLE COMPRISES THE PARTS; THE PARTS COMPOSE THE WHOLE. 'The committee comprises seven members' (the whole comprises the parts). 'Seven members compose the committee' (the parts compose the whole). The trap: 'is comprised of' is widely used in casual writing but is regarded as wrong by careful writers — comprise means 'is made up of' built in, so 'is comprised of' is like saying 'is is made up of of.' Garner puts 'is comprised of' at Stage 3 (widespread but still resisted). The careful form is 'comprises' (active) or 'is composed of' (passive). The committee CONSISTS OF seven members works too.

question: British and American style differ on punctuation after honorifics. Which version follows American convention?
answer: Dr. Smith met with Mr. Jones to discuss the matter.
choices: Dr. Smith met with Mr. Jones to discuss the matter.
Dr Smith met with Mr Jones to discuss the matter.
Dr; Smith met with Mr; Jones to discuss the matter.
Dr- Smith met with Mr- Jones to discuss the matter.
context: American convention puts a period after 'Dr.,' 'Mr.,' 'Mrs.,' 'Ms.,' 'Jr.,' 'Sr.' British convention often drops the period — these are 'contractions' (the last letter is preserved) and don't take the abbreviation period. So 'Dr Smith' (UK) vs 'Dr. Smith' (US). The distinction is subtle but consistent across British vs American typography. For abbreviations where the last letter is NOT preserved (Prof., Capt., Sept.), both styles use the period. The general British rule: full stop after an abbreviation only if the last letter of the abbreviation is NOT the last letter of the original word. The US dropped this finer distinction in the 19th century and put periods on everything.

question: An editor at a literary magazine reads a manuscript with the sentence 'The reason is because he never finished his degree.' What does the editor flag, and why?
answer: Redundancy — 'the reason is' and 'because' both signal causation; replace with 'The reason is THAT he never finished' or 'It is BECAUSE he never finished.'
choices: Redundancy — 'the reason is' and 'because' both signal causation; replace with 'The reason is THAT he never finished' or 'It is BECAUSE he never finished.'
Misplaced modifier — 'because he never finished' attaches to 'is' instead of attaching to 'reason' here.
Subject-verb agreement — 'reason' is plural in older English usage and requires 'are' as the verb.
Tense conflict — 'is' is present but 'never finished' is past, requiring a tense rewrite for the sentence.
context: 'The reason is because' is one of the most-flagged redundancies in copyediting. Both halves signal causation; combined, they do the work twice. The careful forms: 'The reason is THAT he never finished his degree' (subordinate clause introduced by 'that') OR 'It is BECAUSE he never finished his degree' (cleft sentence). Either form makes the causation explicit without doubling it. The redundancy survives in casual speech because it sounds rhythmically natural, but in edited writing it is regarded as a flaw. The structure 'the reason for X is Y' is also clean ('The reason for the delay is staff shortage').

question: Modern English style guides treat 'hopefully' as a contested usage. The traditional reading: 'hopefully' is an adverb meaning 'in a hopeful manner.' The modern reading: 'hopefully' can also serve as a sentence adverb meaning 'I hope that...' Which sentence uses the contested sentence-adverb form?
answer: Hopefully, the package will arrive before the weekend.
choices: Hopefully, the package will arrive before the weekend.
She looked hopefully at the empty mailbox, waiting for the package.
Hopefully signing the form, she gave the clerk a final nervous smile.
The dog approached the table hopefully, watching for falling food.
context: 'Hopefully' as a sentence adverb ('Hopefully, X will happen' meaning 'I hope X will happen') was widely condemned in 20th-century usage guides. Garner originally placed it at Stage 3 in his Language-Change Index; by the 2010s he moved it to Stage 4. The traditional form treats 'hopefully' strictly as a manner adverb ('she looked hopefully'). Other sentence adverbs are largely unobjectionable ('Frankly, I disagree'; 'Sadly, he died'; 'Mercifully, the storm passed'); the special opposition to 'hopefully' is partly historical accident — it became a flagship case in the prescriptive/descriptive wars of the 1960s-70s. Today most usage guides accept it as standard, with notes acknowledging the older objection.

question: The 'data is' vs 'data are' debate has a clear linguistic history. 'Data' was originally Latin plural; 'datum' the singular. How do major contemporary style guides handle the question?
answer: Most accept singular ('data is') for everyday use; many keep plural ('data are') in scientific contexts.
choices: Most accept singular ('data is') for everyday use; many keep plural ('data are') in scientific contexts.
All major guides reject 'data is' as a fundamental error, and require 'data are' in absolutely all contexts.
All major guides require 'data is' and consider 'data are' to be archaic Latin pedantry in modern English.
Style guides ignore 'data' entirely, leaving the choice to individual writers without any guidance ever.
context: Latin singular 'datum,' Latin plural 'data' — preserved in older scientific English ('the data show'). English usage has shifted toward treating 'data' as a mass noun, like 'water' or 'evidence,' taking singular verbs ('the data shows'). Chicago Manual of Style (17th ed.) accepts both, with a slight preference for 'data are' in formal scientific writing. AP accepts both. Garner places 'data is' at Stage 5 (fully accepted) for everyday use, but notes that scientific journals often retain 'data are.' The hyper-correct 'data are' in a casual newspaper article reads as pedantic; the casual 'data is' in a peer-reviewed scientific paper reads as informal. Match the register.

question: The Oxford English Dictionary cites the earliest documented use of every word it defines. What is the OED's policy when a 'first use' citation it published is later antedated by a researcher's discovery?
answer: It updates the entry — antedatings are routinely incorporated, sometimes pushing first uses back by centuries.
choices: It updates the entry — antedatings are routinely incorporated, sometimes pushing first uses back by centuries.
It refuses to change — the first edition's citations are treated as canonical, locked permanently.
It maintains both — listing the original citation as primary and the antedating as a footnote.
It publishes corrections only every fifty years — when a new full edition is being prepared.
context: The OED is continuously updated since it began moving to a full online format in 2000. Antedatings — earlier citations of a word's use found in newly digitized archives, in newspaper databases, in private letters now released — are routinely incorporated. The OED's third edition project, ongoing since 2000, has revised tens of thousands of entries with updated dates. Volunteer 'word-hunters' (analogous to Murray's volunteer readers) continue to send in antedatings. The most spectacular recent finds: 'literally' as figurative intensifier antedated to the 1700s; 'OK' antedated by Allen Walker Read's 1960s research; 'selfie' tracked through Australian internet forums of 2002.

question: Sentence diagramming, invented by Reed and Kellogg in 1877, has both passionate defenders and critics. Which of these is the most-cited educational argument FOR diagramming?
answer: It makes grammatical relationships visible — helping students see how sentences are structured rather than memorizing rules abstractly.
choices: It makes grammatical relationships visible — helping students see how sentences are structured rather than memorizing rules abstractly.
It improves spelling accuracy — students who diagram make 40% fewer spelling errors on tests.
It teaches Latin grammar directly — diagrams in Reed-Kellogg follow Cicero's grammatical analysis.
It accelerates reading speed — diagrammers read three times faster than non-diagrammers on average.
context: Defenders of sentence diagramming argue it gives students a visual handle on syntax — a kid who can draw a sentence understands what the subject is, what's modifying what, where dependent clauses attach. Critics argue it's an artifact of a particular grammatical theory (the Latin-influenced traditional grammar of the 1800s), that the time spent diagramming could be spent writing, and that the diagrams don't help with the actual problems writers face (when to use a comma, how to vary sentence length). The teaching method has waxed and waned — peak popularity 1890s-1950s in American schools, faded in the 1970s with the rise of communicative-method language teaching, revived in classical-education and homeschool curricula since the 1990s.

question: The Plain Language Movement, formalized in the US through the Plain Writing Act of 2010, requires federal agencies to write clearly. Which of these is a Plain Language principle?
answer: Prefer short, common words to longer, more obscure ones, and write in the active voice where possible.
choices: Prefer short, common words to longer, more obscure ones, and write in the active voice where possible.
Use only words drawn from the King James Bible's vocabulary for governmental writing today, always.
Maintain 18th-century legal-prose conventions, establishing tradition over reader accessibility entirely.
Adopt long compound sentences with multiple subordinate clauses for legal precision throughout writing.
context: The Plain Language Movement traces to the 1970s but became US federal law in 2010. Its principles: short common words, active voice, second-person 'you' (when addressing the reader), short sentences, logical organization, plenty of headings and bullets. The result is documents that ordinary readers can use — Social Security forms, tax instructions, agency websites. The movement has analogs in Britain (Plain English Campaign, 1979) and Canada. Critics argue the principles sometimes oversimplify subtle legal language; defenders point to studies showing dramatic reductions in errors, call-center volume, and customer confusion after plain-language rewrites. Strunk and White would have approved.

question: An editor reads: 'The data set is comprised of three subsections.' She flags it. What are the two careful-writing forms she might suggest instead?
answer: 'The data set comprises three subsections.' OR 'The data set is composed of three subsections.'
choices: 'The data set comprises three subsections.' OR 'The data set is composed of three subsections.'
'The data sets are comprised of three subsections.' OR 'The data sets composes three subsections.'
'The data set is comprising three subsections.' OR 'The data set is being composed of three subsections.'
'The data set has comprised three subsections.' OR 'The data set having composed three subsections.'
context: 'Is comprised of' is widely used but flagged by careful writers as a defect — 'comprise' already means 'is made up of,' so 'is comprised of' is redundant. The two careful forms: ACTIVE — 'X comprises Y' (the whole comprises the parts). PASSIVE — 'X is composed of Y' (passive of 'compose'). Or simply: 'X consists of Y.' All three convey the same meaning without the redundancy. Garner's index puts 'is comprised of' at Stage 3 (widespread but resisted). Wikipedia's Bryan Henderson famously made it a personal mission to edit out 47,000+ instances of 'is comprised of' from Wikipedia between 2007 and 2018 — a one-person prescriptivist project of remarkable scale.

question: George Orwell's 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language' offered six rules for clear writing. Which of these is one of Orwell's six?
answer: Never use a long word where a short one will do; cut every word that can be cut.
choices: Never use a long word where a short one will do; cut every word that can be cut.
Always begin sentences with prepositions for varied rhythm in formal writing always.
Use Latin-derived vocabulary whenever possible to convey educated authority in your prose.
Avoid all forms of dialogue in essays; third-person narrative produces clearer political prose.
context: Orwell's six rules from 'Politics and the English Language' (1946): (1) Never use a metaphor, simile, or other figure of speech which you are used to seeing in print. (2) Never use a long word where a short one will do. (3) If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out. (4) Never use the passive where you can use the active. (5) Never use a foreign phrase, a scientific word, or a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent. (6) Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous. Orwell's argument was political as much as stylistic — vague language enables vague thought, and propaganda thrives on jargon. The essay sits alongside Strunk's 'Elements of Style' as one of the most-cited English-prose manifestos.

question: Writing handbooks teach 'nominalization' as a vice — turning verbs into nouns and pairing them with weak verbs. Which sentence shows the nominalized form, and which would Strunk improve to use the original verb?
answer: Original: 'The committee made a decision.' Strunk: 'The committee decided.'
choices: Original: 'The committee made a decision.' Strunk: 'The committee decided.'
Original: 'The committee decided.' Strunk: 'The committee made a decision.'
Original: 'She ran fast.' Strunk: 'She undertook a movement at velocity.'
Original: 'He laughed loudly.' Strunk: 'He produced a vocalization of amusement.'
context: Nominalization: turning a verb ('decide') into a noun ('decision') and pairing it with a weak verb ('made'). The verb does no work; the noun carries the meaning. Strunk and Orwell both target this pattern — 'made a decision' becomes 'decided,' 'reached a conclusion' becomes 'concluded,' 'gave a description of' becomes 'described.' Each substitution saves words and strengthens the sentence. Bureaucratic and academic prose is full of nominalizations because they sound formal — 'The decision was made to undertake the implementation of a review process' instead of 'We decided to review the process.' Writing handbooks teach hunting nominalizations as a daily editing habit. Result: tighter, clearer sentences.

question: A British editor and an American editor disagree about period placement after a quoted single word. Which version follows American convention?
answer: The committee called the proposal "unworkable."
choices: The committee called the proposal "unworkable."
The committee called the proposal "unworkable".
The committee called the proposal (unworkable).
The committee called the proposal: 'unworkable'.
context: American convention puts the period (and comma) INSIDE the closing quotation marks even when the period is not part of the quoted material. British convention (and most logical-punctuation styles) puts the period outside when it's not part of the quoted material. American: 'unworkable."' British: 'unworkable".' The American rule is one of English typography's most non-logical conventions — it was inherited from 19th-century typesetting (the small period was visually fragile when set outside the larger quote mark, so printers tucked it inside). The convention survived even though the typesetting rationale is gone. Both forms communicate the same meaning; the issue is consistency within a publication's style.

question: A careful writer wants to give a date range in formal prose. Chicago Manual of Style endorses one preferred form. Which is it?
answer: An en-dash with no spaces, as in '1995-2025' (using the en-dash mark specifically).
choices: An en-dash with no spaces, as in '1995-2025' (using the en-dash mark specifically).
A hyphen with spaces around it, as in '1995 - 2025' (the older typewriter form).
A comma between start and end years, as in '1995, 2025' (no dash at all in ranges).
The word 'to' between the years, as in '1995 to 2025' (Chicago bans dashes for ranges).
context: Chicago's preferred form for ranges is the en-dash (–), no spaces: '1995–2025,' 'pages 123–145,' 'Monday–Friday.' The en-dash is shorter than the em-dash (—) and longer than the hyphen (-). It can also be replaced by the word 'to' in running prose ('1995 to 2025'). Chicago's logic: a dash compactly carries the meaning 'through' or 'between.' AP uses the hyphen for ranges (1995-2025) — simpler typographically, even if technically less elegant. Word-processing software typically auto-converts double-hyphens into em-dashes; for en-dashes most writers have to insert them deliberately (Mac: Option-hyphen; Windows: Alt+0150).

question: A copyeditor finds: 'Each of the students raised their hand.' What does she do?
answer: Probably accepts it — 'singular they' for an indefinite antecedent is now Stage 5 in Garner's index, fully standard.
choices: Probably accepts it — 'singular they' for an indefinite antecedent is now Stage 5 in Garner's index, fully standard.
Replaces 'their' with 'his' — masculine pronoun is the prescribed default for indefinite singulars.
Replaces 'their' with 'his or her' — only the compound form is acceptable in any formal writing.
Replaces 'their' with 'its' — 'student' takes a neuter pronoun in modern formal English usage.
context: 'Singular they' for an indefinite antecedent ('each student raised their hand,' 'anyone who left their bag') is now widely accepted in formal writing. Garner moved it to Stage 5 (fully accepted) in 2016. The older 'he or she' is regarded as wordy; the older 'he' (generic masculine) is regarded as out of date and exclusionary. 'Their' is the natural form English has been using since at least Shakespeare ('There's not a man I meet but doth salute me / As if I were their well-acquainted friend' — Comedy of Errors). The prescriptive ban on singular 'they' was a 19th-century invention, never reflecting actual educated usage. Modern style guides (Chicago, AP, APA, MLA) all now accept singular they.

question: American Heritage Dictionary's Usage Panel was disbanded in 2018 after fifty years of voting on contested usages. What replaced it as a measure of educated opinion on usage?
answer: Corpus-based analysis of actual usage in edited prose: the empirical method now dominant in usage commentary.
choices: Corpus-based analysis of actual usage in edited prose: the empirical method now dominant in usage commentary.
An online vote where any visitor to the dictionary's website can register an opinion on each usage entry.
A panel of grade-school teachers replaced the original panel of writers and university scholars entirely.
Nothing replaced it; the dictionary now operates without any consultative input on contested usages at all.
context: American Heritage's Usage Panel — 200+ writers, editors, and academics voting on contested constructions — was for fifty years the most explicit prescriptive apparatus in American lexicography. By the 2010s, large corpora (the Corpus of Contemporary American English, the British National Corpus, the COHA historical corpus, Google's Ngram Viewer) offered a more comprehensive way to measure usage — billions of words from edited writing tagged for date, register, genre. Garner's later editions explicitly cite corpus data. The panel was disbanded in 2018; the empirical methods that replaced it are descriptivist in spirit (let the data speak) while still informing prescriptive guidance (here's what educated writers actually do).

question: 'Aggravate' has a strict-traditional meaning and a looser modern meaning. What does the strict traditional meaning preserve?
answer: To make worse — 'the rain aggravated the flooding.' The looser meaning ('annoy') is now Stage 4.
choices: To make worse — 'the rain aggravated the flooding.' The looser meaning ('annoy') is now Stage 4.
To annoy or irritate — 'his constant tapping aggravated her' is the only correct historical sense.
To prosecute legally — 'aggravated assault' is the only formal use of the verb in modern law.
To accelerate — 'the boy aggravated his bike up the hill' is the original Old English meaning.
context: Aggravate comes from Latin 'aggravare' — to make heavier, to worsen. The traditional rule: aggravate means 'make worse' ('the rain aggravated the flooding'); irritate means 'annoy.' The looser modern use of 'aggravate' to mean 'irritate' ('he aggravated me') is widespread and gradually winning — Garner places it at Stage 4. Older usage guides (Fowler, Strunk) condemned the looser use. The 'aggravated assault' legal term keeps the original sense — an assault made worse by an aggravating factor like a weapon. Careful writers preserve the distinction between aggravate (worsen a condition) and irritate (annoy a person).

question: The Chicago Manual of Style's signature feature is its 'rule on rules.' What does Chicago tell editors to do when a stylistic choice is contested and no rule clearly resolves it?
answer: Pick a consistent practice and stay with it across the document; house style trumps abstract correctness.
choices: Pick a consistent practice and stay with it across the document; house style trumps abstract correctness.
Defer to Webster's Dictionary entries for spelling and to Strunk's Elements for usage choices, always.
Vary the choice deliberately, because alternating styles produces livelier prose throughout the work.
Always copy The New York Times's house style for the relevant edition's date of publication exactly.
context: Chicago Manual's underlying philosophy is that English style admits genuine choices — Oxford comma or not, em-dash with or without spaces, '1990s' vs ''90s,' US 'gray' or British 'grey.' Many of these have no objectively correct answer. Chicago's guidance: pick a practice, document it as house style, apply it consistently. A document that switches between styles distracts the reader; one that holds to a consistent style reads cleanly even if the chosen style is not what the reader would have chosen. The 'house style' philosophy explains why magazines and book publishers have distinctive looks — the New Yorker's diaeresis on 'coöperate,' the Economist's UK spellings, the New York Times's distinctive byline format. Style is house identity.

question: Strunk and White famously condemned 'student of human nature' as a pretentious phrase preferable to plain alternatives. Their broader principle has a name in style commentary. What is it called?
answer: Anti-genteelism — Fowler's term for the impulse to use fancier words because the plain ones feel too plain.
choices: Anti-genteelism — Fowler's term for the impulse to use fancier words because the plain ones feel too plain.
Anti-archaism — the principle of choosing modern Latin over Old English Germanic vocabulary.
Anti-nominalism — the principle of preferring abstract nouns over plain verb constructions.
Anti-vernacularism — the principle of resisting colloquial speech in formal published prose.
context: Fowler defined GENTEELISM as choosing a fancier word because the plain one feels too plain — 'expectorate' for 'spit,' 'remuneration' for 'pay,' 'inebriated' for 'drunk,' 'commence' for 'start.' The fancier word implies refinement; the plain word does the job. Strunk and White take the same anti-genteelism stance throughout 'Elements' — prefer the short Germanic word to the long Latinate one when both communicate the same thing. Orwell's third rule ('If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out') has the same flavor. The opposite vice — using needlessly plain language where technical precision is required — is also a vice, but a less common one in everyday writing.

question: Run-on sentences and comma splices are both formal-writing defects. Which of these is the LEAST acceptable fix in formal English writing?
answer: Chain commas plus 'and' through every long sentence, trusting the rhythm to carry the reader through.
choices: Chain commas plus 'and' through every long sentence, trusting the rhythm to carry the reader through.
Split each problem into two complete sentences separated by periods, the surest of fixes.
Use a semicolon when the two clauses are closely related in meaning, an elegant compromise.
Subordinate one clause to the other with a conjunction (because, although, when), changing emphasis.
context: Standard fixes for run-on or comma-spliced sentences: (1) PERIOD — split into two sentences. (2) SEMICOLON — when clauses are closely related. (3) SUBORDINATION — turn one clause into a dependent clause with 'because,' 'although,' 'when,' 'since,' 'while.' (4) COORDINATION — comma plus FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). The bad fix: stringing comma-and-and patterns throughout. 'I went home, and I ate dinner, and I read a book, and I went to bed' is grammatically correct but is the prose of a five-year-old. Skilled writing varies sentence structure — using all four standard fixes alternately to produce rhythm. The defect being fixed is the LONGER VICE of how the sentence connects to its neighbors.

question: The dash family in English typography (em-dash, en-dash, hyphen) has a less-common cousin: the figure dash and the swung dash. Which usage describes the FIGURE dash?
answer: Used in phone numbers and other digit groupings, with the same width as a digit, distinct from a hyphen.
choices: Used in phone numbers and other digit groupings, with the same width as a digit, distinct from a hyphen.
Used in legal documents only, for denoting redacted or omitted material in cited contracts and statutes.
Used as a substitute for repeated words in vocabulary lists, bibliographies, and similar tabular entries.
Used to indicate musical bar lines in vocal lyrics printed beside instrumental scores in printed sheets.
context: The FIGURE DASH (‒) is a typographer's special character with the exact width of a digit — used in phone numbers and other digit groupings where consistent character width matters for alignment ('555‒123‒4567'). Most everyday typography uses a hyphen here, but typesetting purists prefer the figure dash. The SWUNG DASH (~) substitutes for repeated headwords in dictionaries and vocabulary lists — saves space and signals 'same word, new entry.' The HORIZONTAL BAR (―) is the longest dash — used in some European typography to introduce dialogue. Most word processors lack the figure dash and swung dash on the standard keyboard; they're inserted through special-character menus.

question: Webster's Third International Dictionary's 1961 publication caused a national controversy. What specific editorial decision drew the most heated complaint?
answer: Removing usage labels like 'colloquial,' 'slang,' and 'illit.' so that words appeared without judgment markers.
choices: Removing usage labels like 'colloquial,' 'slang,' and 'illit.' so that words appeared without judgment markers.
Adding thousands of new technical terms from physics, chemistry, and biology overnight in the entries.
Dropping all British spellings from American English entries throughout the dictionary's whole vocabulary.
Excluding rare and archaic vocabulary from earlier Webster's editions to save physical printing space.
context: Webster's Third's most controversial editorial decision under Philip Gove was reducing the use of judgmental usage labels. Earlier Websters had marked words 'colloquial,' 'slang,' 'illit.' (illiterate), 'substandard,' 'erroneous' — telling the reader at a glance whether a word was respectable. Gove's W3 mostly dropped these in favor of more neutral notes about register and frequency. Words like 'ain't' appeared without the older 'illit.' label, suggesting they had become acceptable. Conservative critics (Dwight Macdonald in The New Yorker, the Atlantic Monthly's 'Sabotage in Springfield' editorial) read this as a moral abdication: the dictionary's role was to guide, not just to describe. The controversy spawned the American Heritage Dictionary (1969) as an explicitly prescriptive alternative.

question: Restrictive relative clauses provide essential information about the noun; non-restrictive clauses provide extra information. Which sentence demonstrates a restrictive relative clause (the comma test fails)?
answer: The candidates who arrived late were disqualified.
choices: The candidates who arrived late were disqualified.
The candidates, who arrived late, were disqualified.
The candidates (the late arrivals) were disqualified.
The late-arriving candidates were the ones disqualified.
context: RESTRICTIVE: 'The candidates WHO ARRIVED LATE were disqualified' — only the late-arriving candidates; the others weren't disqualified. The clause restricts WHICH candidates we're talking about. NO COMMAS. NON-RESTRICTIVE: 'The candidates, who arrived late, were disqualified' — ALL the candidates arrived late, and all were disqualified; the clause adds information about the whole set. COMMAS. The comma test: if you can remove the clause and the sentence still names the same set, the clause is non-restrictive (commas). If removing the clause changes which set you're naming, the clause is restrictive (no commas). American style adds: use THAT for restrictive, WHICH for non-restrictive.

question: Style guides differ on how to render quoted material that runs more than four lines. Which is the standard treatment in academic prose (MLA/Chicago)?
answer: Block quotation — indent the entire passage, no quotation marks, smaller font often.
choices: Block quotation — indent the entire passage, no quotation marks, smaller font often.
Italic font — render the entire passage in italics regardless of length.
Boldface — render the entire long passage in bold, with quotation marks around it.
Endnote only — long quotations are removed from the main text and placed in endnotes.
context: Block quotations: when quoted material runs longer than four lines (MLA) or about 100 words (Chicago/APA varies by style), the standard treatment is to indent the entire passage from the left margin, drop the surrounding quotation marks (the indentation signals the quotation), and often use a slightly smaller font. The block visually separates the quoted material from the writer's own prose. Short quotations stay integrated in the running paragraph with surrounding quotation marks. The thresholds vary slightly between MLA (4+ lines), Chicago (about 100 words / 8 lines), and APA (40+ words). The principle is the same: visual separation when the quoted material gets long.

question: A literary scholar writes: 'The novel is comprised of three sections, each of which contains numerous chapters, and which together form a complete narrative arc.' An editor flags THREE problems. What are they?
answer: 'Is comprised of' (use 'comprises'); restrictive 'which' should be 'that'; second 'which' has unclear antecedent.
choices: 'Is comprised of' (use 'comprises'); restrictive 'which' should be 'that'; second 'which' has unclear antecedent.
'Is comprised of' is fine; the two 'whichs' both need to be replaced with 'who' for personification.
Sentence is fully correct as written; the editor's three flags would be without basis here.
All three pronouns 'each,' 'which,' and 'which' need to be replaced with explicit nouns instead.
context: Three problems the editor flags: (1) 'IS COMPRISED OF' — careful writers prefer 'comprises' (active) or 'is composed of' (passive). 'The novel comprises three sections.' (2) RESTRICTIVE 'WHICH' — 'each of which contains numerous chapters' is restrictive (selects WHICH sections — the ones containing chapters); American convention prefers 'each of that' but that's awkward; the typical fix is to restructure: 'each containing numerous chapters.' (3) UNCLEAR ANTECEDENT for the second 'which' — does 'which together form a complete narrative arc' refer to the chapters, the sections, or all of them? Rewrite: 'The novel comprises three sections, each containing numerous chapters; together, the sections form a complete narrative arc.' Three issues, one rewrite.

question: The serial-comma debate has a famous Times of London headline from a 1986 broadcast: 'Among those interviewed were his two ex-wives, Kris Kristofferson and Robert Duvall.' What did the missing serial comma create?
answer: The reading that Kris Kristofferson and Robert Duvall were the interviewee's two ex-wives.
choices: The reading that Kris Kristofferson and Robert Duvall were the interviewee's two ex-wives.
The reading that the interview had taken place inside a recording studio in Nashville.
The reading that two-ex-wives was the name of a country band of the era named for divorce.
The reading that ex-wives and Kristofferson and Duvall were four distinct people at the event.
context: The Times of London headline (often cited with slight variations) reads: 'Among those interviewed were his two ex-wives, Kris Kristofferson and Robert Duvall.' Without the Oxford comma, 'his two ex-wives' can be read as an appositive renaming 'Kris Kristofferson and Robert Duvall' — making the male country singer and actor into the interviewee's two ex-wives. With the Oxford comma — 'his two ex-wives, Kris Kristofferson, and Robert Duvall' — they sit clearly in a list of three (or four) items. The headline is one of the most-cited examples of why the Oxford comma is worth the one extra character. AP-style omission of the serial comma works most of the time, but the case where it fails is funny enough to be unforgettable.
